activities.text: French on paper, Greek in everyday life: Aristotelous Square, Thessaloniki’s main square, originated in Ernest Hébrard’s 1918 plans following the great fire of 1917, but was largely built in the 1950s. The twelve buildings lining it have been protected since 1950, and the square opens directly onto the waterfront. Stroll along the water after nightfall, then dine in the small taverns of nearby Athonos Square.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

activities.text: Easy to access and family-friendly, Livadi Beach at the entrance to Armenistis offers fine golden sand, a small lake formed by a mountain stream, and shade from tamarisk trees. The stream flowing down from the mountain makes the water slightly cooler. Sun loungers, umbrellas, and a snack bar are available in summer; come toward the end of the day, as the beach is very popular.

You’ll then follow Messakti Beach, a long stretch of golden sand where the small Myrsonas River forms a wetland before reaching the sea. Shallow water and a lifeguard station make it a good choice for families with children. When the meltemi winds pick up, surfers take over: stay close to shore then.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches

visits.text: Glass floor panels lie beneath your feet: inside Agios Stefanos Church in Arnaia, you walk above the excavations. Built in 1812, as the inscription on its facade confirms, the church burned in 2005; its restoration uncovered a 5th-century Early Christian basilica and a 10th-century Byzantine church. Visit outside service times, then look up at the bell tower, which dates to 1889.

Known as the Yiatradiko, this house from the 1750s is home to the Arnaia Historical and Folklore Museum. Beekeeping equipment, a loom, traditional clothing, and photographs from 1880 to 1950 tell the town’s story, with two curiosities: the first radio to reach the village, in 1941, and a fire pump dating back about two centuries. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Thursdays: arrive before 5 p.m.

As early as the 1790s, Arnaia was weaving rugs from local wool. Across from the folklore museum, the weaving museum occupies an 1870 house and honors Charikleia Dimitrakoudi, a renowned weaver and merchant: her glasses, yarn, and dye recipes are displayed on the ground floor. Then head upstairs to see the “calligraphic” rugs that decorated the walls.

activities.text: Next, wander through the narrow streets of Arnaia, designated a historic site and traditional village in 1987. At an elevation of 600 m, at the foot of Holomontas, its stone and wood houses were rebuilt after 1821, when the town was among the 42 villages burned in Halkidiki. Climb to the Chapel of the Prophet Elijah for a view over the rooftops, then bring home some honey: beekeeping is a long-standing tradition here.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages, Aristotle, and Mount Athos

visits.text: It is best to begin your visit to Arta with its buried past at the Archaeological Museum, dedicated to Ambracia, a colony founded by Corinth in 625 BC. A reconstructed necropolis, a cenotaph honoring warriors who fell in the 6th century BC, and a life-size house bring the city to life. Open from 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM; closed Tuesdays.

In Greece, an endless construction project still brings to mind the Bridge of Arta: according to the ballad, its foundations collapsed every night until the builder walled his wife into them. The current bridge, about 145 m long, dates from the early 17th century; from 1881 to 1912, its highest arch marked the border with the Ottoman Empire. Walk across, then admire it from the riverbank.

Around 1250, Despot Michael II founded Kato Panagia, reportedly to atone for exiling his wife Theodora. On the banks of the Arachthos, 3 km south of the center, the church preserves 13th-century frescoes and an extensive cycle of paintings from 1715. The monastery is home to nuns: keep shoulders and knees covered.

Climb up to Arta Castle, protected by the Arachthos to the north and east. Its walls enclose about 9 hectares, roughly a dozen soccer fields, and feature 18 towers, repaired by Ali Pasha between 1796 and 1820. A hotel built within the walls in the 1960s erased most of the remains inside. Open from 8:30 AM to 4 PM.

A Doric temple beneath the sidewalk: in central Arta, the foundations of the 44 m-long Temple of Apollo Pythios emerge at street level. Nearby, the small theater of Ambracia, built around 300 BC, retains only five rows of seats; it may have served as a council chamber. Look for both around Vasileos Pyrrou Street.

Finish at Agia Theodora Church, on the corner of Vasileos Pyrrou and Agias Theodoras Streets, decorated with ceramic crosses and suns. Theodora, wife of Michael II, became a nun here and was buried here; she became Arta’s patron saint. Near the south entrance, a cenotaph from 1873 is thought to depict her with her son Nikephoros. A procession takes place every March 11.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Ioannina, Arta, and Aromanian Villages

visits.text: Astypalea's Chora is a cascade of cubic white houses tumbling down a rocky hillside to the old port of Pera Gialos. At the summit looms Querini Castle, built of dark stone by the eponymous Venetian family after 1413—contrasting spectacularly with the village's white walls below. The ramparts once served as exterior walls for three-story houses built against them inside. The 1956 earthquake left ruins within, but the monumental entrance remains intact and the view from the top over the two bays forming the island's isthmus is extraordinary. Free admission.

The eight windmills aligned along the ridge of Chora, between the village and the castle, are Astypalea's symbol. Their position allowed them to capture north and south winds interchangeably according to season. One has been converted into the municipal library, another into a shop. In the evening, this is the locals' meeting point before descending to the tavernas.

Pera Gialos, the old port at Chora's foot, is Astypalea's most authentic spot: painted wooden fishing boats, tavernas with plastic tables facing the sea, fish market in the morning. This is where the island truly lives, far from the tourist animation of Chora. Stroll the quay in late afternoon when fishermen return.

The Church of Panagia Portaïtissa (18th century), just below the castle, is considered one of the Dodecanese's most beautiful: its carved and gilded wooden iconostasis was built over nine years by Agios Anthimos of Cephalonia, who was blind according to tradition. A copy of the Panagia Portaïtissa icon was brought from Mount Athos.

Pera Gialos's archaeological museum sits directly on the old port waterfront. It houses finds ranging from prehistory to the medieval era, including pieces from the Kylindra necropolis—a unique burial site where 2,700 infant skeletons interred in jars were discovered on the castle hill's flank, spanning a thousand-year period. A local cult whose significance archaeologists still debate. The museum is small but dense: allow 30 to 40 minutes.

activities.text: From Pera Gialos, drive or ride a scooter to Livadi, an organized beach below Chora, then continue for about 5 km to Agios Konstantinos. The final kilometre follows a passable dirt road. There, alternate swimming with a walk to the small chapel overlooking the cove and a break beneath the tamarisks or in the serviced area. The beach combines sand and pebbles, facing Chora and Querini Castle. On the way back, stop at Livadi to see Chora's white silhouette again from the other side of the bay.

Reserve half a day to reach Vathy by water taxi from Pera Gialos. This natural fjord on the island's east—accessible only by sea or via a poor-condition track—is one of the Dodecanese's most timeless atmospheres: a silent fishing village at the end of a narrow sea arm surrounded by arid hills. A single taverna serves the morning's catch. Boats generally depart late morning.

Have a drink in front of Chora's windmills at sunset—it's the locals' gathering spot. Illuminated Chora gives the impression the village is either climbing the mountain or suspended in the void, depending on the viewing angle. The atmosphere shifts dramatically once night falls.

Astypalea's 'Kopanisti' is a pungent, fermented soft-paste cheese served as mezze. The local 'Pouggia' are filled with almonds and mastiha (mastic resin), a perfumed variation on the specialty you may have tasted in Patmos. Ask for them in Pera Gialos pastry shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos

visits.text: Mustafa Kemal, the future Atatürk and founder of modern Turkey, is said to have been born in 1881 in this pink house on Apostolou Pavlou Street. The Atatürk Museum now stands within the grounds of the Turkish consulate: family furniture, his mother Zübeyde Hanım’s bedroom, clothing, and rare photographs are displayed across two floors. Allow 30 minutes; admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: The Parthenon is why you came. Built between 447 and 432 BC by architects Ictinus and Callicrates under the direction of sculptor Phidias, it took 22,000 tonnes of marble quarried from Mount Pentelicus, 17 km away, to raise it. Notice that the marble contains traces of iron that have oxidized over time—at sunrise or sunset, it turns honey-gold. Arrive as early as possible, right when it opens: crowds thicken after 9:30 AM.

The Erechtheion, built between 421 and 406 BC in Ionic style, houses the famous Porch of the Caryatids. These six statues of young women serving as columns are copies—the originals are in the Acropolis Museum. Take time to walk around the building: the north façade, the most ornate, is the best preserved.

The Propylaea form the monumental gateway to the Acropolis, designed by architect Mnesicles starting in 437 BC, in Pentelic marble. This five-opening portico was so imposing that ancient travelers described it as rivaling the Parthenon itself. Look at the ceiling of the central hall—the coffers painted in blue and gold are still partially visible.

The Temple of Athena Nike, perched to the right of the entrance, was built between 427 and 424 BC to celebrate victory over the Persians. It's the oldest Ionic temple on the Acropolis, and also the smallest: only 8 meters long. It was completely dismantled by the Ottomans in 1686 to build a gun battery, then reconstructed stone by stone in the 19th century.

The Theater of Dionysus, carved into the southern slope of the Acropolis in the 6th century BC, is considered the birthplace of Western theater. This is where Aeschylus, Sophocles and Aristophanes first presented their plays, before 17,000 spectators. The marble seats you see date from the Roman renovation, but the original wooden stage goes back to the Great Dionysia festivals.

The Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009 and designed by Swiss architect Bernard Tschumi, houses 4,000 pieces exclusively from the sacred hill. Don't miss the third floor, oriented exactly like the Parthenon: you'll see 160 meters of friezes presented according to their original arrangement. The empty spaces, marked "BM," remind you that two-thirds of the marbles are still in the British Museum. Book your ticket in advance during high season.

If the Acropolis is Athens' symbol, the Ancient Agora is its brain. Here, on these 25 hectares northwest of the sacred rock, democracy took shape: the Bouleuterion housed the Council of 500 members, the Tholos the standing committee. Socrates paced these very porticoes. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours to tour it completely with the museum—don't skip the latter, it preserves history's first voting ballots.

Take time to climb up to the Temple of Hephaestus, perched at the northwest corner of the Agora: it's the best-preserved Doric temple in Greece, built between 460 and 415 BC. Its survival is due to a lucky coincidence—it was converted into a Christian church in the 7th century, preserving its walls and roof. The north and south friezes recount the exploits of Theseus and Heracles. Athenians themselves often mistakenly call it the “Theseion.”

Entering the Stoa of Attalos, you're walking into history's first shopping mall. Built around 150 BC by Attalos II, king of Pergamon, in gratitude to the city that had welcomed him during his studies, this 116-meter portico on two levels now houses the Agora Museum. Reconstructed identically between 1953 and 1956 by the American School of Archaeology, it retains Doric columns on the ground floor and Ionic upstairs. Look for the ostraka—those pottery shards on which Athenians inscribed the name of the citizen to be banished from the city.

Right next to the Roman Agora, don't miss Hadrian's Library: built in 132 AD by the Roman emperor, it was much more than a library—a vast complex of 122 by 82 meters with reading rooms, gardens and a central pool. Today only the façade with Corinthian columns is clearly visible from the street, but the site merits a brief stop. Entry is included in the combined ticket for Athens' seven archaeological sites.

The National Archaeological Museum, founded in 1829, is Greece's largest museum. If you only have time for one room, go directly to the Mycenaean collection: the gold mask called "Agamemnon's," discovered by Schliemann in 1876 at Mycenae, is one of the most striking pieces of Greek antiquity. Reserve at least 2 hours if you want to cover the Cycladic collection and the bronzes.

The Panathenaic Stadium—Kallimarmaro in Greek, "of beautiful marble"—is the world's only stadium built entirely of white marble. Founded in 330 BC by statesman Lycurgus for the Great Panathenaea, it was completely rebuilt in Pentelic marble under Herodes Atticus in the 2nd century AD (capacity: 70,000 spectators). Fallen into ruin then pillaged for its stones in the Middle Ages, it was restored to host the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. You can run on the track: it's included in the ticket. Caution: in summer, the marble heats up—visit in the morning or late afternoon.

Lycabettus Hill rises to 277 meters, Athens' highest point. From the summit, you have 360° views of the Acropolis, Piraeus and, on clear days, as far as the island of Aegina. Climb on foot from Kolonaki (30 minutes) or by funicular from Aristippou Street. In the evening, it's the city's best spot to watch Athens light up.

Athens' National Garden extends over 15 hectares in the city's heart, planted by Queen Amalia in the 19th century. It's the Athenians' green oasis—ducks, turtles, shaded pergolas—a welcome break between visits. At the southern exit stands the Zappeion, a neoclassical palace from 1888 designed by Theophil Hansen, used for official ceremonies and exhibitions.

The Academy of Athens, the University and the National Library form the Neoclassical Trilogy of Panepistimiou Street, all three designed by Theophil Hansen between 1859 and 1902. The Academy is the most impressive: Ionic columns, colored friezes, statues of Apollo and Athena on their pedestals. It's the iconic photo of neoclassical Athens—and often ignored by tourists hurrying off to the Acropolis.

If you're feeling a bit weary of ancient sites, the Benaki Museum is an excellent antidote. Housed in a beautiful neoclassical mansion in Kolonaki, it traces Greek history from prehistory to the present day—Mycenaean, Byzantine, Ottoman, modern—in one fluid journey. It's also one of Athens' museums with the best exhibition design. Go up to the rooftop café terrace: the view over the gardens and city is worth the trip.

After three days of ancient Greece, pause at the Byzantine and Christian Museum—you'll discover another Greece, just as rich. Icons, mosaics, frescoes, liturgical embroideries: the collection covers fourteen centuries, from the 4th to the 15th. Some gold and tempera icons are stunningly refined. Allow about 1.5 hours to enjoy it unhurried.

Don't miss Kerameikos: it's one of Athens' most moving sites, and one of the least crowded. This former potters' quarter was also the city's main necropolis, used from the 12th century BC through the Roman era. You'll find sculpted funerary steles, marble lions, and the Sacred Way that ran from here to Eleusis. The on-site museum houses the finest steles. On weekdays, you'll often have it to yourself.

Kapnikarea Church, nestled right in the middle of Ermou Street since the 11th century, is one of Athens' oldest Byzantine churches. Its central brick dome and golden interior mosaics contrast sharply with the bustle of shops on the street. Step inside—it's often open in the morning.

Syntagma Square is the heart of modern Athens, dominated by the Parliament housed in the former Royal Palace of 1843. In front, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is permanently guarded by the Evzones, presidential guards in traditional costume—white pleated fustanella with 400 pleats, white stockings and shoes with black pompoms. The changing of the guard happens every hour, and on Sundays at 11 AM in full dress with music.

The Museum of Cycladic Art houses one of the world's most important collections of Cycladic art, dating from 3200 to 2000 BC. These white marble figurines with refined forms—barely sketched silhouettes, smooth faces—fascinated Picasso and Modigliani in the 20th century. The effect is striking: they could be contemporary sculptures.

activities.text: Head up to the Acropolis right when it opens (8 AM in summer). The raking morning light gilds the Parthenon's marble and tourists are still scarce—it's the best window of the day to photograph the site without crowds.

After the Acropolis, descend toward Plaka, the historic neighborhood that stretches at the foot of the rock. Its cobbled lanes and stairways, neoclassical houses and bougainvillea make it one of the most pleasant places in Athens to stroll in the shade. Avoid restaurants directly on the tourist thoroughfares—head into the side streets.

Moussaka is the dish to try in Athens: meltingly tender eggplant, spiced ground meat, and béchamel baked until golden on top. The best versions are found in the tavernas of Plaka or Monastiraki, not in terrace restaurants with laminated photos.
In the evening, head back up toward the Acropolis rock at sunset from the Hill of the Muses or from Filopappou—free views, no crowds, of the Parthenon turning orange. It's the day's spectacle.

Monastiraki, right next to the Agora, is the neighborhood of flea markets, shops of every kind and local bustle. On Sundays, the flea market spills into the surrounding lanes - you can find everything from Byzantine icons to old Greek coins.

Head into the Psyrri neighborhood, just north of Monastiraki. It's the haunt of Athenian artists and night owls: walls covered in graffiti, used bookstores, cafés where people play cards until 3 AM. The neighborhood really only comes alive after 8 PM.

Spanakopita—spinach and feta pastry—is the ideal snack to keep you going between visits. You'll find it in all the market bakeries, still warm in the morning. Pastitsio is the day's main dish: baked pasta, ground meat, tomato sauce and béchamel browned on top—a pasta version of moussaka.

In the evening, try ouzo with a few mezze on a Psyrri terrace: cephalopods, olives, taramosalata. Ouzo is drunk diluted with cold water—it turns cloudy and the anise flavor softens. It's been the Athenians' aperitif ritual for generations.

Kolonaki is Athens' upscale neighborhood, at the foot of Lycabettus. Its cafés in Kolonaki Square are perfect for a midday break to watch well-heeled Athenians—it's a local sport. Greek designer boutiques cluster in the streets around the square.

Plan your Lycabettus ascent for late afternoon, so you reach the summit an hour before sunset. When the light shifts over the Acropolis and the city begins to glow beneath your feet, it's one of the most memorable moments of a stay in Athens. The little café at the summit stays open until nightfall.

Dolmades—vine leaves stuffed with rice, fresh herbs and lemon juice—are often served as mezze in the tavernas of Kolonaki or Plaka. Greek salad is always better here than elsewhere: thick slices of tomato, cucumbers, Kalamata olives, a block of feta and dried oregano on top.

If you like Greek wines, look for an Assyrtiko from Santorini when dining out in the evening: a dry white with pronounced minerality and sharp acidity that comes from the island's volcanic soils. It's Greece's most internationally famous white wine, and one of the best to pair with seafood.

For breakfast or a midday break, look for a café in Syntagma Square or the adjacent alleys for bougatsa—warm pastry filled with custard cream or fresh cheese, dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar. It's the traditional Thessaloniki breakfast that's become popular throughout Greece.

Ermou Street, pedestrianized between Syntagma and Monastiraki, is Athens' main shopping artery. This is where you'll encounter locals doing their shopping—not just tourists. Kapnikarea Church cuts it in two, a symbol of two overlapping millennia.

If you have the energy for an evening out, Exarcheia is Athens' most alternative neighborhood—bookstores, politicized bars, walls entirely covered in political graffiti, cafés open until the early hours. It's a very different Athens from Kolonaki or Plaka, and much more authentic.

For dinner, try keftedes—meatballs flavored with mint and cumin, fried and served as mezze. Mavrodaphne from Patras, a sweet red Greek wine, is the ideal companion to finish the meal with honey-based desserts.

visits.text: It is best to start at the Archaeological Museum of Abdera, in the village of Avdira, before tackling the ruins. Opened in 2000, it covers nearly two thousand years, from the 7th century BC to the 13th century AD, and reconstructs burials with clay sarcophagi and funerary offerings. Note that it is closed on Tuesdays.

Head down to Cape Bouloustra, about ten kilometers south, following in the footsteps of Democritus and Protagoras, both born in Abdera. Founded in the 7th century BC by settlers from Clazomenae and refounded by settlers from Teos around 544 BC, the city retains its defensive walls, a sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, and a quay now buried in sand. Check seasonal opening hours.

Salty air rises to the promontory of Polystylon, the Byzantine acropolis of Abdera, whose name recalls the columns that adorned its buildings. On the western side of the present-day anchorage, look for granite blocks from the ancient harbor. Save this sea view for the end of your visit before taking the road to Porto Lagos.

days_plan.itin_title: Greek Thrace in 5 Days: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini

visits.text: Explore Avgonyma on foot, from its narrow lanes to the paved square where a medieval tower faces the Church of Saint George. Almost abandoned in the 1960s, this village perched at an elevation of about 475 m has since been extensively restored in the traditional style, centered on its cube-shaped stone houses. Allow 30 minutes, ideally before lunch.

activities.text: On a clear day, the view from Avgonyma stretches across the Aegean Sea to the island of Psara. Tradition attributes the village’s founding to workers from Nea Moni in the 11th century, although no documents substantiate this. Have lunch here overlooking the open sea before descending to the west coast via Elinta and Lithi.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni

visits.text: It’s worth knowing the history before viewing the small Kastello in Avlemonas. In September 1802, Lord Elgin’s brig Mentor sank in the bay at a depth of 22 m, carrying seventeen crates of antiquities, including pieces from the Parthenon; no one died, and the marbles were recovered as early as 1804. Admire the small Venetian fort from the surrounding area at the end of the harbor.

activities.text: At Avlemonas, you’ll swim from the rocks or the small beach beside the harbor, where fishing caiques bob on very clear water. The taverna tables are just a few steps away. Save this swim for the end of the day, once you’ve settled into the village.

If the wind is blowing from neither the north nor the east, head down to Kaladi, not far from Avlemonas: more than a hundred steps lead to three pebble coves. A large rock separates the first two; the third, a small open cave, leads to a tiny beach. There’s just one snack bar, at the top: bring water and something for shade.

Paleopoli Beach, the longest on Kythira, stretches out a few kilometers from Avlemonas. Sand and fine pebbles, clear, shallow water: children can wade a long way out before it gets deep. Park in the parking lot at the entrance, then walk toward the undeveloped sections for more space.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves

visits.text: Legend has it that Aziz Aga threatened to have his master builder beheaded if the central arch collapsed a third time. Aziz Aga Bridge has stood firm: more than 70 m long, with three arches, one spanning 28 m, it rises 15 m above the Venetikos and was dated to 1727 by an inscription now lost. Only pedestrians and visitors use it today: bring walking shoes.

Head back toward Grevena via Spanos Bridge, about 16 km southwest of town, between Kosmati and Kipourio. Its five arches cross the Venetikos over roughly 85 m; one bears the date 1846, and cars still cross it. Stop before crossing to take in all five arches at once; the Egnatia highway runs just a few meters away.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena in 3 Days: Mansions and Fossils

visits.text: Standing 7.02 m tall and turned to stone, an ancestor of the sequoia still stands in Bali Alonia Petrified Forest Park: according to the museum, no standing fossil trunk in Europe is taller. Eruptions 17 to 20 million years ago also preserved a fallen trunk more than 20 m long here. Three themed trails wind through the park: arrive before 2 p.m., as it closes at 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Mytilene, Molyvos and the Petrified Forest

visits.text: If the white shelter stretched over the Temple of Apollo Epicurius seems disappointing at first, wait until you step beneath it. Built around 420–400 BC at an elevation of 1,130 m and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986, it combines all three Greek architectural orders and once featured the oldest known Corinthian capital. Its frieze is in the British Museum. In winter, arrive early: the site closes around 3:30 p.m.

activities.text: You will walk around the back of the shelter to follow the red and white trail markers toward Kotilion: roughly 3 km round-trip with 150 m of elevation gain. Below the summit lie the remains of two small temples from the 7th and 6th centuries BC, probably dedicated to Aphrodite and Artemis. The trail is rocky and poorly marked: abandon the hike if mist rolls in.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Tegea, Lousios, and Karytaina

visits.text: “Little she-bears”: at Brauron, the Athenians used the name arktoi for young girls dedicated to Artemis before marriage, who danced and ran in saffron-colored clothing. The sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia features a stoa with re-erected columns and a stone bridge, the only known example of a Classical-period bridge in Greece. Admission €5, open 8:30 AM–3:30 PM except Tuesdays: arrive at opening time to continue on to Marathon and Rhamnous.

Few museums have so much to say about childhood: Brauron’s museum displays statues of children, toys, vases, and figurines offered to Artemis, along with fragments of her cult statue. Look for the “relief of the gods,” which illustrates the founding myth: Iphigenia and Orestes bringing back the goddess’s statue from Tauris. Separate admission of €5; the museum is a five-minute walk from the sanctuary.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis

visits.text: The Temple of Poseidon raises its 15 surviving Doric columns on a promontory 60 meters high, at the southern tip of Attica. Built between 444 and 440 BC—at the same time as the Parthenon, as part of Pericles' program—it served both as a sanctuary to the god of the seas and as a landmark for sailors returning to Piraeus from the Mediterranean. On clear days, you'll make out the islands of Kea, Kythnos, and in good weather, as far as Serifos in the distance. Time your arrival for sunset: the orange light on the white marble is spectacular.

On one of the temple columns, look for the carved name of Lord Byron, who visited the site in 1810. The English poet was so captivated by Sounion that he recorded his reaction in verses from Don Juan (1819)—an ode to this marble promontory battered by waves that he described as the ideal place to listen to the sea in silence. This kind of graffiti would be a crime today—at the time, Byron was simply an enthusiastic Romantic tourist.

Take time to explore the site beyond the main temple: the cape also encompasses the remains of ancient fortifications and, on the adjacent hill, the foundations of a temple of Athena at Sounion destroyed in the 1st century AD. Less documented, this second sanctuary confirms that Sounion was a major place of worship—not just a navigational landmark for sailors.

As you walk the promontory, keep in mind that you're standing on one of Greece's most mythologically charged places: according to legend, this is where King Aegeus threw himself into the sea, believing his son Theseus dead after the expedition against the Minotaur. Theseus had forgotten to change his black sails to white ones to signal his victory. The sea has borne the king's name ever since. Homer himself mentions Sounion in the Odyssey as 'the sacred promontory of Athens.'

activities.text: The coastal road from Athens follows the Athenian Riviera for 70 km - a succession of beaches, coves and seaside resorts. Plan to leave in the morning to enjoy the water before the summer crowds arrive. The beaches of Vouliagmeni and Varkiza, more than half an hour's drive from Cape Sounion, are the most popular with Athenians.

In Vouliagmeni, more than half an hour's drive from Cape Sounion, stop at the thermal lake of the same name: a turquoise body of water fed by underground hot springs, set within a partially open cave. The water stays around 22 to 29°C all year round. There is an entrance fee but the swim is worth the detour, especially if you have spent several days at the archaeological sites.

Arrive at Cape Sounion about an hour before sunset. The site stays open until sunset—check the exact time depending on the season. Warning: there's no shade at the site, bring a hat and water. The terrain is rocky, avoid light sandals.

After sunset, the tavernas along the Sounion coast serve ultra-fresh locally caught fish: grilled octopus with oregano and lemon, Mediterranean fish soup, calamari and scampi. An ouzo or a Greek Alfa beer while watching the last light fade over the Aegean Sea: hard to beat as an end to the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece: Athens, Delphi and the Meteora
What to See in Athens: Acropolis, Museums & Neighborhoods

visits.text: Stop at the historic sliding bridge in the city's heart: you're standing at the narrowest point of the Euripus Strait, where just 38 meters separate island from mainland. Watch the water for a few minutes—the current reverses approximately every six hours, building to speeds of 12 km/h, then achieving eight minutes of eerie stillness before reversing again. This phenomenon, governed by lunar cycles, has mystified scientists since antiquity. Aristotle, whose ancestors hailed from Chalcis, came here to study what seemed to defy the laws of nature. A wooden bridge already spanned this strait in 411 BCE; the current structure dates to 1962.

Karababa Castle towers over the city from the opposite hillside. Constructed by the Ottomans in 1686—just years after they conquered Chalcis from the Venetians—it commands a spectacular vantage over the strait, the bridge, and the terracotta rooftops below. The climb from the center takes about 20 minutes on foot. It's the finest spot for photographing the current phenomenon from above.

Agia Paraskevi Church in the old town is among Greece's rarest surviving examples of Gothic Dominican architecture. Begun around 1250, it housed one of the earliest two Dominican priories approved in the Greek province. The central vault and carved stone sculptures in the southern chapel rank among the finest examples of Italian Gothic in Greece. Don't miss the central arch above the iconostasis.

Chalcis Archaeological Museum holds regional finds: geometric and archaic ceramics, Hellenistic sculpture, and domestic objects from local excavations. The Euboean pottery collection is especially rewarding for understanding Chalcis' pivotal role in Greek colonization. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, Chalcidian colonists founded roughly thirty cities on the Chalcidice peninsula and several in Magna Graecia, including Cumae in Italy.

The historic quarter of Chalcis blends Ottoman lanes, Venetian traces and an old Jewish quarter. The synagogue of Chalcis bears witness to a continuous Jewish presence since Antiquity, one of the oldest in Europe. Stroll through the small streets behind the seafront to find the most distinctive facades.

activities.text: Claim a terrace table facing the old bridge and observe the current shift. Locals do the same—it's free theater and genuinely hypnotic. On "chaotic" days—about 6–7 per lunar month—the current can reverse up to 14 times instead of the usual four. If you hit one of those days, you'll understand why the ancients spoke of Chalcis' "wild waters."

Taste syglino, Euboean smoked pork cured in fat—a highland specialty. Served on local bread with olives, it's the quintessential savory mezze of the region. Pair it with Euboean retsina, that resinous white wine of ancient tradition, here produced locally and superb alongside charcuterie and cheese.

As evening descends, Chalcis' waterfront comes alive. Residents gather at waterfront cafés and tavernas overlooking the strait. Order loukoumades—small fried pastries drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon—and watch pleasure boats navigate against the current.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages
Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South

visits.text: Start with a slow stroll along the Venetian harbour to the lighthouse at the jetty's end – it's the best vantage point over the colourful houses lining the basin. This lighthouse built by the Venetians in the 16th century, then rebuilt by the Egyptians in the 19th century, rises 21 metres and is one of the world's oldest lighthouses still standing. The harbour itself was built around 1320: you're walking on infrastructure that has guided merchant fleets for seven centuries. Plan to return at sunset – the atmosphere is altogether different.

On the harbour itself, don't miss the Hassan Pasha mosque – also called the Janissaries' mosque or Yali Tzami. Built shortly after the Ottomans took Chania in 1645, by an Armenian architect, it's the first mosque ever erected in Crete. Its architecture is distinctive: a cubic building topped with a main dome, flanked by a portico with seven small domes. It's now used as an exhibition space. Just beside it, the Venetian dockyards (Neoria) – 23 vaulted stone halls built in the 16th century to shelter and repair the fleet – are among the few surviving examples of this type in the Mediterranean.

Get lost in the old town lanes beyond the harbour. In the Topanas quarter, look for the Etz Hayyim synagogue, restored in the 1990s after nearly falling into ruin. It recalls a painful chapter: Chania's Jewish community, settled here for centuries, was entirely deported by the Nazis in 1944. Most deportees perished when the ship carrying them was sunk by a British torpedo after being mistaken for a warship.

Just behind the harbour, the Splantzia quarter is Chania's best-preserved – fewer tourists come here, and the atmosphere is more authentic. Look for Saint Nicholas church, a former 14th-century Dominican church converted to a mosque in 1645, which today has the unique distinction of having both an Orthodox bell tower and the old 35-metre Ottoman minaret still standing.

Walk past the Agora, the covered market built in 1913 in the shape of a cross. This dressed-stone building is worth a stop to observe its façade and architecture from outside. It is closed for restoration at the date of this audit: browsing the stalls and shopping inside are not possible. Before travelling, check whether it has reopened; do not plan to buy supplies here for the gorges until the market is operating again.

The Samaria Gorge is among Europe's longest: a 16 km downhill hike from the Omalos plateau (1,230 m above sea level) to the coastal village of Agia Roumeli on the Libyan Sea. The national park, established in 1962 and recognised as a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1981, supports more than 300 plant species, including 70 endemic to Crete. The walls rise up to 600 m, and the narrowest passage - the Sideroportes (Iron Gates) - is just 2.5 m wide. Be sure to organise your return: the last boat to Sougia or Hora Sfakion leaves at 17:30.

The Omalos plateau, at around 1,100 m above sea level, is the last village before the start of the walk. Xyloskalo, the gorge entrance, is 1 km away at 1,230 m. If you're driving, plan to leave Chania around 06:00 – the drive takes about 1 hour 15 minutes and Xyloskalo car parks are free. A few tavernas around the plateau serve breakfast before the descent.

Agia Roumeli, the village at the gorge exit, is accessible only by sea or on foot. A few tavernas and guesthouses welcome hikers who want to avoid the race against time to catch the last boat – a solution we recommend if you're with family or want to enjoy the beach unhurriedly. Otherwise, the evening boat departs around 17:30 for Sougia (45 min) or Hora Sfakion (1 hour 20 minutes), from where buses run to Chania.

If the gorge is too demanding or you prefer an alternative, the village of Loutro on the south coast can be reached by boat from Hora Sfakion (20 min). White houses beside a turquoise cove, no cars, no road - Loutro is one of Crete's most unspoilt corners. A night or an afternoon on its beach is worth all the tourist facilities on the island's north coast.

activities.text: Devote the morning to exploring the harbour and old town on foot. Chania is smaller and easier to explore on foot than Heraklion. Skrydlof Street, parallel to the harbour, is entirely dedicated to leather goods – bags, belts and leather sandals made on the premises. A typical purchase of good quality.

Walk past the covered Agora market to look at its stone building and façade. The market is closed for restoration at the date of this audit: you cannot see its stalls in operation or buy olive oil, aromatic herbs, thyme honey or graviera cheese there. Check whether it has reopened before planning an indoor visit. During the works, this stop remains an opportunity to discover the market's architecture from outside.

For dinner, settle into a taverna on the Venetian harbour by the dockyards – the atmosphere is less touristy than opposite the lighthouse. Taste kouneli stifado (rabbit simmered for a long time with small onions, red wine, cinnamon and cloves), one of the most characteristic slow-cooked dishes of Cretan mountain cuisine. Accompany it with a glass of vidiano, the aromatic local white.

Late evening, wander towards the Splantzia quarter for the more local vibe. The bars and cafés on Splantzia Square are heavily frequented by locals—the atmosphere is distinctly less touristy than at the harbour, and prices a bit more reasonable.

Leave as early as possible – before 07:00 if you can, for two reasons: to avoid the crowds (up to 4,000 people daily in high season in July–August) and to enjoy the coolness of the early hours in the canyon. The first 7 km cross a shaded forest of pines and cypresses and descend gradually; the last 4.5 km, at the canyon bottom, are the narrowest and most striking. Keep an eye out for kri-kri, the endemic wild goats that scale the walls – they're shy but far more visible in the morning. Bring plenty of water (water from the springs along the route is drinkable), good hiking shoes and sunscreen for the last exposed section.

On arrival at Agia Roumeli, the Libyan Sea awaits right ahead. Plunge in—you'll have earned it. The water is clear and the bottom sandy. Take time to lunch in one of the village tavernas before catching the boat.

If you are less athletic or travelling with very young children, there is a reasonable alternative: reach Agia Roumeli by boat, then walk 5 km up the gorge to the Iron Gates – its most spectacular section – and walk back down. Allow 3 hours for the round-trip walk, without the full logistical arrangements.

Rakomelo is the winter version of raki: warmed with honey and cinnamon, it's drunk like a comforting digestif. In the mountain tavernas around Omalos, you'll often be offered it at the start of the meal in the cool morning temperatures—accept without hesitation, it's the local custom.

visits.text: The most beautiful neighborhood in Chios Town is still inhabited behind its ramparts. The Kastro, a Byzantine citadel remodeled by the Genoese and then the Ottomans, is still home to about 650 residents, an Ottoman cemetery, and the tomb of Kara Ali Pasha, whose flagship Kanaris set ablaze in 1822. Enter through Porta Maggiore to the south, then look for the “dark dungeon” where seventy prominent citizens were held before their execution. Come in the morning, when the narrow streets are still shaded.

Circles of light fall from the dome onto marble benches: the Ottoman baths in the Kastro have retained the dim atmosphere of a hammam. Dating to the 18th century, they form the citadel’s largest hammam, with ten rooms covering 365 m², and their restoration was completed in 2012; the foundations still reveal how hot air circulated. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. except Tuesdays: stop by before lunch.

Orthodox icons beneath the dome of a mosque: the Byzantine Museum of Chios occupies the former Mecidiye Mosque on Vounaki Square. Built in the 19th century under Sultan Abdülmecid I, it traces the island’s history from early Christian times, with Genoese and Ottoman artifacts and sculptures in the courtyard. The icons from Panagia Krina catch the eye. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

One hundred thirty thousand volumes downstairs, a 19th-century birthing chair upstairs: the Korais Library brings together an eclectic mix. Founded in 1792 thanks to the scholar Adamantios Korais, it preserves medical texts from the 15th century. Upstairs, the Philip Argenti Museum brings together traditional costumes, embroidery, shepherds’ tools, and portraits of the wealthy Argenti family. Come on a weekday morning: closing time is around 3 p.m.

The Chios Maritime Museum tells the story of an island of shipowners, in a house in the town center donated by the heirs of the Patera family. Paintings of sailing ships and steamships by Aristides Glykas, a native of Vrontados, sit alongside models and photographs; one section explores the Liberty ships that fueled the growth of the Greek fleet after the war. Check the seasonal hours: 9 a.m.–2 p.m. from May to October, 9 a.m.–1 p.m. in winter, and closed Sundays except in August.

The Citrus Museum on the Perivoli estate occupies a house dating to 1742 in the heart of Kampos. Maps, photographs, tools, and packaging tell the story of the citrus cultivation and trade that brought prosperity to the plain, supplemented by a short documentary. Admission is free; check the estate’s hours before visiting and leave some time to try its jams.

It is tempting to believe the legend of Daskalopetra in Vrontados: Homer is said to have taught his students on this rock near the sea. Archaeologists instead interpret it as a rock sanctuary of Cybele dating to the late 6th or early 5th century BC. Access is free; late in the day is the best time to visit.

activities.text: Stroll along Aplotaria Street, Chios Town’s pedestrian shopping thoroughfare, for clothing, souvenirs, and island products. Then head to the harbor, lined with cafés and restaurants that bustle day and night. Look for mastiha, a mastic liqueur protected by a designation of origin in the European Union, to take home rather than drink in direct sunlight. Save this walk for late afternoon, after the museums.

Hop on a bike or walk through the lanes of Kampos, south of Chios Town, between high walls of reddish Thymiana stone. Behind the gates, two- and three-story mansions, most dating from the Genoese period, watch over groves of mandarin, orange, and lemon trees, once irrigated by waterwheels known as manganas. Stay on the lanes: most estates are private.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni
Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni

visits.text: The Agios Polykarpos Folklore Museum, in a village near Christos Raches, tells the story of everyday life in Raches in years past through a wide range of objects. Admission is free, and a visit takes less than 1 hour. Stop by in the morning: it opens daily from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., well before the mountains come alive in the evening.

“The village that never sleeps” is how Christos Raches is described, perched among pine trees at about 500 m above sea level. Its square paved with Ikarian slate, church with a marble bell tower, and the women’s association’s sweets workshop can be explored on foot, with cars left at the village entrance. Return after 9 p.m., when shops and cafés come alive until midnight.

activities.text: Walk 15 minutes from Christos Raches to Litani Rock, a viewpoint known for its sunsets. The path winds through the pines and oaks surrounding scattered houses, with an old mill hidden beneath the trees. The walk stays cool in the morning; return at dusk if you want the evening light.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches

places.name: Corfu

visits.text: Corfu's old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 — a maze of narrow cobblestone lanes known as kantounia, lined with neoclassical facades in pastel hues inherited from centuries of Venetian rule. Venice held the island almost uninterrupted from 1386 to 1797, and it's the Republic that shaped this unique urban fabric, which neither the French nor the British managed to erase. Get up early: the lanes are stunning before 9am, empty and gilded by the morning light.

The Old Fortress (Palaio Frourio) sits on a rocky headland separated from the town by a sea moat — the Contrafossa — which the Venetians dug to turn the citadel into an artificial island. It successfully repelled three major Ottoman sieges: 1537, 1571 and 1716. Inside, don't miss the Church of St George, whose golden facade resembles an ancient temple — the contrast is striking. Climb to the lighthouse at the top for the best panoramic view over the sea and the town.

The New Fortress (Fortezza Nuova), built by the Venetians from 1577 on the hill overlooking the harbour, draws fewer visitors than the Old one — take advantage of that. Its underground galleries, bastions and tunnels carved into the rock form a fascinating labyrinth. The view over the harbour and the Ionian Sea from the battlements alone makes it worth the visit.

The Palace of St Michael and St George, built by the British between 1819 and 1824 in neoclassical style, now houses the Museum of Asian Art — a collection of 11,000 pieces from China, Japan and India, bequeathed by a Greek diplomat. An unexpected combination for a Greek island. The entrance from the People's Garden also offers a fine angle on the Spianada.

The Spianada Esplanade is the largest green public square in Greece. The arcaded Liston that lines its western edge was built during the French occupation, directly inspired by the Rue de Rivoli in Paris. This is where the Corfiots still play cricket, a tradition inherited from the British — one of the few places in Greece where the sport is practised. Late in the afternoon, grab a table on the terrace and watch local life unfold.

The Achilleion is one of the most romantic — and most tragic — palaces in the Mediterranean. Sisi had it built between 1889 and 1891 in a neo-Pompeian style, 10 km south of the capital, on a 200,000 m² plot overlooking the Ionian Sea. She had taught herself Ancient Greek to read Homer in the original and wanted to pay tribute to Achilles, whom she saw as the embodiment of the Greek soul. After her assassination by an anarchist in 1898, Kaiser Wilhelm II bought the palace in 1907 and spent every spring there until World War I. In 1981, the first floor served as the casino set for the James Bond film For Your Eyes Only. Allow at least 1h30 for the gardens and the apartments.

The peninsula of Kanoni, 4 km south of the capital, offers Corfu's most iconic view: in the foreground, Vlacherna Monastery perched on its tiny islet connected to the shore by a causeway, and behind it, the islet of Pontikonisi ('Mouse Island') crowned with dark cypresses. Homeric legend says it's the Phaeacian ship turned to stone by Poseidon after bringing Odysseus home to Ithaca. Arrive in the late afternoon for the best light.

Paleokastritsa, 25 km to the northwest, is one of the most beautiful natural sites in the Ionian Islands: six interlocking bays, crystal-clear turquoise waters and limestone cliffs rising 30 to 50 metres. The Monastery of Panagia Theotokos, founded in 1225 on a rocky headland above the main bay, was according to tradition established after the discovery of an icon of the Virgin. The present buildings date from the 18th century. Modest dress is required to enter — cover-up garments are provided at the door. The view from the monastery gardens over the sea is among the finest on the island.

The hilltop villages of Lakones and Makrades, above Paleokastritsa, offer plunging views over the six coves of the bay - a panorama the locals call the “balcony of Corfu”. These villages of centuries-old olive groves have kept their traditional architecture and their unpretentious tavernas. Plan a day trip from Corfu Town, combined with Paleokastritsa. Stop there for a coffee or a simple lunch on a terrace.

Corfu's Archaeological Museum, in town, houses the pediment of the Artemision, a 6th-century BC temple of Artemis discovered on the island: the central Gorgon stands nearly 3 metres tall and ranks among the best-preserved archaic sculptures in Greece. Allow about 45 minutes.

activities.text: Lose yourself in the Campiello, the oldest neighbourhood in the old town, north of the Old Fortress. It's a tangle of kantounia so narrow that two people can barely pass, with carved Venetian wells popping up in tiny squares. Laundry dries between buildings, bougainvillea spills over ochre walls — the atmosphere is light-years away from mass tourism.

On Orthodox Holy Saturday (in April or early May depending on the year), the people of Corfu celebrate the Resurrection by throwing ceramic jars out of their windows at exactly 11 a.m. - a noisy, festive spectacle unique in Greece. If you are not there for Easter, the religious processions carrying the relics of Saint Spyridon, the island's patron saint, also take place on 11 August and the first Sunday of November, and their atmosphere is worth stopping for.

Pastitsada is Corfu's signature dish: rooster (or veal) braised in a tomato sauce with Venetian spices, served over thick macaroni. The recipe is a direct trace of four centuries of Italian influence. Try it in an old-town taverna — the spots around the Campiello are the most authentic.

Bourdeto is Corfu's other pride: fish (scorpionfish by preference) cooked in a tomato sauce fired up with hot paprika. It's a fisherman's recipe — rustic and bold. Pair it with a glass of Robola, the dry, mineral white from neighbouring Cephalonia, which cuts through the acidity of the sauce.

Book a boat trip from Paleokastritsa to explore the sea caves along the northwest coast. Small boats slip into limestone cavities where sunlight creates blue and green reflections on the water — local guides call one of them the “Blue Light Cave”. The experience is at its best in the morning, when the sea is calm.

Take a dip in Agios Spyridon bay at Paleokastritsa — it's the most accessible beach in the resort, a mix of sand and pebbles with shallow waters. Several outfitters rent sea kayaks to explore the coves that can't be reached on foot. Expect to pay around €25–35 for a half-day kayak rental.

Sofrito is Corfu's quintessential Venetian dish: thin slices of veal pan-fried in a sauce of garlic, parsley, white wine and vinegar. The recipe dates back to 16th-century Venetian cooks. Pair it with a glass of Verdea, the dry white from Zakynthos — slightly oxidised and full-bodied, it holds its own against the bold flavours of the sauce.

Mantolato, a hard nougat made with roasted almonds and thyme honey, is Corfu's traditional confection — old-town delicatessens have stocked it since the 19th century. It's the ideal edible souvenir to bring home: it travels well and keeps for several weeks.

visits.text: The Temple of Apollo immediately gives you a sense of the scale of Ancient Corinth: its columns still tower over the surrounding remains. Dating from the 6th century BCE, it stands alongside the Roman forum, a reminder of another era. Start early on this exposed site, then continue to the museum using the same ticket.

Up close, the objects in the Archaeological Museum of Corinth make the ruins feel less abstract. Built in 1932, the museum houses finds from excavations of the city and stands within the archaeological site. Keep your ticket and enjoy this indoor visit before getting back on the road.

Save some energy for Acrocorinth: the climb is part of the visit. This fortress occupies the rocky height that protected the ancient city; from the ramparts, the ruins and the modern city share the same panorama. Wear shoes with good traction and check the closing time before heading up.

activities.text: Corinth marks the end of the tour, after the drive from Lake Doxa. If you have time before leaving, take a stroll around the town.

Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: Dadia’s bird-of-prey observation hide overlooks the feeding site where rangers leave carcasses for vultures. The park is home to the Balkans’ only natural colony of cinereous vultures, with 36 to 47 pairs according to the Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds (BSPB). A 15-seat minibus heads up at 8:30 AM, 10 AM, 11:30 AM, and 1 PM: book at 25540 32209 and aim for the first departure.

The most striking sight in Dadia remains the forest itself: the August 2023 wildfire swept through it for seventeen days and burned a large part of it. Natural regeneration is underway, and the vultures have stayed. The park information center, 800 m from the village square, introduces the park through an exhibition room and documentaries; open daily from 8 AM to 4 PM.

activities.text: You’ll continue the morning on foot along the marked 5 km loop that starts at the Dadia ecotourism center, follows the edge of the protected area, and returns near the village. The route is easy; another trail climbs to Kapsalo for panoramic views of the forest. Set out before the heat and bring water.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk

visits.text: The stern gaze of the Pantocrator looks down from the dome of Daphni Monastery, on the ancient Sacred Way that led to Eleusis. Its gold-background mosaics, dating to around 1100, have survived many changes in the monastery’s use: a Cistercian presence until 1458, a gunpowder magazine during the revolution of 1821, and later a psychiatric hospital. UNESCO listed the monastery in 1990. Admission is free, every day except Tuesday, until 3:30 PM in winter and 5 PM in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis

visits.text: The Sanctuary of Apollo clings to the slopes of Mount Parnassus at 600 meters—a site that functioned as an oracle for over a thousand years, from the late 7th century BC through the 4th century AD. According to tradition, this is where the omphalos stood, the stone Zeus designated as the center of the world. Don't expect a peaceful museum experience: tour buses arrive early in summer. Plan your ascent for opening time (8 AM) to catch the site while it's still quiet.

The Temple of Apollo you see today dates from the 4th century BC—actually the sixth temple built here, after an earthquake in 373 BC destroyed its predecessor. A Doric structure measuring 60 meters long by 24 meters wide, with six columns on the facade and fifteen along the sides, it housed the Pythia seated on her tripod inside the cella. This is where the maxim Socrates would make famous was carved: "Know thyself." Three columns still stand—they give you a sense of the original building's scale.

The theater, built in the 4th century BC and restored by the Romans in the 2nd century, seated 5,000 spectators during the Pythian Games, held every four years in honor of Apollo. Climb to the upper tiers: the view over the Pleistos valley, the olive groves, and the Gulf of Corinth in the distance is one of the finest at the entire site. Take time to examine the proscenium's bas-reliefs depicting the labors of Heracles before moving on.

Don't rush past this small building in Parian marble: the Athenian Treasury, built between 510 and 480 BC to celebrate the victory at Marathon, is one of the few Delphi monuments completely reconstructed—French archaeologists reassembled it stone by stone between 1903 and 1906. Its friezes depict Theseus, Heracles, and an amazonomachy. And on the exterior walls, carved into the marble, you can still see two hymns to Apollo with their musical notation—among the only sonic documents to survive from antiquity.

After the theater, take time to look at the seating and the Pleistos valley below. The stadium lies higher up the site, but access is currently closed for work to protect against falling rocks. The theater remains a place to imagine the Pythian Games and view the sanctuary of Apollo from above.

The Castalian Spring lies in the ravine between the two Phaedriades rocks, just before entering the sanctuary. Every pilgrim had to purify themselves here before consulting the oracle—washing their hands, or their entire head for first-time visitors. Today it's a basin carved from rock, with water still flowing. The setting, between cliffs rising over 200 meters, has a stark beauty.

Below the main sanctuary, the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia is often less visited—wrongly so. Its most famous monument is the tholos, a 4th-century BC circular building whose exact function remains unknown. Three Doric columns and three interior Corinthian columns have been re-erected—they give the site an almost photogenic appearance. Allow 20 to 30 minutes to descend from the main site entrance.

The gymnasium at Delphi, midway between the tholos and the main sanctuary, was the training ground for athletes competing in the Pythian Games. You can still make out the running track (xystos) and the cold bath basins. A quiet spot, often deserted, that you may have entirely to yourself.

Arachova (960 meters elevation) deserves at least an hour's stop. Its steep alleyways open onto craft shops—hand-woven rugs, cheeses, local liqueurs—and viewpoints over the valley. In winter it's a lively little ski resort; in summer the village is considerably calmer. Look for the overlook above the main church for the best view of the surroundings.

Make the detour to Hosios Loukas, 37 km from Delphi—it's an hour's drive well worth the trip. This monastery founded in 945 by the hermit Saint Luke of Steiris has been UNESCO-listed since 1990 and preserves 11th-century gold-ground mosaics among the best preserved in the entire Byzantine world. The great katholikon, built in 1011, introduced an architectural plan—octagonal inscribed cross—that would become standard throughout Byzantine Greece. Inside, look up at the dome: Christ Pantocrator gazes down at you. The site is open mornings; check hours before departing as midday closures often surprise visitors.

activities.text: Take your time walking slowly along the Sacred Way from the sanctuary entrance to the temple. On either side once stood dozens of statues and treasuries offered by Greek city-states competing for prestige. The empty pedestals you see today once bore bronzes long since melted down. This gradual ascent with the oracle at the end creates an atmosphere that even the crowds can't quite dispel.

The Delphi Archaeological Museum deserves half a day on its own. Its centerpiece is the Charioteer (Hêniokhos): a 1.82-meter bronze discovered in 1896 beneath the Sacred Way, buried during the earthquake of 373 BC. Cast around 470-466 BC to commemorate the tyrant of Gela's victory at the Pythian Games, it's one of only five major classical bronzes preserved worldwide. Look closely at the eyes: irises in brown chalcedony, pupils in obsidian, tear ducts in pink coral—a staggering level of detail for a work 2,500 years old.

In late afternoon, from the heights of the site, the panorama over Parnassus (2,457 meters according to official sources) and the valley of olive trees descending toward the Gulf of Corinth is at its finest. The oblique light brings out the nuances of the temple's honey-colored stone. If you're staying in Delphi or Arachova, you can walk down via the trail along the ravine—allow 30 minutes and wear sturdy shoes.

Formaela from Arachova, a PDO sheep's milk cheese, can be purchased in shops in the neighboring village. Grill it and drizzle with local honey—a combination you won't find everywhere in Greece. Arachova is 10 km from Delphi via a road offering some beautiful valley viewpoints.

Kleftiko lamb—slow-cooked in a paper parcel with herbs and garlic—is the mountain specialty of the region. You'll find it in most tavernas around Delphi and Arachova. The name comes from the "klephtes," brigands who cooked meat underground so the smoke wouldn't give them away.
Agiorgitiko, a red wine from Nemea (Peloponnese), pairs beautifully with the region's mountain cuisine. Full-bodied with soft tannins, it drinks young. You'll find it by the carafe in local tavernas.

The walk through the Pleistos Gorge, the river flowing below Delphi, is accessible from the village and takes 1.5 to 2 hours round trip. The trail winds through thousand-year-old olive groves—some trees are said to be over a millennium old. The quiet contrasts with the bustle of the archaeological site. Hiking shoes recommended; the path can be slippery.

In the village of Arachova, step into the craft shops lining the main street. Hand-woven rugs and kilims are the village specialty going back several generations—red and black geometric patterns you'll only see here. Local cheeses (formaela, fresh goat cheese) are sold directly from producers.

On the route to Hosios Loukas from Delphi, stop in the village of Distomo—known for the 1944 tragedy when the SS massacred 218 residents in reprisal. A sober memorial marks the village center. This context adds another dimension to the monastery visit that follows, a place of cultural continuity and resistance for a thousand years.
Hilopites—square dried pasta typical of the region—are eaten in soup or baked with cheese. A simple, hearty dish you'll find in mountain tavernas around Arachova.

Feta saganaki, pan-fried in olive oil and served with honey and sesame seeds, is a classic appetizer in the region's tavernas. The sweet-salty balance works particularly well with a glass of dry white wine.

Tsipouro from Thessaly, a grape marc eau-de-vie sometimes lightly anise-flavored, is served ice-cold with mezze—olives, cheese, mountain charcuterie. It's the aperitif drink throughout central Greece. Don't confuse it with ouzo: tsipouro is more concentrated and without added sugar.

visits.text: A freighter’s bow juts out of the water off Diakofti: it belongs to the Nordland, a Russian ship that ran aground on the islet of Prasonisi on August 29, 2000. Its stern rests at a depth of around 30 m and attracts divers. View the bow from the white-sand beach while waiting for the ferry.

activities.text: From Diakofti, you’ll take the ferry back to Neapoli Voion, a crossing of about 1 hour 15 minutes, then drive 13 km to Pounta, where the ferry reaches Elafonisos in about ten minutes. Bring water and a snack: the snack bar at Diakofti port was not expected to open in summer 2026.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves

activities.text: You’ll begin the itinerary in Diakopto, a village on the Achaean coast where the Vouraïkos Gorge meets the sea. From Athens, the Olympia Odos highway takes you there by car; by rail, the station, which reopened in 2020, is served by local trains between Kiato and Aigio. No local bus serves the station, so keep the car for the drive up to Kato Zachlorou.

Diakopto brings the route to a close on the shores of the Gulf of Corinth, at the mouth of the Vouraïkos Gorge. From Lake Tsivlou, the road descends to Akrata, then follows the coast. To leave by train, check the local train schedule to Kiato, where you connect for Athens; the station has a small parking lot.

days_plan.itin_title: Kalavryta and Helmos in 3 Days: Monasteries, Lakes, and the Styx
Kalavryta and Helmos in 3 Days: Monasteries, Lakes, and the Styx

visits.text: “The unknown capital of Byzantium”: this is how the Byzantine Museum of Didymoteicho presents the city where Emperors John III Vatatzes and John V Palaiologos were born. The exhibits also explore Plotinopolis, a city founded by Trajan on Agia Petra hill, and end with an illuminated map of the Via Egnatia that visitors can walk across like a game. On Saturdays, it is open from 1 PM to 8 PM; closed Mondays and Tuesdays, admission €5.

Climb to the Kale, Didymoteicho’s citadel, perched on a rocky hill 107 m above the Erythropotamos. Its ramparts have 24 towers; the most famous, Vasilopoula Tower, takes its name from a governor’s daughter who, legend has it, fell from its battlements. At the foot of the hill, cavities carved into the rock served as storerooms and cisterns. Near the Church of Saint Athanasius (1834), a cave is said to have held Charles XII of Sweden captive. Closed-toe shoes are essential.

Small but charming, the Folklore Museum of Didymoteicho is worth a 45-minute visit. Embroidery, woven bedding, traditional jewelry, a raki still, and tools from an old print shop fill the displays; the courtyard is dominated by the giachana, a sesame mill once used to produce oil. Open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 AM to 2 PM and Sunday from 10:30 AM to 1:30 PM.

activities.text: In the evening, the Erythropotamos flows below the ramparts: follow the river, then head into central Didymoteicho, where the Ottoman baths of Oruç Pasha, built in 1398–1399, still stand. In front of these walls in 1352, the Ottomans won their first victory in Europe. View the hammam ruins from the outside, then finish at the central square.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk

visits.text: On the way to Dikella, make a detour through Kavala — a port city built into a hillside descending to the Aegean, facing the island of Thasos. Its old Ottoman quarter of Panagia is best explored on foot from the 270-metre Kamares aqueduct, built in the 16th century under Suleiman the Magnificent. Climb to the citadel for the sea view. In the quarter's streets, look for the birthplace of Mehmet Ali, an Ottoman officer born here in the 18th century and considered the founder of modern Egypt.

Twenty-five minutes north of Kavala, the site of Philippi is an essential stop. Founded in 360 BC by settlers from Thasos, fortified by Philip II of Macedon in 356, it witnessed the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC where Octavian (the future Augustus) and Mark Antony crushed Brutus and Cassius. In AD 50, the Apostle Paul founded the first Christian church in Europe here. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the grounds include an ancient theatre still used in summer, early Christian basilicas, a Roman forum and a museum. Allow at least 2 hours.

Dikella beach, on the northern coast of the Aegean Sea, is a long, well-equipped stretch of golden sand and smooth pebbles — with sun loungers, showers and a gently sloping entry into the water — popular with families from the Alexandroupolis area. It's quiet, not heavily visited by foreign tourists, and offers a peaceful end to the trip before heading back via Kavala.

activities.text: Spend the afternoon at Dikella beach — the water is clean and shallow, the Aegean sunset is serene and crowd-free. Mesi beach, a few kilometres along, is even wilder if you're looking for total solitude.

Finish with a seafood dinner at one of the waterfront restaurants in the nearby village of Agia Paraskevi — octopus, Thracian mussels and grilled fish have been served here for decades by local fishing families. The cuisine of Eastern Macedonia blends Greek, Turkish and Balkan influences in a way quite different from the islands.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: As soon as you arrive, follow a paved path down to the Open-Air Water Power Museum beside the Lousios. A flour mill, fulling mill, gunpowder mill, tannery, and tsipouro still show how water kept the valley running. Open until 5 p.m. in winter and 6 p.m. in summer, except Tuesdays; in 2026, access is partial and admission is free.

“The nation’s powder magazine”: that was the nickname for Dimitsana, whose gunpowder mills ran day and night in 1821. In the lanes of the village, perched at around 950 m, look for the house and statue of Patriarch Gregory V, then the statue of Germanos of Patras. Park before reaching the center: the main street doubles as a regional road.

Around 5,000 volumes before 1821, barely 500 afterward: Dimitsana’s library, founded in 1764, paid a heavy price for the revolution. According to Kolokotronis’s memoirs, paper from the lost books was used to make cartridges filled with local gunpowder. Open to visitors, it now holds some 35,000 works: stop by in the morning, before heading to the gorge.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Tegea, Lousios, and Karytaina

visits.text: Water from the springs of Mount Olympus still flows between the columns of the Dion archaeological park; it helped preserve the mosaics. Here, Alexander the Great sacrificed to Zeus before marching against the Persians, and the sanctuary of Isis retains a canal representing the Nile. In season, the park opens at 8 a.m.: explore it before the heat sets in.

The real showstopper at the Archaeological Museum of Dion awaits upstairs: the hydraulis, a water organ unearthed in 1992 and presented as the oldest known example. In the neighboring Archaiothiki, you can admire the 100 m² Dionysus mosaic—the size of a large apartment—from a gallery. From April through October, the museum opens at 11 a.m.: visit the ruins first.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus in 3 Days: Dion, Litochoro, and Larissa

visits.text: The monastery of Osios Loukas is one of the most beautiful in the entire Mediterranean – and one of the least familiar to French-speaking travellers. Perched on the slopes of Mount Helicon in a bowl of olive and almond trees, it was founded by the hermit Luke of Steiris, born in Delphi in 896, who died in 953 after predicting the reconquest of Crete from the Arabs (a prediction fulfilled eight years after his death). UNESCO-listed since 1990, its katholikon (completed around 1011) houses Greece's most complete 11th-century gold-ground mosaics: Crucifixion, Descent into Limbo – an iconographic programme of rare coherence and beauty. The polychrome marble, jasper and porphyry pavements are also exceptional. The saint's relics remain in the crypt. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

On the road between Thebes and Osios Loukas, a stop in Levadia (Livadia) is worth the detour. From Distomo, allow approximately 22 km and 20 minutes by car. The city centres on the spring of Trophonius, an ancient oracle contemporary with Delphi that made those seeking its advice enter a terrifying cave – Pausanias, the Greek traveller of the 2nd century AD, left a striking description. The springs still gush from the foot of a rocky cliff, where a promenade with watermills and cafés has now been laid out. The medieval castle of Levadia (14th century) overlooks the city from the hill – a 30-minute climb.

activities.text: In the monastery shop, monks sell their honey, olive oil and preserves. These are products of exceptional quality at very reasonable prices. Before leaving the site, have a coffee on the small terrace facing the valley – the view of olive trees descending towards the sea, the silence and the mountain air form a combination you won't find anywhere else on this circuit.

visits.text: Small but exceptionally clear in its presentation, the Archaeological Museum of Drama covers some 50,000 years in three rooms. The oldest tools come from the cave at the Aggitis springs, which you will visit the following day, while a bust of Dionysus attests to the worship of the god of wine in the region. On Tuesdays, opening is delayed until 11 a.m.; full-price admission is €5. The Hellenistic tomb on Troias Street can be visited by appointment through the museum.

The sound of water drowns out the city at Agia Varvara Park, fed by springs that emerge in the heart of Drama. Giant plane trees, small lakes, wooden bridges, and old watermills spread across about six hectares; the Marble House, built in 1875 as a tobacco merchant’s residence, displays photographs of Drama. Return after dark: crayfish can be made out under the underwater lights. Around December 4, the feast of Saint Barbara, candles float on the lake.

Still standing after more than a thousand years, Agia Sofia Church, built in the 10th century, is Drama’s oldest surviving building. Converted into a mosque under Ottoman rule, it retains a bell tower set on the base of the former minaret. Nearby, sections of the Byzantine walls emerge throughout the northern neighborhood, and some still serve as boundaries between private properties. Follow them on foot, looking up as you go.

So inconspicuous that it is easy to miss, the Church of the Taxiarchs on Venizelou Street is worth a detour for its Palaiologan-era frescoes. This single-nave church from the 14th century measures just 7 meters by 3.45; a staircase connects it to the neighboring Byzantine wall. Its age only came to light in 1973, when the porch that concealed it was demolished. Continue to nearby Agia Sofia.

Drama built its late-19th-century prosperity on tobacco. On a 30-minute walk, look for the Portokaloglou (1904), Protopappa (1912), and Spierer warehouses, the last a four-story building designed in 1924 by the Austrian Konrad von Vilas. These warehouses also carry a painful memory: in March 1943, Drama’s Jews were rounded up in tobacco warehouses before being deported, and none of the 589 returned.

If the sky is clear toward the end of the day, head up Korylovos, a hill about 500 m high with Drama spread out at its foot. A 4 km paved road leads to the summit, where the remains of the Byzantine church of Panagia Koryliotissa, dating to around 1050, still stand. On foot, start at the Panorama kiosk, 2.7 km from the center, and follow a marked trail through the pine forest.

activities.text: Leave the city for Adriani, 12 km away, where Ktima Kosta Lazaridi welcomes visitors Monday through Friday. In 1979, its founder planted the region’s first vineyard with trellised rows, earning him the nickname “patriarch” of Drama wines. The tour takes you through the red wine aging cellars and a corridor of marble sculptures before the tasting. Call the day before to arrange a time.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 6 Days: Philippi, Caves, and Elatia

visits.text: You hear the roar before you see the waterfalls of Edessa: Karanos and the double waterfall come into view at the edge of the city’s plateau. The Edessaios River splits into branches in the city before falling into the plain, explaining the abundance of water amid the streets. Follow the open paths and wear shoes with good traction near the spray.

Varosi overlooks the plain of Edessa from the site of the ancient acropolis. This neighborhood retains houses built in the Macedonian architectural tradition and cobblestone streets; its remains are a reminder that the ancient city also had fortifications on the plateau. Explore it on foot after visiting the waterfalls, allowing time for the viewpoints and historical information panels.

Before attracting walkers, water powered the workshops of Edessa: the Open-Air Water Museum tells this industrial history. The mills form a group of buildings near the waterfalls, rather than an exhibition confined to a single room. Check which buildings are actually open on the day you visit before planning to go inside.

activities.text: Head to Kioupri Bridge in Edessa to finish with a walk along the Edessaios River. This arched stone bridge is part of the urban heritage of a city where waterways still run alongside streets and cafés. Plan a short route if you are leaving afterward, and allow extra time to reach your transportation.
