visits.text: Elafonisi isn't really an island: in calm weather, you can walk across the shallow lagoon separating it from shore—the water comes up to your knees. The pink sand is real but nuanced: it's not uniformly pink, but sprinkled with pink grains where the waves deposit crushed shells of micro-organisms called Foraminifera. Local legend says the sand was stained by the blood of an Ottoman massacre on April 18, 1824: several hundred Cretans, including many women and children, were killed here while waiting for a rescue boat. The area is protected by the Natura 2000 network—it's strictly forbidden to take sand, shells, or plants; inspections are real. Arrive before 9:30 a.m.: afterward, tourist buses pour in hundreds of people.

The Monastery of Chrissoskalitissa stands on a coastal rock 10 minutes by car from Elafonisi. Its name means “Golden Step”—legend says a 90-step staircase carved into the rock has one golden step, visible only to those who haven't sinned. The view over the west coast from the terraces is magnificent, and the visit takes only 20 minutes.

activities.text: Walk across the lagoon from the main beach (barely 100 meters, warm and shallow water) and follow the island's northern shore: the beach on the north side is less crowded, the waters slightly deeper and turquoise. Plan to stay until the tourist buses leave around 4–5 p.m.—the site then regains a remarkable calm, ideal for sunset.

If you want to extend this stop, plan a return drive from Elafonisi to Falasarna. This long, wind-exposed white-sand beach offers spectacular sunsets. Two distinct beaches frame a rocky headland with ancient remains.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: Agios Spyridon Chapel, built in 1858 on a rock linked to the village by a small bridge, welcomes boats at the entrance to Elafonisos, near a ruined mill. Spyridon is the island’s patron saint, celebrated on December 12. Stop by on your way back from Simos, then try kakavia, the local fish soup, at the harbor.

Here, the village is simply called Chora: Elafonisos’s main settlement lines the north coast, facing Pounta. In winter, the island has 300 to 350 residents; in July and August, more than 3,000 visitors arrive each day. Pausanias already described this land as a peninsula shaped like a donkey’s jaw, Onou Gnathos. Stroll between the harbor and Kontogoni Beach, sheltered from southerly winds, then order a tsaiti, a pie from Vatika filled with fresh goat cheese and mint.

activities.text: The photos don’t lie: at Simos, almost-white sand and shallow water form twin bays, Sarakiniko, with more facilities, and the more unspoiled Fragkos. Dunes and junipers separate them, 4.5 km from the village of Elafonisos. Climb for about twenty minutes to Simos Cave for the view.

Dunes, junipers, and four islets offshore: Panagia Beach, near Kato Nisi, 5 km southwest of the village of Elafonisos, offers a different setting from Simos. The area, designated a Natura 2000 site, is home to endemic plants such as the sea daffodil. Expect fine sand, warm, shallow water, and beach umbrellas along only part of the shore. Settle in early and stay until sunset, which is renowned here.

A caique will take you where the road cannot: boat trips from Elafonisos harbor reach the islets facing Panagia, including Xeropoules, Prasonisi, and Kassela, as well as Karandreas Sea Cave. In summer, small boats are also available to rent at the old harbor. Book the day before and allow some flexibility: trips depend on the wind, which is common on the island.

When a southerly wind picks up, head to Lefki on Elafonisos’s east coast: it becomes the calmest spot on the island, and small boats come here for shelter. White sand, rocks, and clear water make it a good snorkeling spot to explore in the late morning. Pack your mask and snorkel before setting out.

At 276 m, Vardia is the highest point on Elafonisos; one of the island’s six hiking trails climbs to it from Vigla. Along the way, you’ll look down over Sarakiniko Beach. On a clear day, look for Kythira to the south: its Cape Frangos is just 8.5 km from the island. Set out late in the day, the recommended time for this hike, and bring water and a headlamp for the descent.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves
Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves

visits.text: Elatia Forest Village, 72 km north of Drama, occupies the former summer camp of Sarakatsani shepherds, known as Kalyvia Koutra. It is surrounded by Greece’s only forest of Norway spruce, a northern European species with some trees exceeding 30 meters. Every July 20, the Sarakatsani of Eastern Macedonia gather here. Fill up in Sidironero: it has the last gas station on the road.

The scent of resin gives way to that of water near Vathyrema, a stream lined with alders and willows. The mountain range reaches its highest point at Tsakalos, at 1,826 m, and a birch forest unique in Greece grows on its western flank at Magoula. Come in the fall, when the deciduous trees turn orange and red among the conifers.

activities.text: If you take just one hike in Elatia, choose the Stravorema Valley, east of the forest village, where the stream meanders through a meadow. The path following it downhill is suitable for hikers but remains rough even for a 4x4; it crosses the Megalo Rema forest road. Save some energy for the climb back up, and bring water, a windbreaker, and a picnic.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 6 Days: Philippi, Caves, and Elatia

visits.text: Eleusis calls for imagination, and that is its whole appeal: initiates were forbidden to reveal a word about the Mysteries celebrated here for nearly a millennium. Pass through the Greater and then the Lesser Propylaea and continue to the Telesterion, a columned hall whose foundations survive, designed by Ictinus, the architect of the Parthenon. Admission €10 including the museum; open except Tuesdays, 8:30 AM–3:30 PM in winter and until 8 PM from April through August.

If the Telesterion left you wanting more, the Archaeological Museum of Eleusis, in the heart of the site, puts faces to the cult. Built in 1889, it is among Greece’s earliest archaeological museums and displays large statues of Demeter and Asclepius in sections devoted to “the city around the sanctuary” and “the Great Mysteries.” Save it for the end of your visit, when the sun beats down on the ruins.

activities.text: Next, walk along the Eleusis waterfront, past Palaio Elaiourgeio, a former factory that hosted performances during the Aischylia Festival. Since 1975, this festival has honored Aeschylus, who was born in Eleusis, and the city was a European Capital of Culture in 2023, amid an oil refinery and ancient remains. If you visit from late August through September, check the festival program for performance venues.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis

visits.text: Spinalonga is the most history-laden place in all of eastern Crete. The Venetians began fortifying this 34-hectare rocky islet in 1579 to protect Mirabello Gulf—the fortress was so solid that even after the Ottomans took Crete in 1669, it held out another 46 years before falling in 1715. Entry is through a long dark tunnel that the lepers deported here between 1903 and 1957 nicknamed 'Dante's Gate.' For over 50 years, between 300 and 400 patients lived here as a community—with a baker, a barber, a priest. The last inhabitant, a priest, didn't leave the island until 1962. Allow 90 minutes to explore it fully. From Plaka (5-minute crossing) or from Elounda (20 minutes), boats depart regularly in high season.

Between Elounda and the peninsula, a causeway runs along the ancient city of Olous, submerged since antiquity. At low tide, you can see the mosaics of a 4th-century early Christian basilica with the naked eye—just beneath the surface, among the rocks. Olous was one of the great cities of Minoan and Classical Crete, mentioned as early as 3000 BC. With a mask and snorkel, the walls of the ancient acropolis are visible in shallow water. Swimming in this small lagoon sheltered from the wind is among the most pleasant in the region.

Elounda is the most comfortable base for this day. The resort is upscale—international resorts have set up here since the 1970s—but the waterfront of the original fishing village, the old salt pans between the town and the Olous peninsula, and the fish tavernas at the harbor are worth a detour beyond the hotels. The view of Spinalonga from the lagoon beaches is one of the finest in the region, especially late afternoon when golden light falls on the fortress walls.

Plaka is a fishing village 5 kilometers north of Elounda, facing Spinalonga. It's the closest departure point for the island (5-minute crossing) and also a remarkably preserved village with tavernas on the harbor, colorful boats, and nets drying in the sun. The grilled catch of the day here is impeccably fresh—Spinalonga's residents used to get their supplies here. Reserve a table for sunset over the island.

activities.text: The boat trip to Spinalonga is unmissable—but organize it early in the morning. By 10 AM in summer, groups land in waves and the vaulted passages become packed. Leaving Plaka at 8:30 or 9 AM, you stand a good chance of exploring the fortress in relative calm. Bring water and a hat: there's virtually no shade on the island.

After Spinalonga, swim in the lagoon between the Olous peninsula and Elounda: calm, shallow, and remarkably clear waters. With a mask and snorkel, you can search for the underwater ruins of the ancient city in shallow depths. The sandy beach on the way to the peninsula is one of the least crowded in the area.

For breakfast or brunch, order sfougato at a harbor taverna in Elounda: a thick omelet of zucchini with sheep's cheese and Cretan herbs. Several places serve it in the morning. In season, also look for clusters of octopus drying in the sun outside the Plaka tavernas—order it grilled, it's one of the best things you'll eat on this coast. A white Cretan Assyrtiko, mineral and dry, pairs perfectly with both.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Crete: Minoan Palaces, Gorges and Eastern Coast
Crete Road Trip: Agios Nikolaos, Elounda & Spinalonga

visits.text: The climb to the acropolis of Emporios is worth the effort. On Prophet Elijah Hill, the chief’s megaron and the altar of a temple of Athena survive above an excavated town dating to the early 8th century BC; the view stretches toward Asia Minor, Samos, and Ikaria. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.: climb before your swim, during the cooler hours in summer.

activities.text: The black pebbles of Mavra Volia crunch underfoot and grow hot in the afternoon sun. This beach beside the port of Emporios owes its color to ancient volcanic activity and stretches across three successive bays with deep, dark blue waters. There is no lifeguard: swim carefully, as the seabed drops away quickly, and bring water shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni

visits.text: Potamos beach at Epanomi, 35 km south of Thessaloniki, is a pointed sandy spit jutting into the Thermaic Gulf — its shape recalls Croatia's Zlatni Rat, but with far fewer people. On a clear day, Mount Olympus is visible across the gulf. What makes the site truly unusual is the wreck of a cargo ship that ran aground more than 50 years ago just off the shore: locals say Saint Antonios himself sank the vessel to protect the adjacent 550-hectare wetland, a refuge for migratory birds. Arrive in the morning for the calm before the Thessaloniki families descend.

The Epanomi wetland stretches across 550 hectares between dunes and marshes — a sanctuary for migratory birds, with herons, passing flamingos and numerous aquatic species. A trail runs along the lagoon from the east car park of the beach. The site is especially active in spring and autumn during the migrations.

activities.text: The wreck offshore is reachable by swimming or snorkelling from the beach — the water is clear and shallow here, making it an excellent snorkelling spot suitable for all levels. The west side of the bay, exposed to the wind, is popular with kitesurfers.

The Epanomi area is known for its vineyards: the soil and microclimate produce characterful dry whites. A short drive through the surroundings will take you past several wineries open for visits in summer. End the day at sunset facing the gulf — Olympus turns orange.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: The Theatre of Epidaurus is probably the most impressive surviving ancient theatre in the world. Built in the 4th or early 3rd century BC on the slopes of Mount Kynortion, it originally had 34 rows of seats for 6,200 spectators — the Romans added 21 more rows, bringing capacity to nearly 14,000. Walk to the centre of the orchestra (the circular slab on the ground) and drop a coin: you'll hear it from the back rows, 60 metres away. Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology discovered that the limestone seating filters out low-frequency background noise, allowing voices to travel without amplification. Arrive in the morning to avoid the groups that flood in after 10 am.

Five hundred metres from the theatre, the Sanctuary of Asklepios served for six centuries as the foremost healing centre in the Greek world. Pilgrims came from across the Mediterranean to practise incubation: sleeping in the abaton (a sacred dormitory) in the hope that the god of medicine would appear in their dreams and cure them. Votive stelae found on the site describe cures for hernias, blindness and paralysis that would make a modern doctor smile, yet testify to a thousand-year-old belief. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

The Tholos of Epidaurus, dated to around 360 BC, is the most mysterious building in the sanctuary. This circular building with a triple ring of columns (6 Doric columns on the outside, 14 Corinthian columns on the inside) had a function that no historian has yet clearly established — healing ceremonies, housing the sacred snakes of Asklepios, or an initiation ritual? Don't look for the answer in the museum: it isn't there. Take the opportunity to examine the perfectly preserved Corinthian capitals.

The Epidaurus Museum, at the foot of the site, displays sculptures and architectural elements discovered during the excavations. Don't miss the reconstruction models of the sanctuary — they give an idea of what this complex was like at its Hellenistic peak, far larger than what you've just walked through. Allow 45 minutes.

activities.text: Test the theatre's acoustics for yourself: from the central slab of the orchestra, whisper a sentence. Ask a companion to climb to the top rows - they will hear you clearly. If you are alone, drop a coin onto the slab. It is the experiment every guide has performed for centuries, and it never disappoints. The Epidaurus Festival stages ancient tragedies every Friday and Saturday evening from late June to late August: if you are there at that time, book in advance.

Swimming in the coves between Paleá Epídavros and Nea Epidavros, a few kilometres from the site: small pebble beaches framed by pine trees, with very clear water. The village of Paleá Epídavros has a fishing harbour with seafood tavernas whose terraces overlook the water — ideal for dinner.

Try gemista: tomatoes and peppers stuffed with rice, aromatic herbs and sometimes minced meat, slow-baked in the oven. It's a summer dish found everywhere in Peloponnese tavernas, much better than the name suggests. Pair it with a white assyrtiko — dry and mineral, with a sharp acidity that makes it perfect with stuffed vegetables.

days_plan.itin_title: Peloponnese Road Trip: Mycenae, Epidaurus & Olympia

visits.text: Eretria's archaeological site spreads beneath the modern town—you'll circulate among open-air ruins with a map available at the museum (€5). At the site's heart stands the Temple of Apollo Daphnephoros: its earliest phases date to the late 8th century BCE, with the Doric version of 520–490 BCE destroyed by the Persians during the 490 BCE sack. Foundation stones and sculptured pediment fragments remain. Bring water and a hat in summer—the site offers no shade.

The House of the Mosaics, dated to the 4th century BCE, stands among Greece's finest preserved Hellenistic dwellings. Its floors showcase pebble mosaics depicting mythological scenes—Nereids astride sea creatures, griffins, panthers. Check before visiting: travelers report it's occasionally closed early despite posted hours.

Eretria Archaeological Museum, founded in 1960 and expanded by the Swiss School of Archaeology in Greece (excavating since 1964), displays remarkable finds. Don't miss the sculptured group of Theseus and Antiope, attributed to the Athenian sculptor Antenor (circa 510 BCE), and a black-figure funerary amphora dated 560 BCE depicting Heracles battling Centaurs. Labels appear in Greek and French.

Eretria's ancient theater, with earliest phases from the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, is remarkable for an underground tunnel still visible—actors vanished through it for stage effects, a rarity of ancient theatrical machinery. Climb to the acropolis in the north for a commanding overview of the site and the coastline.

The Persians destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE—Darius sought vengeance for the city's aid to the Ionian Revolt. The male population was slaughtered; women and children were enslaved and deported to Persia. The city rebuilt swiftly, sent 600 hoplites to the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, flourished in the 4th century, then fell to the Romans in 198 BCE and was finally abandoned after 87 BCE. Marshland reclaimed it until 1824, when refugees from Psara resettled the site.

activities.text: Swimming along Eretria and Amarynthos beaches—a neighboring village to the east celebrated for seafood tavernas and grilled shellfish spreads. Waters here are calm and shallow, ideal for children. If you're motoring about, Amarynthos merits a detour for dinner: locals prefer its fish freshness to Eretria.

Sample fava: a creamy yellow-pea purée dressed with excellent olive oil, capers, and lemon juice. It's among Greece's finest yet most underappreciated mezzes. Pair it with local Savatiano white—a dry, fruity Euboean varietal that harmonizes beautifully with legumes.

Pasteli—sesame bars bound with thick honey—sells in waterfront shops and groceries. It's one of Greece's oldest candies, energy-dense and nourishing, perfect to carry for tomorrow's hike to Kymi or Karystos.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

visits.text: A square worthy of a capital on an island of 83.6 km²: Ermoupoli’s Miaouli Square is quite a surprise, paved with marble and planted with tall palm trees. The town hall designed by Ernst Ziller, whose construction began in 1876, overlooks it, while the statue of Admiral Andreas Miaoulis has stood watch since 1889. Return after dark to see the town hall’s illuminated facade.

Behind the town hall’s formal facade lies the Archaeological Museum of Syros, established in 1889. An entire room displays finds from Kastri and Chalandriani, prehistoric sites in the north of the island, while the final room explores the excavations of Christos Tsountas, complete with notebooks. Admission is €5; in summer, the museum closes on Tuesdays but stays open until 9 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

Velvet seats and a ceiling adorned with portraits of poets and composers: Ermoupoli’s Apollon Theater has all the features of a miniature La Scala. Italian architect Pietro Sampò designed it, and the auditorium opened on April 20, 1864; now restored, it seats 350 spectators. Check the schedule before you visit: the theater hosts operas and concerts, especially in summer, and attending a performance remains the finest way to experience it.

Agios Nikolaos Church marks Ermoupoli’s skyline with its brilliant blue dome: it is one of the two churches visible from the ferry. Built around 1870 with the support of Queen Olga, it houses a marble templon and throne carved in 1899 by Georgios Vitalis, an artist from Tinos. Remember his name: you will encounter his work again at the Museum of Tinian Artists in Pyrgos.

Next, walk along Vaporia, the neighborhood stretching behind Agios Nikolaos, where the shipowners and captains of Syros built neoclassical homes that seem to rest on the water. Some conceal frescoed ceilings and walls; several have been restored and turned into guesthouses. Walk here in the late afternoon, when the low sunlight illuminates the facades facing the sea.

The Industrial Museum of Ermoupoli is the most unexpected visit on Syros. Opened in 2000 in an 1888 building that first housed a lead shot foundry and then a paint factory from 1909, it tells the story of the island’s industrial past, when Ermoupoli, home to the Hellenic Steam Navigation Company founded in 1856, had yet to be eclipsed by Piraeus. Look for the first electric car built in Greece, and visit in the morning: the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. most days.

activities.text: Head down for a swim at Asteria, below Vaporia, when the heat rises. There is not a grain of sand: a concrete platform and a ladder leading into the sea, with lounge chairs, umbrellas, and bars, make this one of the city’s liveliest swimming spots. Combine it with your neighborhood walk, wearing your swimsuit under your clothes.

In Ermoupoli, no one leaves the island without a box of loukoumi: vendors even board the ferries to sell it. The first cauldron is said to have arrived on Syros in 1832 with artisans from Chios who came via Constantinople, and mastic was added to the recipe. Try halvadopita, another island sweet, too, and shop at the city’s long-established producers.

days_plan.itin_title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs

activities.text: You will leave Ikaria from Evdilos, the island’s second port and its capital from 1834 to 1912, where ferries depart for Piraeus. While you wait, explore the small harbor, its stately homes, and its stepped lanes. Check the departure time the day before: sailings vary by season and can be disrupted by wind.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches

activities.text: Yellow and red spheres, as smooth as giant pebbles, descend to the sea at Faraklo, on Cape Falakro. Locals call them “frangokefala,” or Franks’ heads; some see lava cooled by contact with water, others sandstone sculpted by erosion. From Propouli, a signposted dirt road leads to the parking lot, then a trail continues to the rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 4 Days: Ancient Cities, Flamingos, and Dunes

visits.text: Drakano Tower watches over Ikaria’s eastern tip: three stories of white marble, about 13 m tall, more than 50 m above the sea. On clear days, Fourni and Samos stand out offshore. Allow 25 minutes for the walk; open from 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m., except Sundays and Mondays.

activities.text: Local legend places Dionysus’s birth near Iero Beach, and a small sea cave still bears his name. This cove of sand and small pebbles remains uncrowded; a freighter wreck lies to the west. Bring a mask and snorkel, and reach the cove via the airport road or the trail down from Drakano.

If you’re traveling with young children, Faros Beach, the largest on the south coast, has a shallow rocky pool where the water stays warm. Pebbles alternate with sand, with large, smooth slabs underwater in places. Park for free a few meters from the village center, then have lunch at a seaside taverna.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches

visits.text: Isaac Komnenos, son of Emperor Alexios I, wanted to live and be laid to rest here: in 1152, he founded a monastery in Feres, of which the Church of Panagia Kosmosoteira survives. Beneath its five domes, military saints bear the features of his relatives, including his father. His typikon provided for 74 monks and barred eunuchs from entering. The church remains active: dress appropriately, and call 25550 22227 if the door is closed.

If you have an extra 30 minutes, head to the Feres aqueduct at the entrance to town, near a former Turkish bath complex. The large Kotza Tsesmes fountain is close by, and a waterfall spills into a pool near the center, beside an old bridge. The aqueduct is illuminated after dark.

activities.text: Endless reeds and still canal waters: a guided trip in a plava, the river’s traditional boat, takes you through the heart of the Evros Delta in two to two and a half hours. Dalmatian pelicans and spoonbills are often spotted around lagoons such as Drana. Expect to pay €10 to €15 per person, and book through the municipal tourist kiosk in Feres.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk

places.name: Fira

visits.text: Fira, Santorini's capital, clings 250 meters above the caldera. The caldera itself resulted from one of the largest eruptions in human history: around 1600 BC, the island's central volcano exploded and collapsed, creating a 12 km diameter crater now filled with sea. The multicolored cliffs - black basalt, red, white pumice - tell the stratigraphy of this catastrophe. If you're afraid of heights, walk carefully along the edges.

The Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira displays objects discovered during Akrotiri excavations - a Minoan city buried under volcanic ash around 1600 BC, comparable to Pompeii. The original frescoes from the city are among the finest in the Aegean Antiquity: fishing scenes, navigation, young men in action. Allow an hour for the visit.

Oia is Greece's most photographed village - its cave houses carved into the cliff, cobalt domes and flowered alleyways make it a worldwide postcard. Arrive early morning, before 9am, to see it almost deserted. Oia's Byzantine castle is the best viewpoint for sunset - plan to arrive 90 minutes early to find a spot.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is often compared to Pompeii: a Middle Bronze Age Minoan city, buried under meters of volcanic pumice around 1600 BC and preserved intact. Unlike Pompeii, no bodies were found here - the inhabitants had time to flee. The two-story alleyways, oil jars still in place, and house structures are protected by a massive covered structure. Allow 90 minutes.

Kamari beach, on the east coast, is Santorini's main black sand beach. This volcanic sand heats up very quickly in summer - wear shoes to walk to the water. The water is clear and quite deep quickly. The beach is long, well-equipped, with seaside tavernas.

Red Beach, west of Akrotiri, is a cove enclosed by bright red lava cliffs that plunge into a deep blue sea. Because of rockfalls and access restrictions, view it only from a distance and comply with any prohibition posted on site.

Pyrgos is the best-preserved medieval village on Santorini, perched at an elevation of 350 meters. Built around a 13th-century Venetian kastro, it has preserved its maze-like lanes and crenellated houses. The chapel at the top offers a 360° view over the entire island. It is far less crowded than Oia.

Megalochori is one of Santorini's most authentic villages, built in the 17th century by merchants and shipowners. Its main square with vaulted arches and small church is one of the island's most beautiful. Much less crowded than Fira or Oia, this is where you'll see the island as it was before mass tourism.

Imerovigli, between Fira and Oia, is nicknamed 'the balcony of the Aegean Sea'. Skaros Rock, a former 13th-century Venetian fortress partially collapsed into the sea during the 1956 earthquake, offers a 270° view over the Kameni islets and caldera - less crowded than Oia castle for sunset.

activities.text: In the evening, settle in Oia for sunset. It's the most famous in the Cyclades: in July-August, hundreds of people crowd the cliff edge. Go anyway, but arrive early and position yourself slightly back from the castle for an unobstructed view without fighting for space.

Santorini fava, yellow split pea puree grown on the island since antiquity and protected by PGI, has incomparable sweetness. Tomatokeftedes, fritters made from cherry tomatoes concentrated by volcanic sun, are worth trying as meze. You'll find both in all Fira and Oia tavernas.

Santorini's assyrtiko, a white grape variety grown in baskets close to the ground to protect it from the wind, produces a mineral, dry and slightly saline wine. Vines have thrived on the island's volcanic soils for centuries. Several estates offer tastings overlooking the caldera.

The Fira-Oia hike along the caldera is one of the most beautiful in the Mediterranean: 10.5 km on the cliff edge, between 250 and 350 meters height, with constant views over the 12 km diameter crater and volcanic islets at the center. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours with breaks. Start early morning in summer - midday heat on the volcanic stones is crushing. The trail passes through Firostefani and Imerovigli before reaching Oia.

Amoudi Bay, at the foot of Oia's cliffs accessible by 300 steps, is the island's most authentic spot for fish. A few fishing tavernas serve dried octopus, sea urchins and grilled fish at the water's edge. You can also dive from the rocks directly into the sea. Avoid going between noon and 3pm - the return climb in the heat is exhausting.

Boat excursion to Nea Kameni volcano in the caldera's center: shuttles depart from Fira's old port (accessible by 580 steps or funicular). On the islet, a trail climbs to the volcanic cone's summit at 150 meters - sulfurous fumaroles remind you the volcano remains active, its last eruption dating from 1950. You can then swim in neighboring Palaia Kameni's natural hot springs, slightly ferruginous and sulfurous water.

Wine tasting in Santorini is a unique experience: vines are cultivated in ground-level basket coils to protect from wind, a millennial technique unique here. The mineral, dry assyrtiko white is most renowned - but vinsanto, sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, is also worth experiencing. Several estates offer tastings with caldera views.

days_plan.itin_title: Santorini Road Trip: Caldeira, White Villages and Minoan Sites
Cyclades Journey: Athens, Santorini, Mykonos & Naxos
Cyclades Journey: Athens, Santorini, Mykonos & Naxos

visits.text: Agios Panteleimon Hill, above Florina, preserves the remains of a Hellenistic city founded in the 4th century BC and destroyed by fire in the early 1st century BC. You can make out house foundations, jars, hearths, and ironworking workshops. The site closes at 4 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays: make it your first stop.

The frescoes removed from Agios Achilleios in 1976 await you at the Archaeological Museum of Florina, near the train station. The displays span the Neolithic period at Armenochori through the Byzantine era, and the exhibition “Prespes: Monuments and Art” covers the 10th–18th centuries. Open from 8 AM to 7 PM except Tuesdays; admission is €5.

Chagall on the banks of the Sakoulevas, who would have thought? Founded in 1977, the Museum of Contemporary Art of Florina brings together more than 700 works, from Moralis and Tsoklis to foreign artists such as Chagall. Admission is free, but the hours are unusual: on weekdays, it opens only late in the day, and never on Mondays.

activities.text: Stroll along the Sakoulevas, the river that runs through Florina between neoclassical houses and cafés. Theo Angelopoulos shot several films in the city, including Ulysses’ Gaze and The Beekeeper; its gray riverbanks evoke something of his long takes. Finish at an outdoor table by the water while waiting for the Museum of Contemporary Art to open.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria, Prespes, and Nymfaio in 5 Days: Icons and Bears

visits.text: Frangokastello Fortress was built by the Venetians between 1371 and 1374 to keep order in the rebellious Sfakia region. The locals never accepted it and renamed it “Frangokastello”—the Castle of the Franks—as a sign of contempt. The rectangular plan with four corner towers still bears the coat of arms of the Lion of St. Mark above the entrance. In 1828, during the Greek War of Independence, 385 Greek fighters led by Hatzimichalis Dalianis were massacred here by the Ottomans. A persistent legend says that every year in May, on the battle's anniversary, the shadows of the dead soldiers—the Drosoulites, literally “dew men”—appear in the morning mist and parade before the castle. The phenomenon has been documented but never fully explained.

activities.text: Imbros Gorge is the southern coast's most accessible hiking route: the descent from the Askifou Plateau to the village of Komitades takes 2 to 3 hours. The walls reach up to fifty meters high in places and the vegetation is dense—a striking contrast to the coastal aridity. The hike is relatively easy, doable year-round.

Frangokastello beach stretches for about 500 m along the castle walls, with fine sand and a gentle slope into calm, shallow water that suits families. To the east, Orthi Ammos beach is wilder, with a rocky seabed suited to snorkeling. You can visit both in one afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: Drive uphill from Toxotes toward Imera and Achladas: about ten kilometers of paved switchbacks lead to the Nestos viewpoint, a wooden gazebo perched above the river’s meanders. On clear days, the view stretches as far as Thasos, and sometimes Limnos. Bring binoculars for birds of prey and take your time on the curves.

activities.text: Easy, but worth taking seriously: the Nestos Gorge trail starts in Galani and follows the east bank along an old railway workers’ path, a branch of the E6 European long-distance trail. The first 3.5 kilometers follow the river; Kromniko Spring is about 2 hours away. Never enter the railway tunnels on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Greek Thrace in 5 Days: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini

places.name: Galaxidi

visits.text: Galaxidi appears around a bend in the coastal road between olive trees and the Gulf of Corinth like a 19th-century print. This port of 1,700 inhabitants has two natural harbours and a collection of neoclassical houses built by ship captains who made their fortunes in the Mediterranean. In the 18th–19th centuries, Galaxidi had a fleet of 350 vessels trading as far as Marseille and the Black Sea – maritime power disproportionate to such a small town. The War of Independence of 1821 largely put an end to this. Today its cobbled alleys and softly coloured façades make it one of mainland Greece's most photogenic villages.

Galaxidi's Maritime Museum occupies a renovated former shipyard – excellent for understanding the port's history in a few well-designed galleries. The collection includes 19th-century sailing-ship paintings (Greece's largest selection), navigation instruments, travel journals and nautical charts. Outside the museum, the PeraPanta coastal promenade leads to the statue of a sailor's wife waving her handkerchief towards the sea – a melancholic image that encapsulates the village's history.

activities.text: The Gulf of Corinth coves below Galaxidi are calm and the water is clean. The coastal walk between the village's two ports (Hiriolakas and the main harbour) skirts small pebble beaches with views of the Byzantine islets opposite. If you're here on a Saturday, Amphissa's market 30 km away merits a morning detour before heading down to Galaxidi.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

map_keywords: Port of Galaxidi Gulf of Corinth

visits.text: Posidonia, also known as Della Grazia after the Catholic church of Santa Maria della Grazia, was a vacation retreat for wealthy Ermoupoli families in the 19th century. Their houses and neoclassical mansions still line the streets of the village in the southwest of the island. Park near the church and take a short loop walk.

Galissas is the busiest beach on Syros, and it’s easy to see why: a U-shaped cove, fine sand, and shallow water awarded Blue Flag status. The best view, though, is from above, at Agia Pakou Chapel, overlooking the entire bay. Bring a mask and snorkel to explore the cove.

activities.text: You’ll then head to Agathopes Beach, near Posidonia: sand, shallow water, and families with young children. The sea daffodils growing in the sand are protected, so don’t step on them. Offshore, the islets of Strongylo and Schinonisi mark the horizon; lounge chairs and a ramp into the sea make swimming easier.

The sun sinks into the sea opposite Kini’s small harbor, 9 km from Ermoupoli, silhouetting the boats moored in the bay. The village viewpoint is an excellent spot for sunset, near the bronze mermaid on the shore. Stay for dinner: tavernas known for their fish line the waterfront.

days_plan.itin_title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs

visits.text: Vathia is the ghost village of the deep Mani: a collective fortress perched on a hilltop, made up of stone tower houses packed so tightly together they form a continuous rampart against rival clans. Vathia had as many as 200 inhabitants in the 19th century; today a few houses have been restored, but it's the abandoned section that is most haunting. The atmosphere is unique — beauty and melancholy intertwined, and not a tourist in sight outside July and August.

Cape Tenaro is the southernmost point of mainland Greece. From the car park, walk 45 minutes along a coastal trail running between two seas: the Ionian Sea to the west and the Aegean to the east merge here. The ancients regarded this cape as one of the gates to the Underworld. You'll find the ruins of a 4th-century BC Temple of Poseidon and a small chapel built on its foundations. The white lighthouse stands 41 metres above the sea.

activities.text: The Diros Caves, 11 km from Aréopoli on the road to Gérolimenas, can currently be visited on a short boat section and in the land section. The boatman rows you past stalactites that almost touch the water. The total mapped network exceeds 14,700 metres. In summer, check visiting arrangements before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South

visits.text: Famous for having been blown up, the Gorgopotamos viaduct has seen no trains since 2018. On the night of November 25–26, 1942, Greek resistance fighters and British saboteurs brought down its spans; rebuilt in 1948, it measures 211 m long and 30 m high. Access is free, but there is no parking: park in the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 Days: Delphi, Hosios Loukas

visits.text: Grevena centers on two squares: the square by the Clock Tower, a downtown landmark, and Aimilianou Square, linked by a broad pedestrian street. At an elevation of about 530 m beside the Grevenitis River, the town has held the title of “City of Mushrooms” since 2007. Take a stroll in the late afternoon before sitting down to dinner.

Mushrooms everywhere, all made of wood: at Grevena Mushroom Park, on the northeastern edge of town along the road to Kozani, sculptures of local species line the paths. Every August, the park hosts the Panhellenic Mushroom Festival. Popular with families, it takes just under 1 hour to visit.

activities.text: Sit down for dinner at a taverna in Grevena: almost every dish features mushrooms, whether in pies, soups, pilaf, trahanas, or even a spoon sweet. More than 2,500 species have been recorded in the regional district, but only about ten make it onto plates. Ask for seasonal species; spring and fall are the best times for mushroom picking.

Our pick for the region’s most original souvenir: the mushroom products sold in Grevena. Producers’ stalls are filled with pickled, oil-packed, or dried mushrooms, liqueur, loukoumi, and even mushroom and truffle chocolates. Buy them on your last evening: a jar travels much better than a tray of fresh mushrooms.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena in 3 Days: Mansions and Fossils

visits.text: Gytheio is the capital of the eastern Mani and the former naval port of Sparta — the Spartans, who scorned the sea, needed a maritime outlet and established their arsenal here. The pastel façades with wrought-iron balconies descending towards the quay, the bustle around the fishing harbour and the tavernas that open at dawn for the fishermen make it one of the most authentic small towns in the Peloponnese. Stroll along the waterfront in the late afternoon when the light is golden.

The islet of Marathonisi (formerly known as Cranae) is linked to the port by a narrow causeway. It was here, according to Greek mythology, that Paris and Helen spent their first night of love before fleeing to Troy. On the island stands the Tzanetakis Tower, built in 1829, which now houses the Historical and Ethnological Museum of the Mani. The octagonal lighthouse at the tip of the island offers a fine view over the gulf.

The museum inside the town hall (1890), on the waterfront, displays archaeological finds from Gytheio and the Mani: ossuaries decorated with reliefs, engraved inscriptions, pottery and sculptures from the Roman period. It's a useful addition to the visit, helping you understand the commercial history of this town, which was one of the main trading centres of the Free Laconians under the Roman Empire.

Take a detour along the Mani coast road to the village of Vathia - one of the best preserved on the peninsula. Its medieval stone towers, built tightly against one another and now almost deserted, tell of the centuries of clan vendettas among the Maniot families, who protected themselves from their neighbours in this way. The road leading there is arid, rocky and spectacularly bare. Allow for a round trip within the day from Gytheio.

activities.text: Mavrovouni beach stretches for several kilometres near Gytheio - a long strip of fine sand with a view of the Laconian Gulf and the peaks of Taygetus in the background. The water is calm in the morning, ideal for a family swim. In the afternoon the sea breeze picks up and makes it a good kitesurfing spot. This is the beach used by Gytheio's residents: simple, authentic.

Synglino is the Mani's iconic cured meat — pork smoked over myrtle or orange wood and preserved in lard. Before the age of refrigeration, every Maniot household kept a supply. The harbour tavernas serve it as a starter, often alongside the orange-spiced sausage. Kakavia, a Mediterranean fish soup with saffron and lemon, is the other must-try for an evening on the quayside.

days_plan.itin_title: Laconia Road Trip: Sparta, Mystras & Monemvasia

visits.text: More modest than its larger counterpart in Constantinople, Hagia Sophia in Thessaloniki saves its finest sight for the dome. The current church dates to the 7th century; high above, a 9th-century mosaic of the Ascension depicts Christ surrounded by the Virgin, two angels, and the twelve apostles. A mosque from 1430 to 1912, it later returned to Orthodox worship. Visit between services with your shoulders and knees covered, and keep your binoculars handy for the dome.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: If you see only one church, choose Saint Demetrios, dedicated to the city’s patron saint. Rebuilt as a five-aisled basilica in 629–634, nearly destroyed by the great fire of 1917, and reconsecrated in 1949, it retains six ancient mosaic panels. Head down into the crypt, a former Roman bath where the saint is said to have been martyred in 303. The church is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; the crypt is closed Tuesdays and closes at 3 p.m. in winter (1 p.m. on Fridays).

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: In 2010, Oedipus Rex rang out in the theater of Hephaistia for the first time in approximately 2,500 years. Carved into the slope in the late Classical period, it was restored between 2000 and 2004 and once again hosts festivals and concerts. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays; last entry is 20 minutes before closing.

Hephaistia is named after the blacksmith god, and Aeschylus placed the first appearance of fire here, before Prometheus’s act. Around the theater, the sanctuary of the Great Goddess, the agora, pottery workshops, and thermal baths from the 4th century BC recall a busy port connecting Thrace, Macedonia, and the Hellespont. Allow 1 hour to walk between these remains and the theater.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 4 Days: Ancient Cities, Flamingos, and Dunes

visits.text: The name is misleading: the Heptapyrgion, the “fortress of seven towers,” has ten at the top of Ano Poli. The Ottomans called it Yedi Kule; converted into a prison in 1890, it held inmates until 1989, and rebetiko songs refer to it as Yedi Koule. Take bus 23 to the Eptapyrgio stop to arrive when it opens, at 8:30 a.m. in winter. Closed Tuesdays; admission €10, free on the first and third Sundays from November through March.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: Only one column remains standing, yet the Heraion of Samos is still staggering: the great temple begun under Polycrates measured 55 m by 108 m, with a peristyle of 155 columns around 20 m tall. The Byzantines quarried the rest for stone, sparing this shaft, probably as a landmark for sailors. Arrive at opening time, before the heat; hours vary by season, so check them the day before.

activities.text: You will then head back down to Ireo, a seaside village one kilometer from the sanctuary, where former fishermen's huts now house tavernas and cafés. Enjoy one last swim and lunch overlooking the water; Samos Airport is just a few kilometers away, between Ireo and Pythagoreio. Allow plenty of time before check-in.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 4 Days: Heraion, Manolates, and Potami Waterfalls

visits.text: At the Heraion of Perachora, ancient remains stand so close to the sea that they change your perspective on a sanctuary. Around the Temple of Hera, surviving structures include an L-shaped colonnade and a large cistern above a small cove. Come in the morning and wear closed-toe shoes for the descent over uneven ground.

Head up to Melagavi Lighthouse for a different perspective on the Heraion of Perachora. Set above the cliffs, the lighthouse overlooks the natural harbor around which the sanctuary was laid out. Stay on the permitted access route and enjoy the views from outside; this walk does not depend on the building being open.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: Plan to arrive at Knossos as soon as it opens at 08:00 – groups arrive from 10:00 onwards and the site quickly becomes stifling in summer. This Minoan palace built around 1900 BC and remodelled after an earthquake around 1700 BC covered more than 20,000 m² with some 1,300 rooms: administrative offices, sanctuaries, workshops and royal quarters, all linked by labyrinthine corridors that probably inspired the Minotaur myth. Pay close attention: the frescoes visible on site are copies; the originals are in the archaeological museum. British archaeologist Arthur Evans, who excavated the site from 1900 to 1935, reconstructed the palace in reinforced concrete – a highly controversial decision that explains the bright, somewhat artificial colours of certain areas.

Visit the Heraklion archaeological museum before or after Knossos – a combined ticket lets you enter both at a better rate. This museum, founded in 1883 and housed in a building whose renovation continued until 2014, is Greece's second most visited museum and holds the world's largest collection of Minoan objects. Don't miss the four highlights: the Snake Goddess in faience (around 1600 BC) discovered at Knossos, the black steatite rhyton shaped like a bull's head with rock-crystal eyes, the Bull-Leaping Fresco, and above all the Phaistos Disc – a fired clay disc discovered in 1908, covered with 242 signs arranged in a spiral, belonging to a script still undeciphered to this day.

The Koules fortress dominates the old harbour entrance, at the end of the jetty. Built by the Venetians between 1523 and 1540 on a site fortified since the 9th century, this massive Rocca al Mare was constructed to counter the Ottoman threat in the time of Suleiman the Magnificent. Its outer walls reach 9 metres thick. It reopened in 2016 with a permanent exhibition—including pieces brought up from the seabed by Cousteau's team in 1976. Climb to the terrace: the view over the harbour and city is Heraklion's best.

Push open the door of Saint Titus Cathedral in the city centre. This church dedicated to Crete's patron saint—Titus, disciple of Saint Paul—has a turbulent history: built in the Byzantine era, converted to a mosque under the Ottomans, it was returned to Christian worship in 1925. It houses a relic of Saint Titus, brought to Venice when the Ottomans took Crete in 1669 and returned to Heraklion in 1966.

Just beside the cathedral stands the Loggia, a Venetian edifice rebuilt in 1628 that served as a meeting place for Candia's nobility (Heraklion's former name). Now the town hall, this building with its Renaissance porticos perfectly illustrates Venice's imprint on the city. Spend a few minutes walking around it—the façade is one of the old town's most elegant.

If Knossos gave you Minoan Crete, the historical museum gives you everything else: Byzantium, Venice, the Ottomans and 20th-century Crete up to the Second World War. Don't miss the room devoted to El Greco – Dominikos Theotokopoulos was Cretan, born around 1541 in Fodélé, and the only work by him kept in Crete is here. Also look for the reconstruction of the library of Nikos Kazantzakis, the author of Zorba the Greek, born in Heraklion in 1883 – an intimate and moving room.

Make the detour to the Martinengo bastion, in the Venetian walls encircling the city – these ramparts rank among the best-preserved in the entire Mediterranean. You'll find the tomb of Nikos Kazantzakis, who chose his own epitaph: “I hope for nothing, I fear nothing, I am free”. You can climb certain sections of the ramparts; the view over the city from the wall walk is worth the effort.

Take a tour down 1866 Street, the liveliest covered market in the city, where locals actually do their shopping. You'll find aged graviera, fresh mizithra, mountain thyme honey, aromatic herbs and marinated olives—all at better prices than at the harbour. Plan to pass through in the morning: some stalls close around 14:00, especially at weekends.

If you have a car, an excursion to the palace of Phaistos (allow for a day trip from Heraklion) is well worth the journey. The second Minoan palace of Crete after Knossos, Phaistos is much less crowded and far more authentic: no concrete reconstruction here, just open-air ruins on a plateau overlooking the Messara plain, with Mount Psiloritis (2,456 m, Crete's highest peak) in the background. This is where the famous Phaistos Disc was found, now in Heraklion museum.

activities.text: Leave for Knossos first thing in the morning – allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours on site. Be sure to use an audio guide or hire a local guide: without explanations, it's very difficult to distinguish original ruins from Evans's concrete reconstructions, and the site loses much of its meaning. A guide will also stop you from missing the Royal Road, considered Europe's oldest paved road.

Follow up with the archaeological museum – ideally after Knossos, to see the originals of the copies you saw there. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes. A practical tip: buy the combined museum + Knossos ticket, valid for 3 days – you save on both admissions and avoid the queue at the museum ticket office.

In the evening, head back towards the old Venetian harbour for golden hour. The tavernas lining the harbour serve seafood and grilled fish facing the illuminated fortress. If you arrive before sunset, walk to the jetty's end: the view over the city and the hinterland mountains is striking.

Take advantage of your Cretan evening to taste dakos, the cornerstone of local cuisine: a barley rusk soaked in olive oil, topped with fresh tomato and feta, scattered with oregano. Accompany it with a glass of raki (or tsikoudia), the local eau-de-vie distilled from grape pomace—served chilled and often offered at meal's end.

The morning in Heraklion is ideal for leisurely exploring the old town streets around Venizelou Square, with its Morosini fountain from 1628—locals simply call this spot 'Lions Square' because of the carvings on the old basin. The surrounding cafés are perfect for a Greek coffee while watching the morning buzz before hitting the road.

If you make the excursion to Phaistos, plan to stop en route at Agia Triada, just 3 km from the palace. This small Minoan site has yielded some of the finest works in Heraklion museum, including the Agia Triada Sarcophagus and the Harvester Vase. Allow 30 to 45 minutes on site.

Cretan vineyards merit a stop: indigenous grape varieties like vidiano (aromatic white with notes of citrus and white flowers) or kotsifali (fruity, sweet red) are found practically only on the island. If you pass through the Messara plain on the way to Phaistos, several wineries offer tastings – ask at your hotel for current recommendations.

In Heraklion, taste kalitsounia, little turnovers made with thin pastry and filled with mizithra and aromatic herbs. They come in both sweet versions – with honey and cinnamon – and savoury ones. Town-centre bakeries generally have them at all hours.

visits.text: A beardless Christ, rare for the period, fills the apse of Hosios David, the former church of Latomou Monastery. This late 5th-century mosaic, known as the Vision of Ezekiel, surrounds him with the prophets Ezekiel and Habakkuk; legend has it that it lay hidden beneath plaster and an oxhide until an earthquake revealed it. The visit is short: set aside ten minutes facing the apse. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: Austere outside, radiant within: the katholikon of Hosios Loukas reveals its colored marble and mosaics to those who step inside. Built around 1011 to house the relics of the hermit Luke, who died in 953, this domed octagonal church became a model for others; its mosaics are among the best preserved from the Macedonian Renaissance, despite the loss of the dome’s Pantocrator. Arrive before noon: last admission is at 3:10 p.m.

The Church of the Theotokos, next to the katholikon, is the older of the two, dating to the second half of the 10th century. The Thebes Museum identifies it as Greece’s first four-column cross-in-square church, with a richly decorated brick facade. In the narthex, look for the Archangel Michael appearing to Joshua: the monastery’s oldest wall painting.

Cool air and dim light greet visitors descending into the crypt of Hosios Loukas, beneath the katholikon. The saint’s original tomb rests against the north wall; surrounding it, 11th-century frescoes display some forty medallion portraits, cleaned in the 1960s. Let your eyes adjust for a few moments before looking for the faces.

Finish at the former refectory of Hosios Loukas, restored to house a collection of Byzantine sculptures that has been on display since 1993. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990 alongside Daphni and Nea Moni of Chios, the monastery was nevertheless damaged and looted during World War II. Allow €10 for full-price admission, and take time to look at the complex’s bell tower, monastic cells, and towers.

days_plan.itin_title: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 Days: Delphi, Hosios Loukas

visits.text: If the hydrofoil from Poros drops you off around 10 a.m., start at the Monastery of the Dormition, whose marble bell tower with a clock watches over Hydra's harbor. Built in the mid-17th century and rebuilt by Venetian architects after the earthquake of 1750, it holds the tomb of Lazaros Koundouriotis in its courtyard. Its small ecclesiastical museum, housed in the former prison, displays the icon of the “Unfading Rose” (1774). Open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from April to mid-November, except Mondays.

An admiral's heart rests in a silver urn at the Historical Archives Museum of Hydra: that of Andreas Miaoulis, master of the fireships of the War of Independence. Figureheads, flags, and weapons recall how Hydra outfitted around 150 ships against the Ottomans. On the waterfront, the museum opens daily from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. (€8). In late June, the Miaoulia festivities reenact the burning of an Ottoman fleet at sea, complete with fireworks.

One house is enough to grasp the wealth of Hydra's shipowners: the Historic House of Lazaros Koundouriotis, on the western side of the harbor. Built in the late 18th century, it belonged to the island's richest captain, who gave his entire fortune to the War of Independence; since 2001, it has been a branch of the National Historical Museum. Landscapes by Panayiotis Tetsis hang upstairs, with paintings by the Vyzantios family in the former cellars. Open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., March 25 through October 31 (€10).

activities.text: You’ll follow Hydra's coastal path west, past the cannons of the 18th-century bastions guarding the harbor entrance. There are no cars or motorcycles—the law prohibits them—and not even a bicycle: donkeys and mules pass walkers along the way. Fishing boats line the shore at Kamini; Vlychos, less than 1 hour away on foot, offers gray pebbles and Agia Paraskevi Chapel on its rock. Swim, wait for sunset, then return by water taxi.

A peaceful place of prayer, yet once a hero's prison: Theodoros Kolokotronis was held for four months at the Monastery of Prophet Elijah. Founded in 1813 by thirteen monks from Mount Athos, it overlooks Hydra's harbor at an elevation of around 500 m, reached after an hour and a half of climbing through the pines. Set out at dawn on the last morning and aim for a late-morning or afternoon ferry: the island has no springs, so bring your own water.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands in 3 Days: Aegina, Poros, and Hydra

visits.text: Ierapetra holds a title few cities can claim: Europe's southernmost, nicknamed 'the bride of the Libyan Sea.' Its position at the southern tip of Crete's isthmus has made it a strategic crossroads since antiquity—the ancient city of Hierapytna was already famous in the 3rd century BC for its piratical tendencies, before being destroyed by the Romans in 67 BC. Climb up to Kales Fortress, rebuilt in 1626, for a view over the fishing harbor—allow 30 minutes. And if you want a local oddity: Ierapetra is also one of Crete's wealthiest towns, thanks to the 13 square kilometers of greenhouses supplying all of Greece with off-season vegetables.

Twelve kilometers offshore from Ierapetra, the island of Chrissi—'the golden island'—is a protected, uninhabited nature reserve, except for a few seasonal caretakers. It's famous for its forest of two-hundred-year-old Lebanon cedars, the only one in Europe, and for its beaches of white sand and intensely turquoise waters. Facing an influx of 200,000 visitors per year, the Greek government imposed access restrictions in summer starting in 2022—prefer May-June or September-October to find it nearly empty.

Wander down into the alleyways of Kato Mera, Ierapetra's old town: a medieval quarter of narrow lanes and dead-ends leading to the fishing harbor. You'll find the Ottoman mosque, a former Christian church converted under Turkish rule, and 'Napoleon's House'—an 18th-century dwelling where, according to local legend passed down since 1798, Bonaparte spent one night during his Egyptian expedition. Undocumented, but locals will tell you the story with infectious pride.

The Archaeological Museum of Ierapetra is small, calm, and often empty—the anti-Heraklion. You'll find collections spanning the Minoan era through the Greco-Roman period: amphorae, decorated sarcophagi, statuettes, and ceramics testifying to Hierapytna's importance in antiquity. Ideal for an hour mid-day, before the Chrissi excursion or after.

If you have time at the end of the day, the coastal road between Ierapetra and Makrygialos offers several wild, quiet beaches, particularly around Agia Fotia. You can also take this direction if you are heading to Sitia Airport (56 km, about 1 hour 5 minutes) or to Heraklion for an international flight (allow at least 1 hour 45 minutes; set off in the middle of the morning so you are not pressed for time).

activities.text: The boat trip to Chrissi Island is the day's highlight in Ierapetra. Book the morning crossing (departure around 10 AM) to maximize your time on the island. Once ashore, follow the marked trails to the cedar forest—the scent of resin beneath the centuries-old trees, with the turquoise sea glittering between the trunks, is striking. Belegrina Beach, covered in a carpet of bleached fossil shells, is a unique natural curiosity. Bring your lunch: the island's only taverna is rudimentary.

Walking exploration of the old town: start from Kales Fortress, then into the alleyways of Kato Mera, the Ottoman mosque, Napoleon's House, the 17th-century Venetian fountain, and the lanes leading to the waterfront. The waterfront promenade runs along a long beach of gray-gold sand to the modern neighborhoods—the perfect spot for a final Cretan swim late in the day.

For dinner, settle into a waterfront taverna and order chtapodi krasato: octopus simmered slowly in red wine with onions and herbs until it's tender—the house specialty at most local establishments. Finish with loukoumades, fried doughnuts served hot and drizzled with honey, dusted with cinnamon. Tsikoudia (Cretan raki) usually arrives unbidden as an end-of-evening digestif.

Return to the airport: if you are flying from Sitia (a small airport with seasonal flights to Athens and a few European destinations), allow about 56 km and 1 hour 5 minutes' drive from Ierapetra. For an international flight from Heraklion, allow at least 1 hour 45 minutes; leave in the middle of the morning to avoid rushing. The faster northern coastal road passes through Agios Nikolaos.

Grand Tour of Crete: Minoan Palaces, Gorges and Eastern Coast

visits.text: A seaside resort below, an ancient city above: in Ierissos, the ramparts of Akanthos still stand 8 m high in places. Founded around 655 B.C. by settlers from Andros, the city welcomed Xerxes in 480 B.C. and helped dig his canal; its necropolis, excavated since 1973, came to light when a bulldozer broke through sarcophagi. From the beach, look for the remains of the old harbor’s quay.

If you are looking for the Canal of Xerxes between Nea Roda and Tripiti, do not look for water: this Persian engineering work, 2 km long and 30 m wide, dug from 483 to 480 B.C. across the Athos isthmus, lies beneath sediment. Only a small valley in the center of the isthmus reveals its course. Stop at Provlakas, on Nea Roda Beach: the canal began here, and ancient walls lie underwater.

activities.text: Here, they call them “karnagia”: the shipyards of Ierissos once ranked among the most important in Greece. In the last century, more than 100 people worked in the four major yards; today, wooden hulls are still shaped in a few sheds, while others are on the verge of collapse. The town itself was rebuilt after the 1932 earthquake. Observe the workshops from the street, then try fish from the harbor at a taverna.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages, Aristotle, and Mount Athos

visits.text: A better introduction than a harborside café, the Archaeological Museum of Igoumenitsa puts Thesprotia in perspective as soon as you step off the ferry. Opened in late 2009, it brings together more than 1,600 objects, from the Middle Paleolithic to the Roman era, with an emphasis on the Hellenistic period. Allow 1 hour: it is a 30-minute walk from the new port terminal and is closed on Tuesdays.

Pines, old walls, and the city’s rooftops at your feet: Igoumenitsa Castle crowns a low hill southwest of the center. Its earliest defenses probably date back to Roman times; the Venetian admiral Morosini partly destroyed it in 1685, and Ali Pasha repaired it in 1798. Allow 30 minutes for the south wall facing the harbor, the best-preserved section with its cannon embrasures.

days_plan.itin_title: The Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Parga, Acheron, and Nicopolis

visits.text: Take the boat from the dock facing the fortress—the crossing takes five minutes and departures are regular. Nisi Island, in the middle of Lake Pamvotis, is smaller than it appears but brings together several Byzantine monasteries and a gripping history: it was in Agios Panteleimon monastery that Ali Pasha took refuge in 1822, pursued by Ottoman troops who had withdrawn the sultan's trust in him. He was executed there at 82, and his decapitated body was buried within the walls. His head was sent on a silver platter to Constantinople. Walking around the island takes 20 minutes.

Ioannina fortress occupies a rocky promontory jutting into Lake Pamvotis—three of its four sides are surrounded by water, making it a naturally defensible position. Justinian laid its first stones in the 6th century; Ali Pasha almost entirely rebuilt it in the early 19th century, completing work in 1815. He made it what you see today. Stroll through the old town's alleys within the walls: at the entrance, by the plane tree where Turks tortured rebels, cafés and silversmiths' shops coexist with the remains of Ali Pasha's palace. One of the few Ottoman town centers in Greece that are still inhabited.

In the fortress's northeast citadel, don't miss the Aslan Pasha mosque—built in 1618 on a Byzantine church's site after the Christian population's expulsion. It now houses the municipal ethnographic museum, documenting the coexistence of Ioannina's three communities: Christian, Muslim and Jewish. What few know is that the city was long one of the great Sephardic Jewish communities of the Balkans. The costumes, silver jewelry and weapons on display give a concrete image of what the city was before the 20th century.

Five km from the center, Perama Cave merits the detour. Discovered by chance in 1940 by villagers seeking shelter during the war, it extends over a kilometer of galleries covering 14,800 m². Archaeologists found the skeleton of a cave bear there—the species is extinct, no worries. Visits are guided group tours (Greek and English), lasting about 45 minutes. Bring a sweater: even in midsummer, the 15°C temperature inside can come as a surprise. Last entry around 5:30 PM.

Head down to the old bazaar's alleys, around the fortress, and step into a silversmith's workshop if you find one open. Ioannina was nicknamed “the city of silversmiths”—an Epirote tradition dating at least to the Ottoman era, with a few artisans still practicing its traditional techniques. The Silversmithing Museum, inside the citadel, displays worked silver pieces from the Ottoman period giving an idea of the region's craftsmanship. The bazaar street is also the best place to buy homemade pita to go.

activities.text: Late in the day, settle on a lakeside terrace by Lake Pamvotis and order local fish: smoked eel, carp, trout—fishermen directly supply the lakefront tavernas. Ioannina is also known for its frogs, exported as far as France. Stay until sunset: the lake reflects the mountains turning violet, and the fortress silhouette stands out against the water.

The walk on the fortress ramparts lets you follow the walls on the lakeside with spectacular views over Pamvotis and the mountains beyond. In the evening, the reflection of the city lights on the water is striking. The café in the elevated Its Kale acropolis is a good place to stop.

Bakaliaros skordalia, fried cod served with a garlic and potato purée, is the signature fried dish of everyday Greek cooking. You'll find it in traditional tavernas around the fortress, often on Fridays—a legacy of the Orthodox calendar.

Ioannina pita differs from mass-produced flaky pitas: a thick pie of homemade phyllo dough, filled with spinach and local cheeses, baked in a wood-fired oven. Each taverna has its recipe. It's THE specialty, wrapped in paper and eaten standing or sitting by the lake.

Epirus tsipouro differs from Thessaly's by the total absence of anise: it's dry, almost neutral, and lets the mezze take center stage. In kafeneia (traditional cafés) around the fortress, you'll be served a small carafe accompanied by a few slices of cheese and mountain charcuterie—a local institution.

visits.text: Less monumental than Corinth, the Sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia calls for a little more attention. Its remains are a reminder that the isthmus also hosted ancient athletic contests, as well as travelers passing through. Start with the site’s information panels to make sense of the foundations, then head to the nearby museum before it closes.

Pictures made of glass rather than paintings on canvas: that is the surprise awaiting you at the Archaeological Museum of Isthmia. Its panels come from the ancient port of Cenchreae, while other objects shed light on the Sanctuary of Poseidon. Save the canal for after the museum: the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

At 6,343 meters long, the Corinth Canal cuts a channel through the land that is easier to grasp from a bridge than on a map. Completed in 1893, it connects the Saronic Gulf and the Gulf of Corinth. Park in a permitted area, head to the pedestrian walkway, and do not count on seeing a boat pass through.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

places.name: Ithaca

visits.text: Vathy, the capital of Ithaca, is a small town of 1,700 people tucked at the end of a horseshoe-shaped gulf — one of the best-sheltered natural anchorages in the Ionian Sea. Most of the Venetian-style buildings were rebuilt to their original designs after the 1953 earthquake; one of the painter El Greco's earliest works is said to be in the local cathedral. Stroll along the harbour, stop at one of the quayside tavernas — the atmosphere is gentle, far from mass tourism.

The Archaeological Museum of Vathy holds over 1,000 objects unearthed on the island, covering the Mycenaean through Roman periods. The star exhibit is a pottery fragment inscribed with the name “Odysseus”, found during excavations at the Alalkomenes site. There is also a small bronze sculpture that some identify as depicting Odysseus himself, along with Mycenaean votive tripods. Admission is free. The museum is closed on Tuesdays.

Aetos Hill, 4 km from Vathy, rises to 380 metres. From the church of Aï Giorgios, a steep trail climbs in 20 minutes to the ruins of the ancient city of Alalkomenes — this is where Heinrich Schliemann dug in 1868 and 1878, convinced he had found the palace of Odysseus. Modern archaeologists are more cautious: the fortifications date from the 7th century BC, after the events of the Odyssey. But the view from the top, over both coasts of the island and Kefalonia across the water, is worth the trip on its own.

Kathara Monastery stands at around 600 metres above sea level, on the mountain Homer called Nirito. Founded in the late 17th century, it offers a 360° panorama of Vathy, the southern part of the island and Kefalonia. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Even if the monastery itself does not interest you, make the trip for the view - it is among the most beautiful in all the Ionian Islands.

The Cave of the Nymphs, known locally as Marmarospilia, lies a few kilometres north of Vathy. According to the Odyssey, this is where Odysseus hid the gifts of the Phaeacians on his return. Its interior is closed to the public: do not plan to enter to see the stalactites or the ancient altar. To explore Vathy's links with the Odyssey without relying on this access, walk along the harbour and visit the archaeological museum of Vathy, which displays finds from the island.

activities.text: Ithaca is tailor-made for gentle hiking. Signposted trails connect the villages through olive groves and scrubland of kermes oak. The island is home to just 3,000 people, and the paths are often deserted — one of the most authentic experiences in the Ionians. Ask in Vathy for details on the marked routes.

Revithokeftedes are chickpea fritters laced with fresh herbs, typical of the Ionian Islands. In Ithaca, they're usually served with yoghurt or skordalia (garlic mash). A simple, delicious vegetarian starter — one of the best things to order in a harbourside taverna in Vathy.

The village of Stavros, in northern Ithaca, is worth a stop: its central square has a bust of Odysseus and a model of his “idealised” castle, while a small archaeological museum displays finds from excavations conducted by the British School of Archaeology in the 1930s. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Do not confuse it with the museum in Vathy - this one focuses on the north of the island and its connections with the Odyssey.

visits.text: If one visit can change how you see the city, it is the Jewish Museum of Thessaloniki on Agiou Mina Street. Opened in 2001 in a 1904 building designed by Vitaliano Poselli, it displays gravestones from the destroyed old Jewish cemetery and dedicates a room to victims of the Holocaust: some 49,000 of the city’s Jews were deported to Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen. Check the museum’s website for opening hours before visiting.

visits.text: If you visit only one sanctuary on Lemnos, choose the Kabirion, set on two terraces above the sea. Each year, mystery rites open to both free men and slaves were celebrated here after sunset for nine days. The Hellenistic initiation hall had twelve Doric columns. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: The Cave of Philoctetes opens beneath the Kabirion, at the end of a narrow path leading down to the shore. According to myth, the Greeks abandoned the wounded hero here on their way to Troy, leaving him to suffer for ten years before they returned. A wide opening lets the sea enter the cave: wear shoes with good traction for the descent.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 4 Days: Ancient Cities, Flamingos, and Dunes

visits.text: The view is worth the climb when the sky is clear: Kaimaktsalan, also known as Voras, rises above 2,500 meters on the border with North Macedonia. The road leads to the ski resort, while the summit is reached on foot. Check the weather and road access; do not try to reach the summit by car.

activities.text: If the trail is dry and the weather is stable, hike to the Profitis Ilias Chapel on Kaimaktsalan. This border monument commemorates the fighting of World War I. Plan a round-trip hike from the ski resort, and bring hiking footwear and a warm layer; give up on the summit if there is snow, fog, or a thunderstorm.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: Perched on the hill above Kalamata, the Castle of Villehardouin is well worth the climb. Built after 1205 by Geoffrey I of Villehardouin on the site of an ancient acropolis, it was the family's fief for two centuries before passing to the Venetians and then the Turks. The ruins are not spectacular, but the panoramic view over the Gulf of Messenia and the peaks of Taygetus rising behind the city is worth the detour on its own. Allow an hour for a leisurely stroll.

The Archaeological Museum of Messenia, housed in the former municipal market hall, has an attractive modern exhibition design. You can follow the region's history from prehistory to the Byzantine era through finds from Kalamata and across Messenia — pottery, mosaics, gold jewellery including a Mycenaean ring dating to the 16th century BC. The English information panels are well done. Allow 45 minutes.

The church of Agioi Apostoloi (Holy Apostles) holds a story of a founding moment: it was here, in this 13th-century Byzantine church, that the oath of the Greek Revolution was sworn on 23 March 1821 — two days before the date recorded in official history books. The façade is unassuming, but the interior retains an intact Byzantine chancel and an atmosphere of contemplation rarely found in such a lively city.

Kalamata's seafront stretches for 2.5 km along the Messenian Gulf. Stroll here at the end of the day, when the low light gilds the neoclassical façades - you can make out German, Italian and Venetian influences in the buildings of the old town. Every Wednesday and Saturday morning, Kalamata hosts one of the finest markets in the region: vegetables, cheeses, dried figs and local olives abound.

activities.text: Kalamata olives have held PDO status since the 1990s — their oblong shape, fleshy texture and deep purple colour set them apart from all other varieties. The region also produces extra-virgin olive oil from the Koroneiki variety, prized for its high antioxidant content. Ask at the delicatessens in the market or at nearby farms for a tasting — you'll surely leave with a few bottles in your luggage.

Kalamata market (Wednesday and Saturday mornings) is one of the richest food markets in the Peloponnese. Messenia is one of the most fertile areas of the country: you will find dried figs, Taygetus honey, pasto (local smoked pork) and, of course, the famous black olives. Arrive early for the atmosphere and for the best pick.

Try Kalamata's pasteli — a dense, crunchy bar of toasted sesame seeds and honey that Greeks have been making since antiquity. Local pastry shops also offer imam baildi, aubergines stuffed with tomato and onion and baked in olive oil until meltingly soft, and the famous marinated olives served with feta. Dinner on the terrace of a waterfront taverna makes for a perfect evening.
