visits.text: In 433 BC, around 270 ships from Corinth, Corcyra, and Athens clashed in these waters, with the Corcyrean fleet based in the Sybota islands. From Sivota’s harbor, the bay looks peaceful today, guarded by four uninhabited islets. Stroll along the waterfront and negotiate your water taxi fare: expect around ten euros per person, depending on the distance.

activities.text: You can reach Bella Vraka in 15 minutes on foot from central Sivota, then wade across the sandbar stretching toward the islet of Megalo Mourtemeno. The shallow water comes up to your knees, making it ideal for families. There is no café on-site: bring water and snacks, and arrive early in the height of summer.

Pisina, nicknamed Blue Lagoon, looks like an emerald pool nestled between Sivota’s islets. Water taxis and small rental boats head there daily from the harbor, making it possible to combine several coves. Bring a mask and snorkel: the neighboring inlets lend themselves to kayaking and leisurely exploration.

If you prefer to stay on dry land, Megali Ammos offers Sivota’s well-equipped beach experience: golden sand, deep, clear water, and water sports. Its neighbor Mikri Ammos offers much the same on a smaller scale. Save this swim for the afternoon, before driving to Parga.

days_plan.itin_title: The Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Parga, Acheron, and Nicopolis

visits.text: Strabo already described Eresos as perched on a hill beside the sea, and its acropolis still overlooks the harbor of Skala Eresou. The visit takes in pre-Classical walls, the ruins of a medieval castle, and the fifth-century Agios Andreas Church with its mosaic floor. Admission is free: climb up in the morning, before the sun heats the hillside.

Housed in a former stone schoolhouse, the Archaeological Collection of Eresos stands beside St. Andrew’s Basilica. A rare statuette of Cybele, a terracotta larnax, and Ionic and Doric capitals tell the story of Sappho’s city, from the Late Bronze Age to the early Christians. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., closed Tuesdays; admission is €5.

activities.text: Sappho’s hometown, Skala Eresou nevertheless revolves above all around its beach: nearly 3 km of Blue Flag dark sand stretching from the small harbor to the western cape. Since the 1980s, lesbian travelers have made it one of their favorite destinations, and cafés and beach bars line the waterfront. Swim in the late morning before the long drive to Kalloni.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Mytilene, Molyvos and the Petrified Forest

visits.text: Panagia Gorgona Chapel seems perched on the rock at the end of the jetty in Skala Sykamias. It inspired Stratis Myrivilis’s novel “The Mermaid Madonna,” published in 1949, which shares the chapel’s name in Greek. Avoid August 15, its feast day, if you are looking for peace and quiet.

activities.text: For lunch, head three kilometers uphill to Sykamia, the birthplace of Stratis Myrivilis, known for its elegant homes and ouzo taverns, many of them a century old. Order hahles, little cups made from trahanas and filled with tomato, feta, and olive oil, the local specialty. Finish with almond candies before taking the road to Molyvos.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Mytilene, Molyvos and the Petrified Forest

visits.text: Skiathos town is a lively little capital whose cobbled lanes wind their way down to the double harbour. It's the most tourist-oriented island in the Sporades — in summer the atmosphere is cosmopolitan and the nightlife is intense, with bars open until dawn on Papadiamanti Street. If you prefer peace and quiet, avoid July–August or arrive in the morning to see the sights before the influx of cruise ships.

The Bourtzi peninsula, linked to the old harbour by a short footbridge, holds a 13th-century Venetian fortification built by the Ghisi brothers to defend the island from pirates. Century-old trees cover the headland, making it a pleasant spot in the evening — concerts are sometimes held here in summer. The view across both harbours of Skiathos from the tip of the peninsula is one of the most photogenic on the island.

Evangelistria Monastery, founded in the 18th century on a hillside 4 km above town, is the most historically charged site on Skiathos. It was here, in September 1807, that the first Greek flag — a white cross on a blue field — was designed, woven, blessed and raised in the presence of the revolutionary hero Theodoros Kolokotronis. The monks who still live in the monastery produce wine, olive oil and honey. The museum housed in the old olive press displays the loom that, according to tradition, was used to weave that first flag. Take the marked trail from town rather than the road — it's more enjoyable and shorter.

Kastro is the former fortified capital of Skiathos, perched on a rocky headland in the north of the island. The inhabitants took refuge here in the 14th century to escape pirate raids and only moved back down to the coast after Greek independence, in 1829. A few churches still cling to the cliffs, including the chapel of the Nativity of Christ, along with a striking view over the Aegean Sea. It can be reached on foot (3 km of track, then a path) or by boat from the port. By car from the overnight stop, the road ends before the site: the last stretch is done on foot.

The Papadiamantis Museum, at number 12 on the street of the same name near the port, occupies the birthplace of Alexandros Papadiamantis, Greece's greatest 19th-century novelist, born on Skiathos in 1851. The two-storey house retains its period interior virtually intact: original furniture, personal library, everyday objects. The cave known as the 'Murderess's Cave' near Lalaria takes its name from one of Papadiamantis's short stories. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30 am to 1:30 pm and 5:15 pm to 8 pm.

Koukounaries, around twenty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, is the picture-postcard beach of Skiathos - ranked among the most beautiful in Greece, with 1,200 metres of fine golden sand edged by an Aleppo pine forest protected under Greek law. Behind the beach lies the wetland of Lake Strofilia, a refuge for rare migratory bird species such as swans and herons. In high season, sunbeds are snapped up early in the morning - arrive before 9am or come in the late afternoon.

Lalaria is Skiathos's show-stopping beach: reachable only by boat from the old harbour, it curves in a half-moon of round white pebbles beneath sheer limestone cliffs that plunge into water of an almost unreal blue-green. A natural arch carved into the rock is the focal point of every photograph of the island. Boats run daily from the port, but if the northerly winds pick up the crossing is cancelled. Bring water and food — there's nothing on site.

The sea caves near Lalaria are every bit as worthwhile as the beach itself. The Blue Cave (Galazia) owes its name to the extraordinary colour of the water inside when the sun hits — reflections off the limestone walls produce an almost supernatural blue glow. The Dark Cave (Skotini), roughly 20 metres long, can only be entered by small boat because the opening is so narrow. Most excursions to Lalaria include a visit to these caves.

Troulos, 8 km west of town, is a family-friendly beach with shallow water and a quiet atmosphere. Pines reach down to the sand, and a few tavernas serve grilled fish. Facing it is the cluster of Troulonisia islets. It's the ideal beach with children if Koukounaries feels too crowded.

activities.text: Papadiamanti Street, the main artery of Skiathos town, is the hub of local life in the evening: craft shops, tavernas with outdoor tables, and ouzo bars. Stroll along it from 7 pm when the locals start to come out — the summer crowds don't descend until after 9 pm. It's also the best spot to order a mezze platter: taramosalata, tyrokafteri, grilled octopus.

Astakomakaronada, the signature dish of the Sporades, is spaghetti with fresh lobster in a lightly spiced tomato sauce. You'll find it at almost every taverna along Skiathos's old harbour — ask whether the lobster was caught that day, as the fishermen deliver directly in the morning. It's one of the island's best combinations of quality and freshness.

Tsipouro, a Greek spirit distilled from grape pomace, is the Sporades' drink of choice. On Skiathos it's served cold, in small glasses, alongside mezze — grilled octopus, feta, marinated olives. The monks at Evangelistria produce an artisanal version available from the monastery shop.

Book a half-day boat trip from Skiathos old harbour to Lalaria and the sea caves — it's the simplest and most enjoyable way to get there. Departures are usually at 9 am or 10 am. In July–August, book the day before: places sell out fast. Options include swimming and snorkelling stops in coves that are impossible to reach on foot.

Revithada, a thick soup of chickpeas slow-baked with olive oil, onion and herbs, is a vegetarian dish from the Sporades often served on Sundays in tavernas. It's a reheated winter dish, though some inns keep it on the menu year-round. With country bread and olives on the side, it makes a complete and very inexpensive lunch.

Retsina is a Greek white wine infused with resin, made according to a tradition stretching back millennia — pine resin once prevented oxidation in amphorae. Its distinctive, slightly terpenic taste pairs perfectly with grilled fish and mezze. It's the cheapest and most authentic bottle you'll be served in the tavernas of the Sporades.

days_plan.itin_title: Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos
Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos

visits.text: Skopelos town is built amphitheatre-style around a deep bay — white houses with red-brown tile roofs tumble down toward the harbour in a setting the filming of Mamma Mia made famous worldwide. The town alone counts 123 Orthodox churches and chapels — nearly as many as days in the year — some dating back to the Byzantine era. Wander the cobbled alleys of the upper town: no two facades are alike.

The Kastro of Skopelos, on the hill above the harbour, is the highest point in town. The Venetian and Byzantine ruins here offer the best panoramic view over the bay, the ferries coming and going, and, on a clear day, the outline of Alonissos on the horizon. Head up towards the end of the day: the light is ideal and the atmosphere calmer than at midday.

The chapel of Agios Ioannis Kastri is perched on top of a sheer rock that drops into the sea, in the north of the island of Skopelos, near the village of Glossa, around 30 km from the overnight stop, a 45-minute drive. To reach it from the car park below, you have to climb 106 steps cut into the rock. This is where the outdoor wedding scenes of the film Mamma Mia were shot in 2007. Arrive early in the morning or after 5pm to avoid the groups of fans who turn up all day long in summer. The view over the Aegean Sea and Alonissos is worth the detour even if you have never seen the film.

The village of Glossa, perched in the hills of Skopelos, around 24 km from the overnight stop, a 40-minute drive, is one of the best-preserved mountain villages in the Sporades. Its Macedonian architecture - overhanging roofs, stone houses, a square shaded by plane trees - contrasts with the white Cycladic houses of the rest of the island. The inhabitants still grow olive and plum trees here. The central square with its cafés is an ideal place to stop on the way to the chapel of Agios Ioannis.

Panormos is a sheltered seaside village tucked into a natural bay, with a fine-sand beach fringed by pines. It's a very pleasant stop for recreational boaters, and its waterfront tavernas serve fresh fish in a peaceful setting. Less crowded than the beaches in the south of the island, it's the perfect spot for lunch by the water.

The beaches of Kastani and Milia are two of the most recognisable Mamma Mia filming locations. Kastani, in particular, hosted the longest scene in the film. These two coves - pebbles or sand depending on the spot, turquoise water, a pine forest running down to the shore - are among the most beautiful on Skopelos, quite apart from their cinematic fame. Milia is windier and ideal for snorkelling. Kastani lies around 15 km from the overnight stop, a 25-minute drive, and Milia just before it on the same road.

The Sendoukia are an archaeological mystery in the hills of Skopelos: four large sarcophagi cut straight into the rock at the top of a hill, linked by local legend to the Greek pirate Glaucus, who is said to have ruled these seas. Their dating and exact purpose are still debated by archaeologists. You drive up from the overnight stop, the last part on a dirt track, to the start of the path, then it is around a 15-minute walk along a waymarked trail. The view from the site alone is worth the effort.

activities.text: The kalderimi trails — old paved paths that once linked Skopelos's monasteries — are the best way to explore the island's wooded interior. The route to the 18th-century Evangelismos Monastery on Mount Palouki passes through a pine forest with panoramic sea views. Set off in the morning to avoid the heat and bring water.

The tyropita on Skopelos is different from the one you know: here, local cheese — a fresh, lightly salted sheep's-milk cheese — is wrapped in homemade puff pastry, not industrially produced filo. It's the island's breakfast speciality, sold in bakeries from 7 am. Don't leave without eating one hot, straight from the oven.

Skopelos plums are recognised for their geographical origin and are the island's agricultural pride. Family orchards produce plums preserved in syrup, sun-dried, or turned into liqueur. You'll find these products in the shops around town — they're the best edible souvenir to bring home from Skopelos.

The ideal day on the west coast of Skopelos: set off by car in the morning for Panormos and a coffee by the sea, head down to Milia for a swim, then on to Kastani for the afternoon. Finish at the small cove of Hovolo, around thirty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, which is less crowded, with flat rocks perfect for snorkelling. Boat hire companies in Skopelos town also offer small motorboats for exploring these coves on your own.

Astakos — lobster simply grilled with lemon and olive oil — is served at the fishermen's tavernas in Panormos and at small harbours like Agnontas. Ask whether it was caught that morning: Skopelos fishermen have a reputation for delivering straight to the local tavernas. Pair it with garlic-rubbed toasted bread.

Loukoumades — small, light doughnuts fried to order, drizzled with honey and sprinkled with walnuts and cinnamon — are the street dessert of the Sporades. You'll find them at the kiosks on Skopelos town's harbour from 6 pm. They're hot, crisp on the outside and airy inside. Eat them standing up with sticky fingers, the way the locals do.

visits.text: Around 1900, Soufli had about 10,000 residents; the 2021 census counted 3,770. In between, silk enjoyed its golden age and then declined, a story told by the Silk Museum in the Kourtidis mansion, built in 1883. Open 10 AM to 6 PM from March to mid-October (5 PM in winter), except Tuesdays; admission €6.

Less solemn than its neighbor, but livelier: at the Art of Silk Museum, live silkworms share the space with working looms. Opened in 2008 by the Tsiakiris family in an 1886 neoclassical building, it follows the thread from cocoon to fabric. Open until 9 PM in season, it’s worth saving for the end of the day; admission €3.

You’ll then stroll past late-19th-century mansions to Soufli’s churches of Saint George and Saint Athanasius, both dating from before the mid-19th century. The Evros River, which marks the border, flows just 500 m from the center. Soufli silk is still sold in town: compare stores before buying a scarf.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk

visits.text: If you experience just one sunset in Attica, make it the one at the Temple of Poseidon on Cape Sounion, perched nearly 60 m above the sea. Built between 444 and 440 BC from Agrileza marble, it has columns with 16 flutes instead of 20, and Lord Byron carved his name into one of them. Admission €20, open from 9:30 a.m. until sunset: arrive 1 hour 30 minutes beforehand; last admission is 20 minutes before closing.

In 413 BC, Athens fortified Cape Sounion to protect its grain supply. From the temple, look for the remains of this fortress, then, a few hundred meters away, the ruins of the sanctuary of Athena, which were reused as early as antiquity. Take this walk in the late afternoon before choosing your spot facing the sunset.

activities.text: Deep, clear water beneath the columns: Sounio Beach, 1.5 km from the temple, is the only beach within walking distance of the site. The Temple of Poseidon towers above swimmers; for a quieter spot, drive from Sounion to the KAPE coast, then walk down a staircase, while the more family-friendly Legrena awaits 5 km away. Expect an extra charge for lounge chairs on beaches with facilities.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis

visits.text: The Archaeological Museum of Sparta, housed since 1875 in a neoclassical building — Greece's first purpose-built provincial museum — holds most of the objects discovered in Laconia, from the Neolithic to the Roman era. Its centrepiece is the marble bust of King Leonidas (5th century BC), wearing the crested helmet of the hoplites. The other treasure is unique in Greece: a collection of votive terracotta masks worn during initiation rites at the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia — old women, bearded warriors, satyrs, gorgons. Allow 45 minutes.

The statue of Leonidas, erected in 1968 at the entrance to the modern city's stadium, depicts the king at a height of 3 metres, helmeted and with a shield on his arm. The pedestal bears the reply ΜΟΛΩΝ ΛΑΒΕ — “come and take them” — which Leonidas is said to have given the Persian king Xerxes when he asked him to surrender his weapons at Thermopylae in 480 BC. It's the quintessential Sparta photo: take it, then continue to the archaeological site just behind.

The archaeological site of Sparta sometimes disappoints those expecting an Acropolis like that of Athens — and that's understandable. The Spartans believed their courage was their best defence and never built fortresses or grand monuments. You'll wander through a park of olive trees among scattered remains: fragments of the theatre, remains of a 10th-century Byzantine basilica, and an Archaic circular building 41 metres in diameter whose purpose remains a mystery.

The Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia lies 800 metres north-east of the stadium, near the River Eurotas, and is free to visit. This is where, from the 9th century BC onwards, Spartan initiation rites took place — notably the ritual flogging of young men before the citizens to prove their endurance. The Romans even had an amphitheatre built in the 3rd century AD to accommodate tourists coming to watch the spectacle.

The Eurotas valley stretches below Sparta, green and fertile, lined with orange and olive trees. This mythological river of Laconia, on whose banks Leda was seduced by Zeus transformed into a swan, flows peacefully between Taygetus and Parnon. An hour's drive south through the valley offers mountain panoramas that help explain why Sparta, without defensive walls, was so difficult to capture.

activities.text: Modern Sparta was re-founded in 1834 by order of King Otto, two years after Greek independence, on a grid plan with wide avenues and citrus trees. This clean, quiet town, far from tourist crowds, is pleasant to explore on foot for its cafés on the squares and its unpretentious tavernas. In the evening, the atmosphere of the central square, with its bars beneath the orange trees, is typical of provincial Greece.

The Mani's orange sausages are the Laconian region's charcuterie speciality: minced pork, orange zest, spices and slow smoking over myrtle wood. You'll find them in local delicatessens and tavernas in Sparta. Pair them with ladera — seasonal vegetables simmered in olive oil and tomato, without meat, which Greeks love to eat at lunchtime.

Laconia Road Trip: Sparta, Mystras & Monemvasia

visits.text: Better than an ordinary stalactite cave: the Cave of the Lakes near Kastria contains a succession of 13 pools on three levels. Explored over 1,980 m, it has a visitor route of about 500 m along a walkway and small bridges. Bones, including those of a hippopotamus, were found on the lower level. The guided tour lasts about thirty minutes: arrive at opening time and bring a sweater, as temperatures inside range from 12 to 17 °C.

Planitero, 7 km from the cave, is home to a plane tree grove sustained by the karst springs of the Aroanios. About 580 m long, it borders the waters that form the river, which runs 12 km to the Ladon and gave Helmos its other name, Aroania. Follow the trails among the springs before lunch, in the shade of the trees.

activities.text: You’ll have trout for lunch in Planitero, where fish farms fed by the Aroanios springs supply the tavernas beside the water. Order it grilled and don’t linger too long: the road to the Helmos ski center then climbs for more than an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Kalavryta and Helmos in 3 Days: Monasteries, Lakes, and the Styx

visits.text: Playful rather than scholarly, and all the better for it: Aristotle’s Park in Stagira turns the philosopher’s Physics into hands-on experiments. Since 2003, a pendulum, prism, sundial, optical disks, and five-note stone have surrounded the statue erected in 1956, at an elevation of about 500 m near the Tower of Madem Aga. Open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.: point the telescopes toward the Gulf of Ierissos and Mount Athos.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages, Aristotle, and Mount Athos

visits.text: Until 1920, it was called Yeni Köy, the “new village.” In Stavroupoli, the Folklore Museum occupies the former tobacco tax office: traditional costumes and a furnished Thracian room are on the ground floor, with everyday objects upstairs, where the antique lamps catch the eye. Since no opening hours are published, call town hall before stopping by.

Stavroupoli may look like a farming town, but it preserves Evangelistria Church, built in 1858, with its carved wooden iconostasis. Traditional houses line the way to the central square, where cafés and pastry shops offer a break before dinner. On Clean Monday, the first day of Orthodox Lent, the square hosts the annual Kamila, or camel, custom.

activities.text: In our view, the Nestos should first be seen from above. Allow for 17 km of paved road from Stavroupoli to the Nestos observation point, a wooden gazebo in the abandoned hamlet of Ano Livera: the river’s meanders unfold between the mountains like a silver ribbon. Feeding stations for birds of prey have been set up nearby; bring binoculars and aim for the late-afternoon light.

visits.text: Stemnitsa, at 1,083 m, still works silver and gold: a public school of goldsmithing and silversmithing has trained craftspeople here since 1976 in a house in the center, and a few workshops sell their jewelry. Among the stone houses and fountains, look for Panagia Bafero, a 12th-century church. In the evening, try portokalopita, an orange cake served on the main square.

In late May 1821, the first Senate of the liberated Peloponnese convened at Zoodochos Pigi Monastery, near Stemnitsa. The church preserves a carved wooden iconostasis from 1805 and 16th-century icons. Walk up from the village the following morning, before taking the road to Karytaina, and wear clothing that provides adequate coverage.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Tegea, Lousios, and Karytaina

visits.text: Entering Gialos harbor, the spectacle hits you all at once: hundreds of neoclassical houses in shades of ochre, pink, blue, and yellow rising in tiers up the hillside, reflected in the harbor water. One hour by ferry from Rhodes, Symi owes this architecture to its 19th-century prosperity, when the island was a major shipbuilding center producing up to 500 vessels a year. The village of Gialos is a classified historic monument—facades are protected in their original state. Give yourself time on the waterfront before climbing toward Chorio.

Chorio, the upper village, is reached from Gialos via the Kali Strata—literally “the beautiful stairs”—500 steps lined with the island's finest manor houses. The climb is worth it as much for the sculpted facades as for the views over the harbor that open at each landing. At the top, the ruins of the 15th-century Knights' castle dominate everything, and Chorio's quiet lanes contrast with the bustle of Gialos below.

Panormitis Monastery, in the island's south, is one of the Dodecanese's most important pilgrimage sites. Founded in the 18th century, it's dedicated to the Archangel Michael, patron saint of sailors. Its baroque bell tower rises above a sheltered bay accessible only by sea or by winding road. Inside, the walls are covered with ex-votos offered by grateful sailors—bells, silver boats, objects recovered after shipwrecks. Several boat excursions from Gialos stop here.

The Maritime Museum of Symi, near Kampos Square, recounts the history of this island of sailors and sponge divers. Diving suits, archive photographs and nineteenth-century diving equipment show how dangerous the trade was: decompression accidents were frequent and left many men disabled. It is a short visit (30 to 45 minutes), but it gives valuable context to what you see around you.

Symi's beaches are mostly pebbles rather than sand, accessible mainly by taxi-boat from Gialos. Agios Georgios Dyssalonas, Nanou, and Agia Marina are among the island's most beautiful coves—turquoise waters, cliff backdrops, no roads leading to them. Check at the harbor in the morning for departures and the last return boat.

activities.text: Position yourself on the ferry deck as you approach Symi—the entrance to Gialos harbor with its amphitheater of houses is one of the Dodecanese's most photographed moments. If you're spending the night on the island, enjoy the evening calm when day-trippers from Rhodes have caught their boat back: tavernas empty by half and lanes regain their silence.

Take a taxi-boat from Gialos to reach one of the isolated coves on the island's south or east coast—Nanou or Agia Marina are best for swimming. It's the only way to access these bays unreachable by road. Ask at the harbor about the last return boat before departing.

Symi's specialty is tiny local shrimp (garides Symis)—minuscule, caught in the deep waters around the island, crispy and delicious eaten whole. They're served fried with a squeeze of lemon and a glass of ouzo. Every harbor taverna offers them—quality varies, but it's the dish you can't miss. Finish with galaktoboureko, that pastry of semolina cream wrapped in phyllo, soaked in lemon syrup.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos

visits.text: Syrrako can only be explored on foot: cars stay outside, and you enter over a stone bridge. On July 10, 1821, the Ottomans destroyed the village; only five buildings, including Panagia Church, survived. Busts of local sons Ioannis Kolettis and the poet Zalokostas take pride of place in the square with the statues. It is uphill all the way: wear good shoes.

activities.text: Follow Syrrako’s lanes to the statue of Kostas Krystallis, a poet born here in 1868, then continue to Agios Nikolaos, the village’s largest church, with an iconostasis carved by artisans from Metsovo. The old trail to Kalarrytes, across the ravine, takes 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours: save it for a longer stay.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Ioannina, Arta, and Aromanian Villages

visits.text: You need a little imagination when viewing the Temple of Athena Alea, reduced to its foundations in the middle of the village of Alea. After the fire of 394 BC, Scopas of Paros rebuilt it in marble; its east pediment depicted the Calydonian boar hunt. Start here, then head to the nearby museum to see images of what these stones once looked like.

The Archaeological Museum of Tegea will help you understand the sanctuary. Founded in 1908, it reopened in 2014 after a complete redesign. Four rooms trace the city from prehistory to the late Roman period, including an entire room devoted to Athena Alea and Scopas. Recognized by the European Museum Forum in 2016, it deserves 1 hour, including the interactive displays.

The Church of Palaia Episkopi stands on the seating tiers of Tegea’s ancient theater, whose remains can be seen beneath the altar. Restored from 1884 to 1888 based on a study by Ernst Ziller, it incorporates reused blocks from the ancient city; its frescoes date to 1935–1936. Free parking is available on-site, and a major Feast of the Dormition celebration takes place around August 15.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Tegea, Lousios, and Karytaina

visits.text: The scent of pine and golden limestone: the Temple of Aphaia crowns a 160 m hill in eastern Aegina. Built around 500 BC, this Doric temple retains 24 of its 32 columns, and the Acropolis is visible in the distance on clear days. Most buses to Agia Marina stop here; from April through August, the site opens at 8 a.m. (admission €10).

Aphaia’s pediments are in Munich, yet the site’s scientific collection is well worth half an hour. Removed in 1811, the statues were sold the following year to the future King Ludwig I of Bavaria; here, the reconstructed entablature of the earlier Archaic temple and copies of sculptures put them in context. Included in admission, the collection is closed on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands in 3 Days: Aegina, Poros, and Hydra

visits.text: To reach Thasos, take the ferry from Keramoti, 35 km south-east of Kavala — the crossing takes just 35 minutes and departures run every 30 minutes in season. It's by far the quickest and cheapest option. Once in Limenas, the capital, head down to the ancient agora: it sits right in the heart of the modern town, surrounded by the ruins of sanctuaries dedicated to Heracles, Dionysus, Artemis and Poseidon, with a medieval tower occupying one corner. Information panels at the entrance show a reconstruction of what the square once looked like — helpful for grasping the scale.

The ancient theatre of Thasos, built into a natural hollow in the hillside north-east of town, dates in its earliest phases from the late 4th century BC. In the 1st century AD it was converted into an arena for gladiatorial combat. It has been fully restored in recent years using white marble from Thasos — the same stone used in antiquity, quarried on the island. The view from the upper tiers over the harbour of Limenas and the Aegean is one of the finest on the island.

The Archaeological Museum of Thasos, founded in 1935 and renovated between 1989 and 2000, is the oldest museum in the Eastern Macedonia and Thrace region. Its centrepiece is the Kouros of Thasos: an archaic statue standing 3.5 metres tall, depicting a young man carrying a ram — a masterpiece of the 6th century BC discovered in 1911 in five pieces inside a Byzantine wall, where it had been reused as building material. The museum also holds a fine head of Alexander the Great and an Aphrodite with a Dolphin regularly lent to major international exhibitions.

The acropolis of Thasos dominates the town from its rocky spur. Climb up from the theatre along the signposted path: you'll pass the sanctuaries of Apollo and Athena, then the Sanctuary of Pan carved directly into the rock face. Along the way, look for the Cyclopean ramparts of white marble — some blocks are fitted so precisely that you still can't slide a credit card between them. The view from the top sweeps across the entire northern coastline of the island.

The village of Panagia, perched in the mountains 10 km south of Limenas, is one of the most beautiful on the island: stone fountains, century-old plane trees, tile-roofed houses and cobbled lanes on the hillside. It's the birthplace of the local dance and one of the best-preserved villages in Eastern Macedonia. Arrive on a Sunday morning to see the locals in traditional dress after Mass.

The village of Theologos, which calls for a day trip from Limenas, was the island's medieval capital under Genoese and Turkish rule. This is where the population took refuge to escape pirates. Its narrow lanes, stone houses with enclosed gardens and old fountains distinguish it from the modernised coastal villages. Allow 45 minutes to walk around the whole village.

The marble quarries of Alyki, on the cape of the same name 32 km south-east of Limenas, are an exceptional archaeological site: the extraction of Thasian white marble — one of the most prized in antiquity — is documented here from the Archaic period through to Byzantine times. Half-cut blocks have been waiting in the rock for twenty centuries. This white marble with its glittering crystals was used, among other things, to build the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki. From the beach at Alyki, submerged blocks are visible beneath the water.

activities.text: Swim at Makryammos, 2 km east of Limenas: a crescent-shaped cove with fine sand, emerald-green waters and maritime pines reaching down to the sea. This is the picture-postcard image of Thasos - the blend of dense vegetation and clear sea that earned the island its nickname, “the Emerald Island”.

In the evening, settle into a café on the harbour at Limenas and order a local retsina — the resinated white wine produced on the island, slightly bitter, served chilled with olives and goat's cheese. It's here that you understand why ancient Greece regulated its wine production by law: Thasian amphorae bearing inspection seals have been found across the entire Mediterranean basin.

Drive around the island: the coastal road covers 95 km and can be comfortably done in a day with stops. Don't miss Golden Beach (Chrisi Amoudia) on the east coast — a long beach of golden sand with deep-blue water, considered one of the most beautiful in the northern Aegean. Behind the beach, archaeologists uncovered a well dating from the 3rd century BC, and on the headland above, the ruins of a 4th-century BC lighthouse.

Sample roast goat with mountain herbs at a taverna in Theologos or Panagia: it's the island's traditional festive dish, oven-roasted or spit-roasted with wild herbs gathered from the slopes of Mount Ipsarion. The mountain-village tavernas are cheaper and more authentic than those on the beaches.

Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi

visits.text: The modern city is built directly over the ancient Cadmée - the acropolis of the mythical city - which explains why ruins appear among ordinary streets. According to mythology, Héraclès and Dionysos were born here, OEdipe ruled here, and Antigone was sentenced to death here. In 335 BC, Alexander the Great destroyed the city following a rebellion, killing or enslaving its 30,000 inhabitants. The renovated Archaeological Museum is remarkable: the painted funerary stelae from ancient Démétrias are an absolute rarity in Greece, and the Linear B tablets (Mycenaean writing from the 15th century BC) attest to the site's antiquity. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

500 m east of the museum, Megalo Kastelli Park contains Mycenaean burial chambers from the 14th–13th centuries BC, dubbed the “tomb of Oedipus's children” by local tradition – a legendary attribution, but the architecture is real. Along Pindarou Street (named after the Theban poet Pindar, 518–438 BC), remnants of ancient Cadmea emerge between houses. The medieval tower visible at the museum entrance dates from the 13th-century Frankish occupation.

activities.text: Thebes attracts few tourists – precisely what makes it an authentic stop. The cafés on the central square are frequented exclusively by locals. Have lunch in a taverna in the centre before continuing towards Distomo in the afternoon: for Osios Loukas, allow for a same-day round trip from Thebes.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

activities.text: Warm currents suddenly rise beneath your arms near the cave at the southern end of Therma Bay. Saline and rich in radon, these springs, at 45 to 52.8 °C, mix with seawater here in a pool enclosed by rocks. From the small harbor, it is just a thirty-meter swim; do not soak for more than twenty minutes.

You can walk to Therma in about 15 minutes along the coastal path that starts at the Agios Kirykos police station. Therma Beach, divided by a fishing pier, stretches below the village square and is at its best when the wind blows from the north. Finish on a terrace overlooking the harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches

visits.text: The Leonidas Monument marks the spot where the final phase of the battle of 480 BC unfolded. The bronze statue of the Spartan king, created by Vasos Falireas and erected in 1955, is flanked by two marble figures representing the Eurotas River and Mount Taygetus. Come early in summer: in July, average highs on the plain exceed 33 °C.

Climb Kolonos Hill, opposite the monument, where the last defenders are said to have fallen. On the battlefield, a stone lion bore the epigram by Simonides: “Stranger, go tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here, obeying their orders.” Turn toward the sea: in 480 BC, it bordered the pass; today, a plain about 5 km wide separates the two.

If the landscape makes the battle difficult to picture, the Thermopylae Historical Information Center puts the armies back in position. Opened in 2010, this 850 m² building shaped like a spearhead takes you through a film, digital tables, and a 3D projection. Allow 1 hour and €3; the time of the last screening varies by day.

activities.text: A sulfur smell hangs at the foot of Kallidromo: the hot springs of Thermopylae, opposite the monument, gave the “Hot Gates” pass its name. Legend has Heracles bathing here after being poisoned by the tunic of the centaur Nessus. Access is free, with no facilities: bring a towel and sandals, and test the water near the spring before settling in.

days_plan.itin_title: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 Days: Delphi, Hosios Loukas

visits.text: Day 1: Marvel at the iconic White Tower, Thessaloniki's most recognizable landmark rising 34 meters on the stunning waterfront promenade. This cylindrical Ottoman fortification, once known as the “Tower of Blood” for its dark history as a prison, now houses a fascinating museum chronicling the city's rich heritage from antiquity to modern times. Climb to the top for panoramic views stretching across the Thermaic Gulf and the city skyline.

Day 1: Stand in awe before the Arch of Galerius, a magnificent triumphal arch built in 303 AD to celebrate Emperor Galerius's victory over the Persians. The marble reliefs depicting battle scenes and symbols of Roman power remain remarkably preserved after 1,700 years. This monumental gateway once connected to a vast imperial palace complex along the ancient Via Egnatia.

Day 1: Enter the Rotunda of Agios Georgios, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and possibly one of the oldest Christian churches in the world, built around 306 AD. Originally intended as Emperor Galerius's mausoleum, this massive domed structure features early Byzantine mosaics of exceptional beauty. The 6-meter-thick walls have withstood earthquakes for seventeen centuries, preserving this architectural marvel.

Day 1: Explore the Roman Forum and Agora, the ancient heart of Thessaloniki's social and political life unearthed only in the 1960s. The remarkably preserved Odeion theater, built around 200 AD, once hosted poetry recitals and musical performances for the aristocracy. Walk among the remains of Roman baths and marketplaces that reveal daily life in this thriving ancient city.

Day 1: Discover the Palace of Galerius ruins, an open-air museum revealing the grandeur of imperial Roman architecture. The surviving mosaics and wall fragments hint at the opulence that once characterized this vast complex connected to the Rotunda and Arch. The recently restored Apsidal Hall provides fascinating context through exhibits and reconstructions of the palace's original splendor.

Day 2: Wander through Ano Poli, Thessaloniki's enchanting Upper Town that miraculously survived the devastating 1917 fire that destroyed two-thirds of the city. This atmospheric neighborhood of winding cobblestone streets, colorful Ottoman-era houses, and traditional tavernas preserves the authentic character of old Thessaloniki. Discover UNESCO-protected Byzantine churches including the 5th-century Church of Hosios David and the 14th-century Vlatadon Monastery hidden among the labyrinthine lanes.

Day 2: Climb to the Trigonion Tower, known as the “Balcony of Thessaloniki” for its spectacular panoramic views over the entire city and Aegean Sea. This 15th-century artillery tower along the Byzantine fortifications offers the most sweeping vistas in the city, particularly magical at sunset. The well-preserved defensive walls stretching from this point encircle the historic Upper Town.

Day 2: Explore the imposing Heptapyrgion fortress, the “Fortress of Seven Towers” crowning the highest point of the city walls. This Byzantine citadel turned Ottoman fort served as Thessaloniki's main prison until 1989, its cells still bearing witness to a turbulent history. The panoramic views from this strategic position reveal why it was crucial for the city's defense for centuries.

Day 2: Enter the Basilica of Agios Dimitrios, dedicated to the city's patron saint, who was martyred on this very site in AD 306. This UNESCO World Heritage Site preserves superb early Byzantine mosaics depicting Saint Demetrius and seventh-century church officials. Descend into the atmospheric crypt where the saint was imprisoned and executed, which later became a pilgrimage site renowned for its miraculous myrrh.

Day 2: Visit the Hagia Sophia of Thessaloniki, a 7th-century church modeled on its famous namesake in Constantinople and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The magnificently restored Byzantine mosaics dating from the 10th to 12th centuries rank among the most breathtaking in Greece. This architectural treasure survived centuries as a mosque and multiple fires; its dome was only reconstructed in 1980.

activities.text: Day 1: Stroll along Thessaloniki's magnificent seaside promenade stretching from the White Tower to the port, where locals gather for evening walks and coffee. Pause at The Umbrellas, George Zongolopoulos's iconic 1997 sculpture of stainless steel umbrellas suspended 13 meters high, a symbol of modern Thessaloniki. This waterfront boulevard offers perfect sunset views over the Thermaic Gulf with Mount Olympus visible on clear days.

Day 1: Photograph the imposing bronze statue of Alexander the Great astride his legendary warhorse Bucephalus in the Garden of Alexander. This 6-meter masterpiece by sculptor Evangelos Moustakas commemorates the Macedonian king born in nearby Pella who conquered an empire spanning three continents. The dramatic pose captures the warrior spirit of history's most celebrated military commander.

Day 2: Immerse yourself in Greek history at the Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki, housing treasures spanning from prehistory to late antiquity. Marvel at the Aravissos Hoard of gold artifacts from 4500 BC, Macedonian royal jewelry, and a striking statue of Emperor Augustus. The eight permanent exhibitions illuminate the remarkable civilizations that flourished in Macedonia over millennia.

Day 2: Explore the Museum of Byzantine Culture, an award-winning modern museum presenting Macedonian treasures from the early Christian through the post-Byzantine periods. Eleven thoughtfully curated exhibitions showcase stunning mosaics, religious artifacts, and artworks revealing how Hellenistic culture merged with Eastern Orthodox Christianity. This comprehensive collection vividly brings to life the Byzantine Empire's thousand-year impact on Thessaloniki.

Day 2: Experience the vibrant atmosphere of Aristotelous Square, Thessaloniki's magnificent central plaza overlooking the waterfront. This architectural triumph, designed after the 1917 fire to rival great European squares, features elegant neoclassical arcades housing cafés and restaurants. Linger over Greek coffee as locals have done for generations in this beloved heart of the city.

Day 2: Discover the colorful Ladadika district, a revitalized Ottoman-era bazaar now bursting with tavernas, bars, and nightlife. The restored former olive oil warehouses create an atmospheric maze of cobbled streets perfect for sampling Greek cuisine and experiencing traditional rebetiko music. This compact neighborhood transforms after dark into Thessaloniki's liveliest entertainment quarter.

places.name: Tinos

visits.text: On January 30, 1823, residents of Falatados clearing foundations struck an icon: the Panagia Evangelistria of Tinos grew out of this discovery, which tradition links to a vision of Sister Pelagia. The icon measures just 20 by 30 cm, but the three-aisled church, completed around 1830, overflows with gold and silver votive offerings, including a fleet of ships donated by sailors from all over Greece. Come early in the morning, before the tour groups.

The museums surrounding the Evangelistria deserve almost as much attention as the church itself. Seven museums and galleries surround the church, featuring Byzantine icons, 19th-century religious art, sculpture, and a small archaeological collection. A chapel commemorates the torpedoing of the cruiser Elli in the harbor on August 15, 1940, by an Italian submarine: nine sailors died. Allow 1 hour to explore them.

Large jars covered with reliefs depicting scenes from the Theogony greet visitors at the Archaeological Museum of Tinos, on the avenue leading up from the port to the Evangelistria. The centerpiece is a multifaceted sundial signed by Andronicus of Cyrrhus in the 1st century BC, sometimes presented as a precursor to the Antikythera mechanism. Admission is €5; open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

If you visit between April and October, head to Kionia, 3 km west of town: the sanctuary of Poseidon and Amphitrite was founded here in the late 4th century BC. Excavated by the Belgians Demoulin and Graindor beginning in 1902, it features a Doric temple built of local marble, a fountain, an altar, and a large portico. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: From the quay, walk up Megalocharis Avenue: an 800 m route that pilgrims still follow on their knees to the church. The contrast between the docking ferries and this slow progress is striking. At the top, a mosaic courtyard made with stones from Tinos and Paros leads to the church. Set out early in the morning, before the heat, and always leave room for those ascending on their knees.

An ancient temple on one side, beach towels on the other: Kionia Beach, a few steps from the sanctuary of Poseidon, rounds out your visit with a swim. The temple’s sculptures depicted dolphins and tridents, a nod to the god of the sea. Go in the late morning, after visiting the site, and bring sun protection.

days_plan.itin_title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs

map_keywords: Sanctuary of Poseidon and Amphitrite Kionia

visits.text: First stop on the road: the Corinth Canal. Dug between 1882 and 1893 (plans date back to antiquity — Nero himself launched construction in 67 AD before giving up), it connects the Gulf of Corinth to the Aegean Sea over a length of 6.4 km. What really strikes you are the sheer vertical walls: 79 meters of limestone sliced clean. The width is only 21 meters — enough for small cruise ships, but not for supertankers. Park on the road bridge and look straight down: vertigo guaranteed.

The Theatre of Epidaurus is often described as the most perfect in antiquity, and for once, that's not an exaggeration. Built around 330 BC by the Argive architect Polykleitos the Younger, it originally had 34 rows of seats (6,200 capacity), with 21 additional rows added in Roman times to bring the total to 12,000 spectators. Climb to the very top row and ask someone at the bottom to whisper or crumple a sheet of paper: you'll hear it perfectly from 22 meters above. Researchers still debate the exact acoustic explanation — the limestone may filter out low frequencies while letting high ones through. Arrive early in the morning to beat the cruise ship coaches from Athens.

The Sanctuary of Asclepius, god of medicine, is considered the first major healing center of antiquity — the "Lourdes" of the ancient Greek world. The sick traveled from across Greece to practice incubation: they slept in the abaton (a 70-meter-long portico) hoping that Asclepius would appear in their dreams to reveal a cure. The complex also included a gymnasium, baths, a 180-meter stadium and a library — embodying the idea that body and soul heal together. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

The small Archaeological Museum of Epidaurus, at the entrance to the site, displays ancient medical instruments, stelae carved with accounts of miraculous healings, and a remarkable statue of Hygieia dating from the 4th century BC. The inscriptions on the stelae are particularly gripping: they describe cures, visions and resurrections — a blend of real medicine and faith. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.

End the day in Nafplio, the first capital of independent Greece in 1829, nestled at the head of a sheltered gulf. Its Venetian center is one of the most beautiful in the Peloponnese: cobblestone lanes, ochre and burgundy façades, cafés lining the local Syntagma Square. If you still have energy, climb up to Palamidi Fortress — 999 steps according to some, 216 according to others. The view over the bay and the floating fort of Bourtzi is worth every step.

Tiryns is often overlooked in favor of Mycenae — unfairly so. This Mycenaean citadel from the 14th century BC boasts the best-preserved Cyclopean walls in the ancient world: up to 14 meters thick, with vaulted galleries carved into the walls themselves. The ancient Greeks believed only the Cyclopes could have assembled such massive blocks. Homer called it "Tiryns of the mighty walls." It's a UNESCO site and far less crowded than Mycenae: chances are you'll have the place to yourself.

From Tolo, allow about 29 km and 35 minutes on the road to reach the site. Mycenae was the city of Agamemnon, the king who led the Greeks against Troy. Founded, according to legend, by Perseus, it reached its height between 1400 and 1200 BC and influenced the whole eastern Mediterranean. Entering through the Lion Gate, erected around 1250 BC, you pass beneath the oldest monumental relief in Europe: two lionesses (their metal heads long gone) flank a Minoan-style column. The cyclopean blocks of the ramparts weigh several tonnes each and are fitted together without mortar. Arrive early - in high season the car park fills up by 9am.

Don't miss the Treasury of Atreus, 300 meters from the main gate — it's actually a royal tholos tomb dating from 1250 BC. You enter through a 36-meter open-air corridor (the dromos), flanked by walls 6 meters high. The circular chamber measures 14.50 meters in diameter and 13.20 meters in height: it was the largest dome in the Western world until the Pantheon in Rome was built five centuries later. The acoustics inside are eerie and mesmerizing — try clapping your hands.

Head back down to Nafplio to explore its Venetian old town. Palamidi Fortress, perched 216 meters above the harbor, was built by the Venetians between 1711 and 1714 in a record time of three years. From its upper bastion, the view sweeps across the entire Gulf of Argolis. If you're only going to climb one fortress at sunset on this trip, make it this one: the golden light on the gulf is stunning.

activities.text: In summer, the Athens & Epidaurus Festival programs performances of ancient tragedies and comedies on Friday and Saturday evenings at the Theatre of Epidaurus. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides performed in their original setting, under the open sky, with the Argolid mountains as a backdrop — an experience unlike anything else. Check the program before your trip and book well in advance.

The bay of Tolo, a small seaside resort a few kilometers from Nafplio, makes the ideal base for the night. The waterfront tavernas serve grilled fish straight off the morning boats. Order some psarosoupa (fish soup) and saganaki (fried cheese) with a glass of local white wine.

Nafplio deserves real time on foot. Cross Syntagma Square, ringed by Venetian and Ottoman houses, pass the Trianon, a former mosque now a theatre and exhibition hall, then follow the harbour to the Bourtzi fort, built on an islet in the middle of the bay. Water taxis get you there in a few minutes.

Argolid cuisine is generous: lamb kleftiko (slow-braised lamb), crispy spanakopita, local cheeses drizzled with Peloponnesian honey. The tavernas along Nafplio's harbor are among the best in the region — look for the ones without a laminated menu posted by the door.
