activities.text: You’ll set out from Galani, at the mouth of Nestos Gorge, along the paved trail that railroad workers built above the river in the late 19th century, a section of the E6 European long-distance path. Allow about 2 hours to reach Kromniko Spring and the same amount of time to return. Wild horses graze near this abandoned village. Never enter the railroad tunnels, even with a flashlight.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 6 Days: Philippi, Caves, and Elatia

visits.text: The city founded by Trajan on the Via Egnatia has left behind its baths, while the Evrenos Bey caravanserai, a travelers’ inn built between 1370 and 1390, forms a long building measuring 38.8 m by 13 m.

Next, you’ll visit the Evros Delta Information Center beside the thermal baths. Admission is free, and the center introduces a wetland of about 200 km², protected under the Ramsar Convention since the 1970s, where more than 300 bird species have been recorded. Open daily from 8 AM to 4 PM: ask for details about arrangements for the following day’s boat trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk

activities.text: You’ll then walk downhill along the acropolis walls to Trigonion Tower, at the northeastern corner of the city walls. It was the last refuge of the city’s Byzantine defenders, then served as an arsenal and artillery post after the Ottoman conquest. From the nearby walls, the view takes in the rooftops of the lower city and the gulf: this is the best place to get a sense of Thessaloniki’s sloping terrain.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: Trikala is little known to foreign travellers — which makes it one of the best "real" towns in Thessaly. The Byzantine fortress on the hill above the city has ancient origins: this is the site of the Sanctuary of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine whose mythical birthplace was Trikala. The current fortress dates from the 4th century, with later Byzantine and Ottoman modifications. The Ottoman clock tower, still standing at the eastern corner, has become the symbol of the city.

The Varousi quarter, at the foot of the fortress, is the old Ottoman neighbourhood with its narrow lanes, overhanging houses, and old churches. The Asclepieion of Trikala — the remains of the ancient healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius — is visible in the park below the fortress. The Koursoum Mosque (16th c.), one of the best preserved in Greece, stands in the lower town — it's no longer active but its Ottoman architecture is remarkable.

On the banks of the Litheos river, the Matsopoulos mill (19th century) is a singular industrial monument: built of imposing stone, it is still standing. The footbridge across the Litheos opposite the mill is the locals' favourite meeting place in the evening - with views of the water and the lights of the old town.

activities.text: Trikala is known for its spiced sausage (loukaniko Trikalinon) seasoned with herbs from nearby Mount Koziakas, its mountain feta cheese, and its tsipouro. The tavernas in the centre are affordable and packed with locals — a welcome break after the tourist prices of Kalambaka. The Tuesday morning market in the lower town draws producers from across the region.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Tripoli, the capital of Arcadia at 650 metres above sea level, deserves a brief stop for its Areos Square: a large neoclassical square with fountains, cafés with terraces and the archaeological museum building designed by architect Ernst Ziller, who also designed the Royal Palace in Athens. Tripoli may not look like much at first glance, but it makes an ideal base for exploring the surrounding mountains of Arcadia.

The Tripoli Archaeological Museum houses collections from ancient Arcadia: sculptures, inscriptions, ceramics and mosaics from local sites such as Tegea and Mantinea. The Mycenaean collections from Arcadia are displayed here, offering an insight into a region often overlooked on classical itineraries. Allow 40 to 50 minutes.

Dimitsana, a mountain village 50 km from Tripoli, is perched on a rocky spur above the Lousios Gorge. Its cobbled lanes, stone tower houses and numerous churches make it one of the most beautiful villages in Arcadia. The library founded in 1764 held 5,000 volumes before the 1821 revolution — according to the memoirs of Kolokotronis, their pages were used to make cartridges with local gunpowder.

The Open-Air Water Power Museum of Dimitsana, opened in 1997, is the only one of its kind in Greece. It showcases the restored buildings of a flour mill, a tannery, a gunpowder mill (which supplied the 1821 revolutionaries with ammunition) and a still. The working hydraulic mechanisms, explained with scale models, paint a vivid picture of pre-industrial life in Arcadia.

activities.text: Hike in the Lousios gorge between the monasteries of Prodromos and Philosophos: a trail of 45 minutes to 1 hour between two limestone walls blackened by damp, above a river that Pausanias said had the coldest waters in Greece. The Prodromos monastery (16th century), still inhabited by monks, literally clings to the cliff - its wooden balconies overhang a drop of several dozen metres. The Philosophos monastery (rebuilt in 1691) is the easiest starting point. Allow for a day trip there and back from your overnight stop.

Tasting in Dimitsana or Stemnitsa: hilopites, egg pasta cut into small squares and dried in the sun, and trachanas, a dried preparation made from flour and fermented milk — the two mountain specialities of Arcadia most often cooked as winter soups. In summer, tavernas serve them in a lighter form with grated cheese. Arcadian fir honey, dark and thick, is among the best in Greece.

days_plan.itin_title: Peloponnese Road Trip: Mycenae, Epidaurus & Olympia
Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Tegea, Lousios, and Karytaina

visits.text: Tsagarada, on Pelion's east side facing the Aegean, is one of the most beautiful villages on the peninsula. Its central square is dominated by a plane tree that locals say is over 1,000 years old — its circumference exceeds 14 m and its shade covers half the square. It was under this tree that villagers gathered for centuries to hold the agora, settle village affairs, and debate politics. Have your morning coffee here, facing the Aegean Sea glimpsed between the trees — it's one of the finest terraces in Greece.

Damouchari, below Tsagarada, is one of those tiny Pelion harbours that look like a postcard of the ideal Mediterranean: a bay split in two by a headland topped with the ruins of a medieval castle, fish tavernas right on the jetty, water so clear you can see the bottom at 5 metres. Several scenes from the film "Mamma Mia" were shot here — the producers didn't have to look far.

activities.text: Mylopotamos beach, reached from Tsagarada via 7 km of side road followed by a 15–20 minute walk along a forest trail, is one of the most beautiful on the Greek mainland: white sand, rocks splitting the beach into two coves, turquoise water, and pine trees reaching down to the shore. The walk through Pelion's dense forest is as good as the beach itself. Plan on spending the afternoon — the descent is easy, the climb back takes a good 30 minutes of effort.

The inter-village trails of Pelion (monopatia) are paved with grey schist slabs and date largely from the Ottoman period — they connected villages when there were no roads. The Damouchari–Tsagarada section (roughly 45 minutes one way) is one of the finest: dense forest, waterfalls, and sea views. The trail is waymarked and manageable for everyone.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Schinoussa is even smaller than Iraklia—8 km², fewer than 300 residents. Its main village, Chora (or Panagia), perches 1.5 km from Mersini port: a single street you can walk down in 5 minutes, lined with family tavernas and geranium-draped houses. Here, everyone knows everyone and newcomers quickly blend in. Come evening, Chora comes alive on the central square: locals and the Greek vacationers who make up most of the island's clientele gather over a warm rakomelo. Push open the door of kafeneio Xara—an institution.

Tsigouri beach is Schinoussa's most accessible beach, 600 m from Chora along a paved road. Golden sand, shallow water and tamarisk trees for shade. A beach bar serves drinks and mezedes. For a wilder experience, Psili Ammos beach is worth the 45-minute walk from Chora: an unspoiled bay with water of unreal clarity and no facilities. Arrive early in summer.

activities.text: Swimming and lounging at Tsigouri—or swim out to the small islet 200 meters offshore for absolute solitude.
A short coastal hike to Livadi or Aligaria beach: Schinoussa's paths connect the beaches, all less than a 40-minute walk from Chora.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Porto Katsiki ('Goat Port') is one of the most photographed beaches in the Mediterranean. A concave limestone cliff drops sheer onto a strip of white pebbles and sand, lapped by water of an almost unreal blue-turquoise hue — locals attribute the colour to the geological composition of the seabed. From the car park at the top of the cliff, roughly a hundred steps cut into the rock lead down to the beach. Arrive before 10am in July–August: after that, the beach fills quickly and the staircase becomes a queue.

Egremni, a few kilometres north of Porto Katsiki, stretches for almost 2.5 km of golden pebbles at the foot of 150-metre-high cliffs. The earthquake of 17 November 2015 destroyed the old staircase of 347 steps and buried part of the beach under a landslide. A new staircase was built in 2021, but the municipality closed land access in 2025 because of ground instability, and the February 2026 storms damaged the steps: the beach is reached by boat from Vassiliki, which keeps it wilder and less crowded than Porto Katsiki. The waves can be powerful: take care with children.

Vassiliki is a world-class windsurfing destination — the reliable afternoon thermals that blow across the bay from the open sea draw competitors and enthusiasts from around the globe. In the morning, the bay is a mirror-flat playground for beginners; from 2pm, the wind picks up and sails multiply. Dozens of windsurf and kitesurf schools cater to all levels.

Karya, a mountain village in the centre of the island at 550 metres above sea level, is famous throughout Greece for its handmade embroidery - the village women carry on a tradition dating from the 19th century with intricate floral patterns. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. The local folklore museum traces this history. In summer, an artisans' market livens up the central square. The view from the heights takes in both coasts of the island.

Kathisma beach, halfway between the capital and Porto Katsiki on the west coast, is the largest organised beach on the island: golden sand, sun loungers, beach bars and sometimes paragliding sessions from the nearby hill. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. If Porto Katsiki feels too chaotic, Kathisma offers the same turquoise water with a little more comfort.

activities.text: Take a windsurfing lesson in Vassiliki — it's one of Europe's most renowned spots to learn or improve. Conditions are close to ideal: calm mornings for the basics, steady thermal winds in the afternoon for practice. Book your slot the day before — schools fill up fast in high season.

Head out early by boat from Vassiliki to Egremni and Porto Katsiki — the perspective from the sea on those white cliffs plunging straight down is completely different from the view at the top. Water taxis and small excursion boats leave from the harbour from 9am.

Savoro is a traditional preservation dish of Corfiot and Lefkadian fishermen: fish (sardines, mackerel) is fried, then marinated in vinegar, raisins and rosemary. The result is a surprisingly tangy-sweet preparation served cold — perfect for a light lunch after the beach.

Pasteli, a sesame-and-honey bar, is the traditional beach snack of the Ionian Islands — people have been eating it since ancient Greece. Simple, energising and utterly unprocessed. Pick up a few from a grocery shop in Vassiliki before heading down to Porto Katsiki: you'll need the fuel for the climb back up.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South
Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada

visits.text: Nothing prepares you for coming face-to-face with the Samos kouros: more than five meters of marble, dedicated around 580 BC by a certain Isches and discovered in 1980 beneath the Sacred Way of the Heraion, with its head only resurfacing in 1984. The Samos Archaeological Museum displays it alongside the Geneleos votive group. Allow 2 hours; the museum is closed on Tuesdays. A modernization project has been announced, so check the hours before visiting.

A Boeotian lion stands guard over an Ionian harbor: the statue in Pythagoras Square in Samos is a copy of the Lion of Chaeronea. Unveiled on August 6, 1921, for the centennial of independence, this Pentelic marble sculpture still bears the scars of a 1943 bombing. Have a coffee in the square when you arrive—it is the heart of the lower town.

Head up to Ano Vathy in the late afternoon, when the lanes of the old quarter perched above the harbor begin to cool down. Designated a “traditional settlement,” it preserves the post-Byzantine church of Agios Giannakis at its highest point, where Samos joined the War of Independence on April 20, 1821. Allow 1 to 2 hours and wear sturdy shoes; the slopes are steep.

The scent of oak and sweet wine fills the air: in Malagari, the Samos Wine Museum occupies a former wine cellar where the cooperative stored its wines and made its barrels. The largest wooden vat holds 80 tonnes, and the manual wine presses date from 1910. The €5 ticket includes a tasting of Muscat, the sole grape variety of the Samos appellation, established in 1970. Closed on Mondays.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves
Samos in 4 Days: Heraion, Manolates, and Potami Waterfalls

places.name: Vergina

visits.text: Gold gleams in the dim light of the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai in Vergina. The grave goods from the tomb attributed to Philip II include a gold larnax weighing 11 kilograms; the exhibition also protects the funerary monuments in their original locations. The museum is concealed beneath a tumulus-shaped covering. Let your eyes adjust to the lighting before examining the details, then check the terms of the combined ticket.

Much more than an annex, the central building of the Polycentric Museum of Aigai deserves a separate visit from the royal tombs. Inaugurated in 2022, it broadens the focus to the inhabitants, queens, and daily life of the ancient Macedonian capital. The objects tell the story of a city, not just a dynasty. Plan this visit after the tombs to better connect the collections, and check the opening times for each part of the site.

Designed for public life, the Palace of Aigai looks less like a royal residence than a gathering place. Its peristyle courtyard and mosaic decoration help you imagine how the Macedonian capital functioned in the 4th century BCE. Architecture made power visible. Visit the accessible areas in the morning, bring water, and wear shoes suitable for the ground at archaeological sites.

Peaceful today, the Theater of Aigai nevertheless preserves the memory of an assassination that changed Macedonian history. Philip II was killed here in 336 BCE during the celebrations for his daughter’s wedding; Alexander succeeded him. The remains add context to the neighboring palace. Make this stop after visiting the palace and check the permitted route rather than trying to cross excavation areas.

activities.text: Next, walk through the Royal Necropolis of the Temenids at Aigai to place the treasures in their funerary landscape. This complex belongs to the Polycentric Museum and reveals another part of the royal cemetery, separate from the tombs displayed beneath the tumulus. Here, the visit takes place outdoors. Check whether it is included in your ticket and bring a hat: this walk complements the museums, with a different level of sun exposure.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Greece Tour: Thessaloniki, Macedonia and Meteora
Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella
Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

map_keywords: Museum of the Royal Tombs Aigai Vergina

places.name: Veria

visits.text: The colors are the first thing to catch your eye in the Church of the Resurrection of Christ in Veria. Dating to 1314–1315, this small church preserves frescoes by Georgios Kalliergis; the richness of its decoration contrasts with the simplicity of the building. Check opening times with the Byzantine Museum before heading there, as access to the churches depends on visiting hours.

A peaceful place for a walk, but also a place of remembrance: the Jewish quarter of Barbouta borders the Tripotamos River in Veria. Its traditional houses surround a synagogue dating to 1850, a reminder of the city’s Jewish community. Explore the narrow streets on foot and inquire before your visit if you would like to see inside the synagogue.

A pleasant surprise: the Byzantine Museum of Veria offers as much to see in its building as in its collections. Housed in an industrial building from the early 20th century, it presents the city’s Christian heritage, from the early centuries through the post-Byzantine periods. Save this visit for the hot hours of the day and check the official opening times.

activities.text: Follow the narrow streets of Panagia Dexia in Veria to find the Tripotamos River between the old houses. This traditional neighborhood combines homes and passageways near the river; the urban landscape becomes less dominated by stone as you walk. Wear shoes with good grip on the cobblestones and save this walk for late afternoon.

If you enjoy syrup-soaked desserts, try Veria’s revani at a pastry shop downtown. This local specialty is served plain or with a scoop of ice cream; the contrast makes a noticeable difference to the tasting experience. Ask for a small portion to start and enjoy this break before resuming your walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

map_keywords: Church of the Resurrection of Christ Veria

visits.text: Icy turquoise water emerges in the final section of the gorge: these are the springs of the Voidomatis, a river that flows on to join the Aoos. In April, its temperature is around 7 to 10 °C. Dip your feet in to soothe your legs before the final climb to the village of Vikos, which is steep and exposed to the sun.

activities.text: Leave Monodendri early to hike through Vikos Gorge, ranked by Guinness World Records as the world’s deepest canyon relative to its width. The trail descends steeply to the bed of the Voidomatis, follows the wooded canyon floor, then climbs to the village of Vikos: roughly 12 kilometers and 5 to 7 hours of hiking. Carry two liters of water per person.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Pindus in 4 Days: Metsovo, Zagori, and Vikos Gorge

visits.text: Ano Poli’s finest balcony may belong to monks: Vlatades Monastery offers a view over the entire city. Founded in the 14th century by the brothers Dorotheos and Markos Vlattis, it remains Thessaloniki’s only active Byzantine monastery and has housed the Patriarchal Institute for Patristic Studies since 1965. Speak softly in the courtyard, as this is a place of prayer, and save your camera for the overlook.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: Santorini—the caldera and its hilltop villages seen from the sea offer one of the Mediterranean's most spectacular arrivals by sea. Vlychada harbor on the south coast is calmer than the crowded caldera and ringed by white cliffs with lunar shapes. It's the best overnight anchorage. The volcanic sand beach of Perissa and Perivolos stretches 7 km: burning-hot black sand (bring sandals), crystal-clear water, and a gently sloping sandy bottom. In high season, it's one of the island's liveliest.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is Santorini's equivalent of Pompeii—a Minoan city buried under meters of volcanic ash during the catastrophic eruption around 1500 BC. Excavations began in 1967 under Spyridon Marinatos. Beneath a massive protective dome, you wander the ancient city streets: two-story houses with sewer systems, murals depicting daily life, pottery, tools. No bodies were found, suggesting inhabitants fled before the eruption.

At Red Beach, a blood-red cliff plunges vertically into the sea, creating a striking contrast with the blue water. The beach is narrow and busy; access is restricted because of rockfall risks. Enjoy it from the sea.

activities.text: Swimming on the volcanic beach of Perissa or Perivolos—the black sand absorbs heat, consider water shoes. Water is deep and clear.

Wine tasting in Santorini—the island's vineyards produce assyrtiko, a mineral white wine unique in the world, with vines trained into baskets (kouloura) on volcanic soil. Several estates are accessible from the anchorage or by road.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: “The debris from an ancient cannonball battle between Titans”: that’s the explanation Discover Greece offers for the rocks of Volax. These almost perfectly spherical gray granite boulders dot the plateau around a village with 51 residents recorded in the 2011 census. Walk the trail winding between the boulders early in the morning, before the stone heats up.

Until 1715, the Venetians controlled Tinos from Exomvourgo, a 641 m peak they called Castello di Santa Elena. The commander eventually negotiated its surrender to the Ottomans, who dismantled the fortress; only ruins remain, perched above the plateau. Allow about twenty minutes for the climb from the Iera Kardia Iisou sanctuary, and wear hiking shoes.

Kechrovouni Monastery is worth a detour for one particular room: the cell of Sister Pelagia, the nun who, according to tradition, was guided by a vision to the icon of the Evangelistria. Dedicated to the Dormition, it is said to have been founded in the 10th or 11th century by three daughters of a wealthy family. Wear clothes that keep you covered and combine your visit with Exomvourgo on the same morning.

Built for pigeons, tended like manor houses: Tinos is said to have around a thousand dovecotes. The Tarampados valley brings together several of the best-preserved examples, restored and connected by trails; the first written mention of these two-story stone towers dates to 1726. Leave your car in the village and walk down into the valley.

activities.text: In the narrow streets of Volax, you’ll find the workshops of basket weavers who preserve a long tradition of woven baskets. The village also has a small stone open-air theater and a folklore museum. Buy directly from a workshop: it’s a chance to exchange a few words with the artisan.

days_plan.itin_title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs

visits.text: Few walls remain standing, but what a view: the foundations and a few ruined towers of Volissos Castle crown the village. Tradition attributes it to the 6th-century general Belisarius; research instead dates it to the 11th century, before a Genoese restoration in the mid-15th century. Admission is free: climb the path that starts near the church.

For the July 22 feast day, many pilgrims from Chios walk to the Monastery of Agia Markella from Vrontados, 50 km away. Built beside the beach, 8 km from Volissos, it honors the island’s patron saint, who was born in that village and, according to tradition, martyred by her own father. Avoid this date if you are looking for peace and quiet.

activities.text: Follow the path at the end of Agia Markella Beach to the site of the martyrdom, where a warm spring flows into the sea. The sand-and-pebble beach faces Psara; the water here stays cool and deep. There is no lifeguard or beach equipment, but a nearby taverna serves lunch.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni

visits.text: Volos stretches between the sea and the first slopes of Pelion - a setting that gives it a character of its own in Greece. Start with the Athanasakeion Archaeological Museum, built in 1909 thanks to the fortune of Alexios Athanasakis, a Pelion merchant who made his money in Egypt. The collection will surprise you: the painted funerary stelae of ancient Demetrias, their colours still vivid, are an absolute rarity in Greece - the pigments survived because the stelae were buried. You will also see Neolithic pieces from the sites of Dimini and Sesklo, located less than 15 km from the town.

The old Palia quarter, a former Byzantine fortress fortified in the 4th century, grew around the port from the 19th century onwards. The Ottomans held it from 1423 until the liberation of Volos in 1881 — nearly 460 years. Behind the train station, the Volos City Museum occupies the former Papantou tobacco warehouse (1920), restored in 2014: the glass floor on the first level reveals 6th–7th-century water channels beneath your feet. The building alone is worth a visit for its industrial architecture.

activities.text: In the evening, Volos reveals its true self through its tsipouradika — tsipouro bars, named after the local grape spirit, where you eat mezze while sipping slowly. It's an institution here: Volos is widely regarded as the Greek capital of tsipouro. The waterfront (Argonauts' promenade) is packed with these places, at their best around aperitif hour. The city owes its mythological name to Iolcos, from where Jason and the Argonauts are said to have set sail in search of the Golden Fleece — a myth that looms over the entire region.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Two fires, in 1999 and 2020, failed to destroy Vrontiani Monastery, rebuilt in 1566 on the site of an earlier monastery and counted among the island’s oldest. Perched at about 450 m, roughly 2 km southeast of Vourliotes, it preserves a carved wooden iconostasis embellished with gold. Cover your shoulders and knees; the monastery’s feast day falls on September 8.

Vourliotes takes its name from Vourla, ancient Clazomenae in Asia Minor, where its founders came from in the late 16th century. On the square, tavernas serve wine from the Muscat vineyards surrounding the village: ask to taste the local wine. Head up for lunch, then wander the lanes lined with restored Samian houses.

activities.text: Continue to Pnaka Spring, 1.6 km from the Vourliotes turnoff, for shade, cool water, and a taverna. It is a simple stop to break up the day before the drive to Manolates; 30 minutes is enough, or longer if you have lunch there.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 4 Days: Heraion, Manolates, and Potami Waterfalls

visits.text: Vovousa Bridge spans the Aoos with a single arch in the heart of the village and has linked its two banks since 1748. Alexis Mitsios, a merchant from Zagori, funded its construction with a donation. Walk across it, then head down to the riverbank to see the arch in profile, more elegant when viewed from below.

Băiasa is the Aromanian name for Vovousa, a Vlach village built at an elevation of around 1,000 m, with the river dividing it into two neighborhoods. Barely more than a hundred people live here, surrounded by beech and fir trees. Stop by Agios Georgios Church, which dates to 1814, and return in midsummer for the village festival, which combines music, theater, and hikes.

activities.text: Valia Kalda has a misleading name: “warm valley” in Aromanian, yet it is one of the coldest and wettest areas in the region. A national park since 1966, this basin of black pines and beeches is home to brown bears, wolves, and chamois. From the Valia Kalda refuge near Vovousa, follow the E6 European long-distance trail toward the heart of the park, then retrace your steps.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Pindus in 4 Days: Metsovo, Zagori, and Vikos Gorge

visits.text: Until a road opened in the 1970s, the Vradeto Steps, a mule route with around a thousand steps, remained the village’s only link to the outside world. At 1,340 m, Vradeto is the highest village in Zagori. Take in the switchbacks from above before heading toward Beloi.

activities.text: Walk from Vradeto’s square to the Beloi viewpoint on the eastern rim of Vikos Gorge: a nearly level 2.8 km round trip. At the end of the trail, the plateau drops away abruptly and the canyon opens beneath your feet. Allow 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes, depending on your photo stops, including the gentle climb on the way back.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Pindus in 4 Days: Metsovo, Zagori, and Vikos Gorge

visits.text: The White Tower is the best place to begin your stay: its museum traces Thessaloniki’s history from its founding in 316–315 BC, with a different theme on each floor. Standing about 34 m tall, the tower was called Kanlı Kule, the “Tower of Blood,” when it served as a prison under the Ottomans; rebellious Janissaries were massacred there in 1826. Climb to the roof for views over the gulf. In winter, it opens from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.; admission is €8.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina

visits.text: The old town of Xanthi (Palia Poli) is one of the largest preserved traditional settlements in Greece: 380,000 m² declared a protected zone in 1976, with over 1,200 buildings listed as monuments. It was rebuilt after two devastating earthquakes in 1829 and reached its zenith between 1880 and 1925 thanks to basma tobacco — an exceptional aromatic variety that supplied imperial courts and European markets. The Epirote and Macedonian craftsmen who built it blended Baroque, Neoclassical, Romanesque and Ottoman elements into a result the Greeks then nicknamed “Little Paris”.

Walk up the main street to Demokratias Square to see the clock tower, erected in 1870 by the Pomak Hadji Emin Aga. The Greek authorities wanted to demolish it in 1972 — protests by Muslim residents forced a reversal. It stands as a symbol of Xanthi's particular brand of coexistence, where Greek Orthodox Christians, Turks and Pomaks have shared the same streets for centuries.

The History and Folklore Museum of Xanthi occupies the Kougioumtzoglou House, a former double residence built in the 1860s by the Kougioumtzoglou brothers, major tobacco merchants. It's a rare example of a three-storey semi-detached house in the local style. The collections feature traditional costumes, embroidered textiles, craft tools and archives from the tobacco era. Allow an hour to do it justice.

At the entrance to the train station, the former tobacco warehouses (the Mandra) bear witness to Xanthi's economic might at the turn of the 20th century. The most notable, shaped like the Greek letter Pi (Π), housed the Ottoman tobacco monopoly's operations until 1912. It's currently being converted into a cultural venue. If you travel through the neighbourhood by car or bus, their imposing red-brick silhouettes are visible from the road.

activities.text: Walk through the lanes around Antika Square in Xanthi: this is where terrace cafés, grocery shops fragrant with eastern spices, leatherworking workshops and Turkish coffee shopfronts cluster. The morning atmosphere is particularly authentic - residents meet here before going to work. A thick Greek coffee, served with a glass of cool water, is the customary ritual.

Excursion into the Rhodope Mountains to the Pomak villages, an hour's drive north: Sminthi with its white mosque and stone lanes, Echinos set amid deep forests, Ottoman bridges over mountain torrents. These villages, isolated in the folds of the Rhodopes, have preserved architecture and traditions virtually unchanged since the 19th century. The road itself is spectacular — wooded gorges, crystal-clear rivers, not a tourist in sight.

Try soutzouk loukoum, Xanthi's signature sweet: Turkish delight flavoured with walnuts or rose, sometimes coated in a layer of toasted hazelnuts. It's the Thracian version of a widespread Ottoman confection, but Xanthi's sweet shops have a well-established regional reputation. Pair it with a lightly anise-flavoured Thracian tsipouro — milder than ouzo.

visits.text: Zakynthos Town — dubbed “the Flower of the East” (Il Fiore di Levante) by the Venetians — was completely destroyed in the 1953 earthquake and rebuilt in a neo-Venetian style with arcades and colonnaded façades. Solomos Square, the largest in town, opens directly onto the Ionian Sea. Here you'll find the Byzantine Museum, a statue of the poet Dionysios Solomos (who penned the Greek national anthem in 1823), and the town hall. This is where the action is in the morning; in the evening, head up to Bohali.

The Church of Agios Dionysios is dedicated to the island's patron saint. Founded in 1708, it houses his relics in a silver reliquary and features a gilded carved iconostasis along with fine Byzantine frescoes restored after 1953. The bell tower overlooking the harbour is one of the defining landmarks of Zakynthos. Every year on 24 August and 17 December, thousands of worshippers gather here for the saint's feast days.

The Byzantine Museum of Zakynthos, on Solomos Square, is one of the richest in the Ionians. It brings together carved wooden Byzantine icons, original frescoes from the 15th to 17th centuries rescued from churches destroyed in 1953, and 18th-century paintings by artists of the Ionian School such as Doxaras, Koutouzis and Kandounis. Some canvases depict the town before the earthquake — a striking comparison with what it looks like today. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The Venetian Castle of Bohali, perched on the hill above the town, was built in the 15th century by the Venetians on even older foundations. The enclosure among the pines overlooks the harbour from 150 metres — from the ruined ramparts you can take in the entire bay, the port and the mountains of the hinterland in a single glance. Drive up or walk (25 minutes from Solomos Square). At sunset, locals from the village of Bohali settle on terraces with a drink — join them.

Zakynthos National Marine Park (NMPZ), created to protect Caretta caretta turtles, encompasses Laganas Bay and the nesting beaches in the south of the island. The turtles lay their eggs on these beaches between May and August - access is regulated, but glass-bottom boat excursions allow you to observe them in their natural habitat without disturbing them. If you visit in summer, do not miss a trip out to sea.

Navagio Bay - also known as “Smugglers' Bay” - is the most photographed image in all of Greece. It takes its name from the wreck of the cargo ship Panagiotis, which ran aground here on the night of 2 October 1980 after being chased by the Greek navy during a storm. The ship had left Argostoli carrying contraband goods. The white limestone cliffs rise more than 200 metres above the white-sand beach and turquoise water. Warning: landing on the beach and swimming in the bay are prohibited because of rockfall risks. Viewing from a boat remains subject to access restrictions. For the view from above, allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town, via Anafonitria or Volimes, to the clifftop viewpoint, subject to permitted access conditions.

The Blue Caves are a series of arches and tunnels carved by the sea into white limestone cliffs in the north of the island, between Agios Nikolaos harbour and Cape Skinari. Their name comes from the electric colour of the water inside, caused by sunlight reflecting off submerged limestone - a phenomenon very similar to the Blue Grotto on Capri. The walls and even your body underwater take on a vivid blue hue. They can only be reached by small boat (maximum 50 passengers to enter the arches). From Zakynthos town, allow for a return road trip to Agios Nikolaos harbour or Cape Skinari, followed by the boat visit.

Cape Skinari is the northern tip of Zakynthos, facing Kefalonia - on clear days, Mount Ainos on the neighbouring island is clearly visible. The lighthouse dates from 1897 and stands 9.5 metres tall. This is a departure point for boat excursions to the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach the cape. The cape's characteristic windmills have become one of the island's symbols.

Anafonitria Monastery, inland in the northwest, dates from the 15th century. It is one of the island's oldest and is famous for having welcomed Saint Dionysios as a monk before he became the patron saint of Zakynthos. It is surrounded by groves of century-old olive trees and a medieval defensive tower that still stands. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town for this visit. The atmosphere is peaceful, far from the beaches.

Xigia Beach is a natural curiosity: sulphur springs emerge directly into the sea from the rocks, giving the water a milky hue and a faint characteristic smell. The therapeutic properties of these sulphurous waters have long been known locally. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Xigia. The beach is small, wild and lightly visited - a good alternative to Navagio for those who want a different bathing experience.

activities.text: Roma Street, the main pedestrian thoroughfare leading off Saint Mark's Square, is lined with local shops where you can pick up mandolato nougat (almonds, honey, egg white — the island's signature sweet), ladotyri (a hard cheese aged in olive oil, Zakynthos PDO) and olive-oil products. It's also the place for evening outings — the tavernas come alive from 8 pm.

Facing Saint Mark's Square stands the Solomos and Kalvos Museum, housed in the island's former casino and open since 1968. On the ground floor lie the tombs of the two poets — Dionysios Solomos, author of the national anthem, and Andreas Kalvos. Upstairs: manuscripts, personal belongings and period documents. A must for anyone interested in Greek literature.

Fritoura is a traditional sweet from Zakynthos: a thick mixture of semolina and water, cooled, cut into pieces, fried and sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon. You can taste it from vendors who prepare it, especially during the island's festivals. In Zakynthos, look for the kiosk in front of Saint Dionysios Church to discover this speciality, served warm and crisp on the outside, with a soft centre.

Verdea is Zakynthos's AOC white wine, made from local grape varieties (pavlos, goustolidi). Dry, with lively acidity and a slightly bitter finish - it contrasts with the rounded whites of most islands. Ask for it at the taverna with local cheeses.

The ideal plan for this last day: leave early in the morning for Cape Skinari and board a small boat to the Blue Caves (allow 2 hours). Then head inland to Volimes and Anafonitria, passing through olive groves and mountain villages. In the afternoon, make the detour to the Navagio viewpoint for the photo, then finish at Xigia Beach for a dip in the sulphurous waters before returning to Zakynthos Town.

The hill village of Volimes is known for its textile artisans - rugs, embroidery and lace are displayed in the small shops along the main street. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Volimes. This is also where the best local products are sold: mountain honey, olive oil and handmade mandolato. The sellers are often the producers themselves.

The boat excursion combining the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay (viewed from offshore) lasts between 3 and 4 hours, depending on the option chosen. Boats depart from Agios Nikolaos harbour or Zakynthos's main port. For a departure from Agios Nikolaos, allow for a return road trip from Zakynthos town to this harbour in the north of the island. Book the day before in summer - places sell out quickly. Small boats carrying 12 to 50 passengers can enter the caves; larger ones can only pass around them.

Ladotyri is the AOC cheese of Zakynthos: a hard cheese made from sheep's and goat's milk, aged in olive oil — hence the name (lado = oil, tyri = cheese). It has a firm texture, a dark rind and a powerful, slightly fruity flavour. It is eaten at the end of a meal with local honey, or diced with an aperitif.
